why.D: That is the reasoning behind the signal, offered before any result is reported.

context: The writer’s claim that a trait may outlast its original cause rests on the point that:

choices.text: the yellow pigments are present in the leaf throughout the summer.
something cheap to keep need not be held up by what first favoured it.
aphids arriving in autumn have no way of judging a tree’s defences.
nitrogen withdrawal takes about a fortnight in most of the species studied.

why.A: Summer carotenoids explain yellow and have nothing to do with a trait outlasting a cause.
why.B: Correct — the final paragraph states it as the reason two jobs can coexist.
why.C: The passage says the opposite: the display is honest and worth the insect reading.
why.D: The fortnight measures how long the sunscreen would be needed, not how traits persist.

context: The two accounts differ most fundamentally in that only the signalling account holds that the pigment:

choices.text: costs the tree resources it might otherwise keep.
appears most strongly on the southern face of a canopy.
acts on something outside the tree entirely.
is manufactured late in the life of the leaf.

why.A: Both accounts turn on the expense; they disagree about what the expense buys.
why.B: The southern face is the sunscreen account’s prediction, not the signal’s.
why.C: Correct — the passage says the pigment does nothing to the leaf and talks to an insect.
why.D: Late manufacture is the shared puzzle that both accounts set out to explain.

context: As used in the third paragraph, "honest" most nearly means:

choices.text: sincere in the intention behind it.
plainly visible from a long distance.
accurate in every biological detail.
impossible to fake cheaply.

why.A: A tree has no intentions, and the passage never attributes any to one.
why.B: Visibility is how the signal reaches the aphid, not what makes it trustworthy.
why.C: Detail accuracy belongs to descriptions, and a pigment describes nothing.
why.D: Correct — the sentence grounds the honesty in a weak tree being unable to pay.

context: The description of the pigment as "talking to something outside the tree" is used to:

choices.text: mark the difference between a shield and a message.
suggest that trees communicate with one another through colour.
imply that the aphids respond to sound as well as to sight.
concede that the signalling account cannot be tested directly.

why.A: Correct — the clause before it says the pigment is doing nothing to the leaf itself.
why.B: The audience named is an insect choosing a tree, not another tree.
why.C: Talking is a figure for signalling, and nothing in the passage involves sound.
why.D: The next paragraph gives a testable prediction for exactly this account.

context: The writer calls the mixed result "the least satisfying result available" chiefly to:

choices.text: express regret that the protective account was not confirmed.
admit its awkwardness while accepting it as probably true.
dismiss the studies that produced it as poorly designed.
urge that the two accounts be tested again more carefully.

why.A: Exposure predicting redness within a tree is the protective account holding up.
why.B: Correct — the same sentence calls it probably the true one, which is not a complaint.
why.C: No study’s design is criticised, and the results are taken at face value.
why.D: Nothing calls for retesting; the paragraph moves on to what the result implies.

context: As used in the second paragraph, "early" most nearly means:

choices.text: painted before the sleeve it rests on.
produced at the start of the painter’s career.
finished ahead of the schedule she had set.
crude in the way a first attempt is crude.

why.A: Correct — the fingers should sit on top of the fabric, so the hand came after the sleeve.
why.B: The word describes one hand in one copy rather than any stage of anyone’s career.
why.C: Obregón works to no schedule; she has spent eleven years on forty-three copies.
why.D: The passage rules this out in the same breath: not badly drawn, early.

context: As used in the second paragraph, "arithmetic" most nearly means:

choices.text: a budget too small to pay for more ship time.
a limit that follows from the numbers themselves.
a calculation the researchers performed incorrectly.
the simple mathematics taught to young children.

why.A: Cost is never raised; the obstacle given is forty years of a single vessel searching.
why.B: Correct — a ship’s speed against an ocean’s size makes the count impossible, not anyone’s fault.
why.C: The paragraph blames no error, and says outright that the effort is not carelessness.
why.D: The word is figurative here, and no elementary mathematics appears in the passage.

context: As used in the second paragraph, "keeping" most nearly means:

choices.text: holding on to rather than selling or leaving.
supporting financially over many years.
upholding at a daily and unremarked cost.
storing safely somewhere out of the way.

why.A: Selling and leaving arise only once the narrator has arrived to empty the place.
why.B: No money is mentioned; the cost named is the work of tending the house itself.
why.C: Correct — the sentence likens it to keeping a promise: daily, without ceremony, at some cost.
why.D: Treating the house as a container is the belief the narrator says she had backward.

context: As used in the fourth paragraph, "read" most nearly means:

choices.text: be interpreted correctly by the city council that set it.
be printed clearly enough on a receipt to notice.
be studied by economists once the results are in.
strike a shopper as one thing rather than another.

why.A: The reading that matters belongs to the shopper at the register, not to the city.
why.B: Receipts never appear, and nothing turns on how legibly a price is printed.
why.C: Economists supply the prediction at the start, which the measured result overturns.
why.D: Correct — the charge has to come across as deliberate rather than as an accident.

context: As used in the fifth paragraph, "work" most nearly means:

choices.text: a useful effect the funding formula cannot register.
employment for the staff who carry out the sweep.
labour of a kind that is unusually difficult to do well.
a task the state has assigned to that collection.

why.A: Correct — a shelf moved two thousand times and borrowed eleven is doing something unseen.
why.B: The staff’s rounds are the method of counting rather than the thing being counted.
why.C: Difficulty is never at issue; visibility to the funding formula is what is at issue.
why.D: The state assigns nothing to collections, and asks the system for one number only.

context: As used in the fifth paragraph, "housekeeping" most nearly means:

choices.text: a domestic chore carried out inside a nest.
routine upkeep of the tissue the cells sit in.
the tidy arrangement of the crystals in the beak.
clerical work done by laboratory assistants.

why.A: Nests never appear, and the cells are within the bird rather than around it.
why.B: Correct — macrophages patrol tissue and take up iron as an ordinary part of that patrolling.
why.C: Nothing is arranged; the cells were merely mistaken for crystal-bearing neurons.
why.D: The word describes what the cells do inside the bird, not what anyone in a lab does.

context: The statement that researchers “count sightings, and then they reason backward” means that they:

choices.text: infer the population from what was seen, using estimates of what was missed.
go back over earlier surveys in reverse order to check their totals.
start from the most cited figure and adjust the sightings to fit it.
follow each whale’s route back to where it spent the winter.

why.A: Correct — the next paragraph spells it out: a chain of estimates about diving, detection and distribution turns sightings into a population figure.
why.B: No earlier surveys are rechecked. “Backward” runs from the evidence to the number, not through old records.
why.C: The thirty-animal figure is the output of this reasoning, not its starting point.
why.D: Migration routes never come up; what is worked back to is the population size, not any whale’s path.

context: When the narrator writes that “The house and I negotiated,” the sentence that follows shows that she means:

choices.text: the work went slowly, one room given up for each afternoon spent.
she bargained with a buyer over what the house was worth.
she argued with her mother about which things to keep.
she paid workers to repair the house before she sold it.

why.A: Correct — the next sentence states the bargain: “It gave up a room; I gave up an afternoon.”
why.B: No buyer appears and no price is discussed. The other party to the negotiation is the house itself.
why.C: Her mother appears in one phone call, and the two do not argue about what to keep.
why.D: No workers or repairs are mentioned; the narrator does the clearing herself, and no sale is described.

context: When the writer says that one of the field’s most reproduced images “quietly stopped meaning what it had meant,” the point is that:

choices.text: the beak-cell pictures no longer counted as evidence for a needle.
the image had been faked by the researchers who first published it.
journals removed the picture from print once it was examined again.
later photographs showed the crystals in the beak far more clearly.

why.A: Correct — the sentence before it explains: the cells were macrophages doing housekeeping, not navigation, so the picture stayed the same while its meaning changed.
why.B: Nobody is accused of faking anything. The cells were real; they were simply taken for the wrong kind of cell.
why.C: Nothing is withdrawn. “Quietly” marks that the picture stayed in circulation while what it showed changed.
why.D: The re-examination found immune cells, not clearer crystals, which is why the mechanical candidate lost ground.

context: According to the passage, Marguerite was unable to perform because she:

choices.text: slipped on a wet flagstone and hurt her ankle.
was replaced by the stage manager at short notice.
had missed a cue during the Thursday run.
chose to give the part to a younger actor.

why.A: Correct — the third paragraph names the wet flagstone and the bad ankle.
why.B: The stage manager delivers the news to Nadia but does not remove Marguerite.
why.C: It is Ivo who misses a cue, and that happens during rehearsal, not in performance.
why.D: Nothing in the passage suggests Marguerite had any say in who went on.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: the physical dangers of working backstage in an old theatre.
the gap between knowing a part and being able to act in a play.
the unfairness of casting understudies who never get to perform.
a rivalry between two actors competing for the same role.

why.A: The fall is a plot device occupying three lines, not the passage’s subject.
why.B: Correct — the closing lines set eleven weeks learning a part against one hour learning a play.
why.C: Nadia does perform, and the passage treats the chance as a shock rather than a grievance.
why.D: Ivo and Marguerite are colleagues throughout; no competition is described.

context: The comparison to "a road you have walked and never driven" chiefly conveys that Nadia’s knowledge was:

choices.text: acquired more recently than the rest of the company’s.
dependent on directions she had been given by someone else.
thorough but untested at the speed the part would actually move.
incomplete in places she had never troubled to rehearse.

why.A: Eleven weeks is presented as unusually long preparation, not as a late start.
why.B: The image is about the pace of travel, and Nadia prepared alone with no one directing her.
why.C: Correct — walking and driving cover the same ground, and the next paragraph has Ivo going faster than she had ever heard.
why.D: The same sentence insists every turn was hers, which rules out gaps in coverage.

context: As it is used in the last paragraph, "diagnosis" most nearly means:

choices.text: a prediction of a future illness.
a formal medical examination.
an unkind remark meant to wound.
a naming of what had been wrong.

why.A: The remark is about the performance just given, not about anything still to come.
why.B: The everyday clinical sense is displaced here; Marguerite is speaking about acting.
why.C: Marguerite says it plainly and Nadia accepts it, with no suggestion of malice.
why.D: Correct — it is set against "compliment", so the remark identifies a fault rather than praising.

context: The "small cold clarity" Nadia arrives at on the bus is best understood as the recognition that:

choices.text: her finished preparation will have to be done again, differently.
she was given the part only because no one better was available.
Marguerite had meant the remark as an insult after all.
her performance in the second act had been a failure.

why.A: Correct — the sentence it introduces is that she would have to learn it all again, in front of people.
why.B: Nothing questions why she was cast as understudy or how she was regarded.
why.C: She reclassifies the remark as a diagnosis, which is a judgement about herself, not about Marguerite.
why.D: Twice in the second act what she said was better than what she had planned.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward Nadia is best described as:

choices.text: detached, reporting the evening without ever evaluating it.
sympathetic but unwilling to soften what she has missed.
impatient with an actor who has wasted eleven weeks.
admiring of a performance that went entirely to plan.

why.A: The closing paragraph evaluates directly, calling the corridor’s teaching incomplete.
why.B: Correct — the narration credits the two good moments and still ends on what the corridor failed to teach.
why.C: The eleven weeks are treated as real work, and the second act is said to be not worse.
why.D: The first act goes plainly wrong: her central line lands somewhere behind her.

context: The description of the corridor and its pipes serves mainly to:

choices.text: explain why Nadia was easy for the stage manager to find.
suggest that Nadia is disliked by the rest of the company.
stand for an audience that asks nothing of her.
establish that the theatre is poorly maintained.

why.A: She is indeed found there, but that is one clause against a paragraph built on the sound.
why.B: Afterwards the company says generous things to her in that same corridor.
why.C: Correct — the pipes sound like applause, and the passage notes it never coughed and never arrived late.
why.D: The state of the building is never a subject; only the sound of the pipes is described.

context: The passage says that when Ivo missed a cue in the Thursday run, Nadia:

choices.text: supplied the missing line from the corridor.
did not notice until the scene had finished.
was rehearsing elsewhere and heard about it later.
sensed it slightly before the silence arrived.

why.A: She is only described as feeling the gap; she says nothing during the run.
why.B: The point of the detail is precisely how early she registered it.
why.C: The passage places her close enough to feel the moment as it happened.
why.D: Correct — she felt it a half-second before the silence, like a step that is not there.

context: The passage is organised as:

choices.text: a long preparation, one displacing event, and a later reinterpretation.
a single performance recounted in strict order from curtain to curtain.
alternating scenes from rehearsal and from opening night.
an argument about acting, illustrated by a brief anecdote.

why.A: Correct — eleven weeks, then the summons at ten past six, then the meaning arrived at on the bus.
why.B: The first two paragraphs precede the performance by weeks, and the last follows it.
why.C: The rehearsal material is given once, at the start, and is not returned to.
why.D: The passage narrates throughout and never argues in its own voice.

context: The difference between Nadia’s first act and her second act is chiefly that in the second she:

choices.text: followed the staging that Marguerite had worked out in rehearsal.
responded to the other actor instead of delivering what she had prepared.
remembered lines that had escaped her earlier in the evening.
spoke more loudly so that the audience could hear her.

why.A: Marguerite’s staging is never described, and the change comes from listening to Ivo.
why.B: Correct — she stopped reciting and started listening, and her lines bent to accommodate Ivo.
why.C: No missed or forgotten line of hers is mentioned at any point.
why.D: Volume is never raised as an issue in either act.

context: According to the passage, ridership rises steeply once the wait between buses drops below about:

choices.text: twelve seconds.
two minutes.
twelve minutes.
thirty minutes.

why.A: The passage discusses waits between buses, which are measured in minutes.
why.B: Two minutes is never mentioned; the threshold the passage gives is twelve.
why.C: Correct — the third paragraph names twelve minutes as the threshold.
why.D: No half-hour figure appears anywhere in the passage.

context: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.text: frequent service on straight corridors is the correct design for every city.
transit planners lack the data needed to draw a defensible network.
bus networks should be designed by councils rather than by consultants.
a technical-looking network decision is really a choice about whom to serve.

why.A: The fourth paragraph sets out what a purely ridership-driven network sheds.
why.B: The ridership case is described as strong and mostly empirical, so data is not the problem.
why.C: The consultant asks the council to set the number; he is not said to be the wrong person to design to it.
why.D: Correct — the opening calls it an argument about who is worth being late for, and the close says the choice is political.

context: As it is used in the third paragraph, "utility" most nearly means:

choices.text: something used without being planned around.
the usefulness a service provides to a rider.
a company that supplies water or electricity.
a measure of the satisfaction a choice produces.

why.A: Correct — it is the opposite of an appointment, so it names a service you simply turn to.
why.B: The everyday sense is on offer here, but the sentence contrasts two ways of using a bus, not two amounts of benefit.
why.C: The commercial sense would make the bus a water company, which the sentence does not support.
why.D: The economists’ sense would be a quantity; the sentence is describing a change in how riders behave.

context: The passage suggests that the ridership measure misjudges the low-density route because it:

choices.text: assumes that every household lives within walking distance of a stop.
treats a rider with a car and a rider without one as the same rider.
undercounts the passengers who actually board in the suburbs.
ignores the cost of running buses over longer distances.

why.A: That is the aim of coverage, not an assumption built into the ridership measure.
why.B: Correct — the fourth paragraph says it counts a rider who would otherwise drive the same as one who would otherwise not go.
why.C: The count of eleven an hour is accepted; what is disputed is what the count means.
why.D: Distance and operating cost are not raised as flaws in the measure.

context: The sentence about cities that redrew their networks and saw ridership climb functions mainly to:

choices.text: show that unchanged budgets are the main obstacle facing planners.
introduce the consultant whose method the passage goes on to describe.
supply the evidence behind the claim that the frequency case is empirical.
concede a point to the supporters of coverage before rebutting them.

why.A: The unchanged budget is what makes the result impressive, not an obstacle being complained of.
why.B: The consultant appears two paragraphs later and is not connected to these cities.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph opens by calling the case mostly empirical, and this is the observed result that backs it.
why.D: It strengthens the frequency case; the coverage case is not raised until the next paragraph.

context: The author’s attitude toward the consultant who refuses to recommend a split is best described as:

choices.text: critical of an expert avoiding the work he was hired for.
uncertain whether the method produces workable networks.
amused by a position the author considers unworkable in practice.
approving of a refusal the author regards as honest.

why.A: He does the technical work; he declines only to answer a question the passage calls political.
why.B: No doubt is expressed about the networks his method yields.
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph is played for humour or treated as impractical.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph introduces him among the planners called "the honest ones".

context: According to the final paragraph, frequency and coverage differ chiefly in that each:

choices.text: means something different by fairness.
appeals to a different body of evidence.
suits a different size of city budget.
was proposed at a different point in history.

why.A: Correct — both appeal to fairness, one treating riders as interchangeable and the other as neighbours.
why.B: The evidence problem is raised earlier and applies to coverage alone.
why.C: The paragraph holds the budget fixed, which is what forces the choice.
why.D: The passage gives neither approach a date or an origin.

context: The passage states that a fixed budget can buy:

choices.text: neither, unless the network is redrawn first.
frequency or coverage, but not both.
both frequency and coverage, at reduced quality.
coverage first, and frequency once ridership grows.

why.A: Redrawing the network is how a city acts on the choice, not a precondition for affording anything.
why.B: Correct — the second paragraph says the same money buys either one and cannot buy both.
why.C: The passage rules the combination out rather than offering a diluted version of it.
why.D: No sequence is proposed; the choice is presented as standing.

context: The opening phrase "an argument about who is worth being late for" chiefly suggests that network design:

choices.text: has no effect on how long any rider actually waits.
is conducted by people who are themselves frequently late.
decides whose time the system treats as costly.
is usually settled by whoever complains most loudly.

why.A: Waiting times are the central quantity the whole argument turns on.
why.B: The lateness belongs to riders left waiting, not to the planners.
why.C: Correct — waiting is the cost, and the design decides which riders are made to bear it.
why.D: The passage attributes the outcome to budgets and councils, not to complaint.

context: Which of the following best supports the passage’s claim that declining to choose is itself a choice?

choices.text: The consultant makes councils name a percentage before he designs anything.
Ridership climbs on an unchanged budget once the routes are straightened.
A route carrying eleven passengers an hour counts as a failure by one measure.
A city that does not decide has the budget decide, one service cut at a time.

why.A: This shows one way of forcing a choice, not what follows when none is made.
why.B: This supports the frequency case and says nothing about indecision.
why.C: This illustrates the limits of the ridership measure rather than the cost of not choosing.
why.D: Correct — this is the passage’s own closing statement of what happens in the absence of a decision.

context: According to the passage, a chilling requirement is measured in:

choices.text: hours spent near freezing.
centimetres of soil above the seed.
the number of warm weeks in autumn.
days between flowering and fruit set.

why.A: Correct — the second paragraph gives it as a number of hours near freezing.
why.B: The two centimetres of soil describe where the seed sits, not what it counts.
why.C: Warm spells are exactly what the mechanism is built to ignore.
why.D: Flowering and fruit set describe the orchard symptom, not the measurement.

context: The passage is mainly about:

choices.text: why plants of the temperate zone cannot survive a January frost.
how seeds time germination by counting cold, and why that is now failing.
the chemical pathway by which abscisic acid and gibberellins interact.
the losses orchardists have suffered in recent low-chill years.

why.A: A November sprout dying in January is the premise of the first line, not the subject.
why.B: Correct — the first three paragraphs establish the counting, and the last two show it being starved.
why.C: The chemistry occupies one paragraph and is offered in outline to explain the counting.
why.D: The orchards are introduced as the visible case of a wider problem.

context: The passage suggests that measuring cold is more reliable than measuring warmth because:

choices.text: cold accumulates faster than warmth in the temperate zone.
warm weather is harder to predict than cold weather.
warmth arrives in autumn too, but a winter’s worth of cold does not.
seeds buried in soil cannot register warm temperatures at all.

why.A: No rate of accumulation is compared anywhere in the passage.
why.B: Prediction is not the issue; the seed is measuring what has already happened.
why.C: Correct — a warm November is the false signal the counter is designed not to be fooled by.
why.D: Warmth after enough cold is what triggers germination, so the seed plainly registers it.

context: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, "starved" most nearly means:

choices.text: deprived of nutrients in the surrounding soil.
exhausted of the reserve the seed carries.
kept from light for too long a period.
left short of the cold the seed requires.

why.A: The nutritional sense is the everyday one, but soil chemistry is never discussed.
why.B: The finite reserve appears in the last paragraph as a consequence, not as what is withheld.
why.C: A buried seed is described as having no eyes and no access to light in any case.
why.D: Correct — it answers the previous sentence about the counter, and the paragraph goes on to describe shorter, milder winters.

context: In calling the ratio of the two chemicals "the clock face", the author chiefly means that it:

choices.text: is the part of the mechanism that shows how much winter has passed.
moves at a steady rate regardless of the surrounding air temperature.
governs the time of day at which germination will occur.
is visible to researchers without dissecting the seed.

why.A: Correct — a clock face is where an accumulated quantity can be read off, which is what the ratio records.
why.B: The whole point is that the ratio moves only with prolonged cold.
why.C: The passage works in seasons and hours of chilling, never in times of day.
why.D: Nothing is said about how the ratio is observed or measured.

context: The passage identifies which pair of substances as governing dormancy?

choices.text: Gibberellins and carbon dioxide.
Abscisic acid and gibberellins.
Chlorophyll and anthocyanin.
Nitrogen and abscisic acid.

why.A: Gibberellins are named, but carbon dioxide is not.
why.B: Correct — one holds the seed shut and the other opens it, and the ratio between them is the clock face.
why.C: Neither pigment is mentioned anywhere in this passage.
why.D: Nitrogen plays no part in the mechanism as the passage describes it.

context: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: indignant at the orchardists who first raised the alarm.
detached, listing outcomes without weighing any of them.
measured concern about a failure that goes unnoticed.
confident that wild plants will adapt within a few seasons.

why.A: The orchardists are credited with noticing first and are not criticised.
why.B: The paragraph weighs plainly, calling the wild case larger than the visible one.
why.C: Correct — the consequence is called harder to see and probably larger, and the paragraph ends on it passing for patience.
why.D: The seed is described trying again against a winter likely to be warmer still.

context: The sentences about peach and cherry trees serve mainly to:

choices.text: explain why orchard species evolved a longer chilling requirement.
argue that commercial losses matter more than losses among wild plants.
establish that warming winters affect cultivated species only.
give a documented instance of a failure that is otherwise hard to observe.

why.A: The orchard trees are said to run on the same system, with no separate evolutionary account.
why.B: The passage calls the wild consequence probably larger.
why.C: The paragraph after it extends the same problem to wild plants.
why.D: Correct — the next paragraph says the wild consequence is harder to see, which is why the visible case comes first.

context: The closing sentence implies that the danger to wild seeds is difficult to detect because a seed that has failed:

choices.text: behaves exactly as a seed that is still waiting on purpose.
decays quickly enough that no trace of it remains.
germinates early and is then killed by the following frost.
produces visible damage only in the second year of drought.

why.A: Correct — an unmet requirement leaves the seed shut, which is what ordinary dormancy also looks like.
why.B: The passage has the seed persisting and trying again the following year.
why.C: Germinating early is the outcome the whole mechanism exists to prevent.
why.D: Drought is never mentioned; the variable is the amount of cold.

context: Compared with the effect on orchard trees, the effect on wild plants is presented as:

choices.text: smaller, because wild seeds can wait indefinitely.
less visible but probably greater in scale.
more visible and easier to put a figure on.
identical, since both run on the same mechanism.

why.A: The seed spends a little more of a finite reserve each year, so waiting has a cost.
why.B: Correct — the last paragraph opens by calling it harder to see and probably larger.
why.C: It is the orchard case that is measurable, in ragged leafing and lost fruit.
why.D: They share a mechanism, but the passage separates them precisely on visibility and scale.

context: The narrative is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a driver finding a use for time the timetable had already allowed her.
a driver investigating why a passenger rode a route to no destination.
the difficulty of keeping a late bus running on a schedule.
the friendship that developed between a driver and a regular passenger.

why.A: Correct — the last paragraph names the slack, says nobody had ever asked what she did with hers, and closes on having found something to spend it on.
why.B: She asks once, is answered vaguely, and deliberately lets it alone; the mystery is never pursued.
why.C: The schedule is described as roomy rather than tight, and she is never shown struggling to keep to it.
why.D: They exchange almost nothing across years; she does not learn where he goes, and hears of his leaving from a clerk.

context: According to the passage, Mr Ahearn boarded the bus:

choices.text: at the terminus, twice a month.
at the fourth stop, on Fridays.
at the fourth stop, every night of the week.
at Renshaw Street, on Fridays.

why.A: The terminus is where he got off, and no interval of a fortnight appears anywhere.
why.B: Correct — the second paragraph opens with a man who got on at the fourth stop on Fridays.
why.C: The passage is specific that it was Fridays, and the narrator later speaks of the Friday bus.
why.D: Renshaw Street is where the route begins, not where he joined it.

context: The narrator’s remark that she had "used mine" most strongly suggests that she believed:

choices.text: Mr Ahearn had lied to her about liking the window.
other passengers had already asked him the same thing.
her question had been answered as fully as it was going to be.
she had been rude and could not repair it.

why.A: She neither doubts the answer nor tests it; the point is that she stops asking, not that she disbelieves.
why.B: No other passenger is mentioned anywhere on the empty late bus.
why.C: Correct — she says there is a kind of question you can only ask once, and she lets it alone rather than pressing.
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph suggests offence was taken; he answers her and the two go on as before.

context: The narrator’s calculation of the forty-minute uphill walk serves mainly to:

choices.text: explain why she eventually decided to hold the bus for him.
show that she had been trained to think about her route in detail.
suggest that he was too frail to have made the journey on foot.
establish that his riding to the terminus made no practical sense.

why.A: The holding of the bus comes years later and is not tied back to the walk.
why.B: The detail is about him rather than about her professional habits.
why.C: His health is never discussed, and the clerk later says explicitly that he was not ill.
why.D: Correct — the sentence before it says he ended two miles from where he started with no way home, and the walk is what makes that cost concrete.

context: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word "slack" most nearly means:

choices.text: spare time deliberately built into the schedule.
a lack of effort on the part of the drivers.
a rope or line hanging loosely.
a falling off in the number of passengers.

why.A: Correct — the passage explains it as room left in the schedule for weather, roadworks and the drunk who cannot find his pass.
why.B: The narrator is describing a property of the timetable, and she is if anything exceeding her duties.
why.C: This is the rope sense of the word, which has no place on a bus route.
why.D: Passenger numbers are low throughout and are never presented as something that changed.

context: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: anxious about what the depot clerk would think of her waiting.
plainly stated and unsentimental about something she cannot explain.
bitter about the years she spent waiting for nothing.
triumphant at having outlasted the timetable.

why.A: The clerk delivers news and then disappears from the passage entirely.
why.B: Correct — she says outright that she could not have told you what she was waiting for, and reports the rest in flat declaratives.
why.C: She describes the year without complaint, and nothing is blamed on anyone.
why.D: There is no victory claimed; the bus simply went on running without him.

context: The passage is organised as:

choices.text: an argument for a change to the timetable, supported by an anecdote.
two parallel accounts of the same route, years apart.
a habit, then one passenger, then his absence and what it left.
a single night recounted in order from the depot to the terminus.

why.A: She never proposes changing anything; the slack she uses is already in the schedule.
why.B: There is one account, moving forward, and no second vantage point on it.
why.C: Correct — the first paragraph describes years of empty driving, the middle ones introduce Mr Ahearn, and the last two follow the night he stopped coming.
why.D: The passage spans twenty-two years, and the one night described is not followed stop by stop.

context: Which detail best supports the idea that the narrator’s four minutes cost the service nothing?

choices.text: The bus is usually empty by the time it reaches the third stop.
She had driven the same route for twenty-two years.
The terminus lies two miles from where Mr Ahearn started.
The timetable has slack built in for weather and roadworks.

why.A: An empty bus explains why nobody minded, but not why the timetable could absorb the delay.
why.B: Length of service speaks to her experience rather than to the schedule’s tolerance.
why.C: That distance describes his journey and has no bearing on the timetable.
why.D: Correct — the built-in allowance is precisely what she is drawing on, and she says that on that route four minutes is nothing.

context: The narrator contrasts driving an empty bus with driving a full one mainly to make the point that:

choices.text: habits formed on empty runs are dangerous when a passenger finally appears.
empty runs are more tiring than crowded ones over a long career.
passengers on late buses behave differently from daytime passengers.
the route should have been shortened once demand fell away.

why.A: Correct — she says you stop taking the corners as though someone might be standing, and then one night someone is.
why.B: Fatigue is never raised; the contrast is about how she handles the vehicle.
why.C: Only one late passenger is described, and his behaviour is not compared with anyone’s.
why.D: No change to the route is suggested at any point.

context: The passage is primarily about:

choices.text: the case for employing more pharmacists at busy outpatient counters.
a change that left the average wait untouched and the sense of fairness transformed.
a method by which a pharmacy cut its average waiting time substantially.
the difficulty of measuring how long patients actually wait for prescriptions.

why.A: Staffing is explicitly held constant, and no argument is made for changing it.
why.B: Correct — the mean holds at fourteen minutes throughout, and the researchers call the finding one about justice rather than speed.
why.C: The passage states twice that the mean wait did not move.
why.D: Waiting times are measured without apparent difficulty; what is hard to see is the people who leave.

context: In the year after the change, the slowest one in twenty patients waited:

choices.text: forty-one minutes or more.
six minutes or more.
twenty-two minutes or more.
fourteen minutes or more.

why.A: Forty-one minutes is the figure from the year before the change.
why.B: Six is the number of counters and of the original queues, not a waiting time.
why.C: Correct — the third paragraph gives forty-one minutes before the change and twenty-two after.
why.D: Fourteen minutes is the mean wait, which was the same in both years.

context: The passage implies that a patient in one of the six original queues was frustrated largely because that patient:

choices.text: was served by pharmacists who worked at noticeably different speeds.
had been assigned to a counter rather than allowed to choose one.
was waiting substantially longer than patients wait under a single queue.
could not tell whether a neighbour’s faster progress was luck or something else.

why.A: The passage says the same six pharmacists filled prescriptions at the same rate.
why.B: Under the old system patients chose their own queue; it is the new one that calls them forward.
why.C: Mean waits were identical under both systems.
why.D: Correct — the fourth paragraph says such a patient can see only that somebody else is doing better, with no way to know why.

context: The sentence explaining that six servers at one speed get through the same number of people serves to:

choices.text: show the unchanged mean was expected, not a disappointment.
argue that the change should not have been attempted.
introduce the finding about the spread of waiting times.
establish that the pharmacy was understaffed for its volume.

why.A: Correct — the passage calls the unchanged mean exactly what arithmetic predicts, which frames it as a confirmation rather than a failure.
why.B: The change is presented as worthwhile, with complaints falling by two thirds.
why.C: The spread is introduced by the sentence that follows, beginning with what changed.
why.D: Volume and staffing adequacy are never assessed.

context: As it is used in the final sentence, the word "dispense" most nearly means:

choices.text: scatter widely.
hand out.
do without.
excuse from a rule.

why.A: Scattering describes spreading something about, which is not what happens at a pharmacy counter.
why.B: Correct — the counter dispenses prescriptions, and the line turns on fairness being the one thing it cannot hand over.
why.C: That sense appears only in the phrase "dispense with," and the sentence does not use it.
why.D: This is the sense in which an authority grants an exemption, which nobody in the passage is doing.

context: The final paragraph’s attitude toward the single queue is best described as:

choices.text: neutral, presenting figures without drawing any conclusion.
enthusiastic, treating the design as a solution without drawbacks.
favourable but careful to name what the measurements miss.
sceptical that the reported improvement occurred at all.

why.A: The paragraph makes a judgement, saying the queue is made harder to look at.
why.B: The cost is stated in the paragraph’s first sentence.
why.C: Correct — it calls the line honest and then notes that those who leave never appear in a waiting-time statistic.
why.D: The improvement is accepted; what is questioned is whether the statistics capture everything.

context: The passage moves through which sequence?

choices.text: a hypothesis, an experiment designed to test it, and its confirmation.
two competing designs weighed side by side throughout.
a history of the pharmacy followed by a proposal for its future.
the old complaint, the change, the figures, the reason, the cost.

why.A: Nobody sets out to test a stated hypothesis; the change is made and then studied.
why.B: The old design is described and then replaced, not held in balance against the new one.
why.C: No future proposal is offered, and the history goes back only to 2011.
why.D: Correct — the paragraphs run in exactly that order, ending with the patients who left without joining.

context: Which finding best supports the claim that the improvement was about fairness rather than speed?

choices.text: The mean wait was unchanged while recorded complaints fell by two thirds.
The slowest one in twenty patients waited twenty-two minutes after the change.
A small number of patients left without joining the single queue.
The same six pharmacists worked the same hours after the change.

why.A: Correct — complaints collapsing while the wait stayed put is precisely the pattern that rules out speed as the cause.
why.B: The improved worst case is a real gain, but on its own it is a change in waiting time.
why.C: That is offered as a cost of the design rather than as support for the claim.
why.D: Unchanged staffing establishes that the comparison is fair; it does not show what patients valued.

context: Compared with six queues of seven people, one queue of forty is presented as:

choices.text: identical in every single respect the study was able to measure.
no slower, but more discouraging to look at from the door.
slower, and for that reason more discouraging.
faster, and therefore easier for arrivals to accept.

why.A: The study measured a large difference in the spread of waits.
why.B: Correct — the final paragraph says it looks worse from the door while the arithmetic of throughput is unchanged.
why.C: Throughput is set by the six counters, and the passage insists the mean did not move.
why.D: Nothing in the passage claims the single queue is faster.

context: The central claim of the passage is that Warde was caught because:

choices.text: a second version of a known painting appeared on the market.
he confessed to a curator in Amsterdam after four years.
his inventions were better composed than the paintings he imitated.
his pigments and canvases could not withstand close laboratory testing.

why.A: That is the risk of a copy, which the passage explicitly contrasts with what Warde made.
why.B: The interview comes after he has served his sentence, not before he was caught.
why.C: Correct — the fourth paragraph states that a forgery is exposed by what it improves, and the curator’s suspicion begins with skies that are too well organised.
why.D: The second paragraph says the materials can be sourced and found, and treats them as the easy part.

context: According to the passage, the curator’s suspicion began with:

choices.text: a chemical analysis of the pigments in one canvas.
a document showing where the canvases had come from.
a comparison with a signed work by the same painter.
an irritation at how neatly the skies were arranged.

why.A: The passage says she did not begin with the paint.
why.B: Provenance documents are never mentioned.
why.C: She compares the suspect group with one another rather than with a signed original.
why.D: Correct — her notes record an irritation that the skies were too well organised.

context: The passage suggests that a forger attempting what Warde attempted must be able to:

choices.text: suppress his own judgement about what would make a picture better.
work faster than the painters whose manner he is adopting.
restrict himself to painters whose work survives in small numbers.
avoid any subject the original painter is known to have attempted.

why.A: Correct — the second paragraph requires choices made without preference, and the last says his eye was what gave him away.
why.B: Speed is never raised as a requirement or a difficulty.
why.C: Scarcity is not discussed; the thirty-one canvases simply had no originals.
why.D: Warde painted the same kind of landscapes his models painted, and that is the point.

context: The description of the painters as "working men filling orders" functions to:

choices.text: argue that forgery does less harm when the originals were made for money.
explain why their pictures contain untidy elements Warde would never have left.
suggest that their work was of lower quality than Warde’s.
establish how many paintings they were able to produce in a year.

why.A: The morality of forgery is not weighed against the originals’ commercial purpose.
why.B: Correct — the sentence that follows says they left things in because the things were there.
why.C: The passage credits Warde with pictures that are too good, which is a criticism rather than praise.
why.D: No figures for their output appear anywhere.

context: As it is used in the first paragraph, the word "hand" most nearly means:

choices.text: a round of applause from an audience.
a unit used for measuring height.
a painter’s individual manner of working.
assistance given to another artist.

why.A: The applause sense has no place in a description of a canvas.
why.B: That unit is used for horses and is unrelated to painting.
why.C: Correct — the phrase describes new paintings in an old hand, meaning canvases made in another painter’s style.
why.D: Nobody helps Warde, and the sentence is about how the pictures look rather than who made them.

context: The passage’s attitude toward Warde is best described as:

choices.text: admiring, presenting him as an artist wronged by the law.
contemptuous, dwelling on the dishonesty of his trade.
detached, declining to draw any conclusion about him.
analytical, treating his failure as a consequence of his ability.

why.A: His four years are reported without objection, and nothing suggests the sentence was unjust.
why.B: The passage never condemns him; it is interested in how he was found out.
why.C: It reaches a firm conclusion about why he was caught.
why.D: Correct — the last paragraph says there was no version of him that had the eye without the flaw it produced.

context: The second paragraph is structured as:

choices.text: a dismissal of the expected difficulties followed by the real one.
a list of the materials a forger must obtain, in order of cost.
a chronological account of how Warde learned his craft.
a comparison between two forgers working in the same period.

why.A: Correct — pigments and canvases are disposed of in one sentence, and the difficulty is then named as making choices without preference.
why.B: The materials appear once, with no prices and no ordering.
why.C: His training is never described.
why.D: No second forger appears anywhere in the passage.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that Warde’s problem was consistent rather than confined to one picture?

choices.text: He said he had never been able to look at a real one without wanting to move something.
The curator went through the group and found the same tidiness everywhere.
A bird in the upper left balanced a church tower in the lower right.
He painted at least thirty-one landscapes between 1951 and 1964.

why.A: His remark explains the cause and comes years after the pictures were examined.
why.B: Correct — examining the whole group and finding it everywhere is what turns one impression into a pattern.
why.C: That is the single canvas that prompted the suspicion, not the evidence that it generalised.
why.D: The count establishes how many pictures existed, not what they had in common.

context: The passage distinguishes a forgery from a copy on the ground that a copy:

choices.text: is generally made from cheaper period materials.
can be sold only to buyers who know what it is.
has an original in existence that exposes it.
requires more technical skill to produce convincingly.

why.A: Materials are discussed only in connection with what Warde used.
why.B: Who might buy a copy is never considered.
why.C: Correct — the first paragraph says the original is in a museum and a second one answers the question before it is asked.
why.D: The passage argues the opposite, that inventing in another hand is the harder thing.

context: The passage is chiefly concerned with:

choices.text: how deep an ice core must be drilled to reach usable air.
the evidence that carbon dioxide rose before the last warming.
the reasons ice cores are more reliable than tree rings.
why an ice core carries two clocks that must be reconciled.

why.A: Depths are given, but only to explain where the firn ends and bubbles begin.
why.B: The passage raises that question as an example and pointedly does not answer it.
why.C: Tree rings appear once, as a way of describing counting layers, and are never rated against ice.
why.D: Correct — the closing image is a calendar with two hands, and the fourth paragraph calls the alignment most of the work.

context: According to the passage, the firn is:

choices.text: compacted snow whose spaces are still connected to the surface.
the layer of solid ice immediately beneath the bubbles.
a band of trapped air found at the base of an ice sheet.
the annual layer counted downward like a tree ring.

why.A: Correct — the second paragraph defines it as old snow, compacted but still porous, with its spaces connected to one another and to the surface.
why.B: The firn lies above the ice that holds bubbles, not below it.
why.C: Air moves through the firn freely; it is sealed only when the pores pinch shut beneath it.
why.D: Layers are counted through the whole core, and the firn is a zone rather than a layer.

context: The passage implies that a core drilled at a site with very heavy snowfall would:

choices.text: record past temperature less reliably than a dry-site core would.
have a smaller gap between the age of its air and its ice.
contain no usable bubbles at any depth.
require a deeper drill to reach the same year.

why.A: Nothing is said about snowfall affecting the temperature signal.
why.B: Correct — the third paragraph ties the offset to how fast snow piles up, giving thirty years at a heavy-snowfall coastal site.
why.C: Heavy snowfall closes the pores sooner, which produces bubbles earlier rather than not at all.
why.D: Heavier layers do mean more depth per year, but the passage never raises drill depth as a consequence.

context: The question about whether carbon dioxide rose before the warming is raised mainly to:

choices.text: suggest that the record is too uncertain to be worth collecting.
introduce a disagreement between two groups of researchers.
show why the two clocks have to be aligned before anything can be concluded.
summarise what ice cores have already established about the last century.

why.A: The final paragraph states plainly that none of this makes the record less valuable.
why.B: No researchers are named and no dispute is described.
why.C: Correct — the sentences around it say temperature is read from the ice, carbon dioxide from the bubbles, and the two are on different clocks.
why.D: The passage offers it as an open question rather than a settled result.

context: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word "younger" most nearly means:

choices.text: less compressed by the weight above it.
nearer to the surface of the ice sheet.
more recently discovered by researchers.
sealed off from the atmosphere more recently.

why.A: Compression is what closes the pores; it is not what the comparison of ages measures.
why.B: The air and the ice being compared sit at the same depth, which is the whole difficulty.
why.C: Discovery dates play no part in the paragraph.
why.D: Correct — the air kept exchanging with the atmosphere while the ice around it was being buried, so its clock starts later.

context: The passage’s stance toward the ice-core record is best described as:

choices.text: confident in its value and insistent about how it must be read.
doubtful that the record can support any firm conclusion.
impatient with researchers who have failed to align the clocks.
indifferent, reporting the method without evaluating it.

why.A: Correct — it says nothing else on Earth offers actual samples of the atmosphere, and warns against a reader who forgets the two clocks.
why.B: The final paragraph denies that the complication reduces the record’s value.
why.C: The alignment is described as genuinely hard work rather than as neglected.
why.D: Judgements are made in almost every paragraph, ending with an explicit warning.

context: The passage develops by:

choices.text: tracing the history of ice-core science in the order of its discoveries.
presenting a unique strength, a complication, and what it costs.
following a single core from the drill site to the laboratory.
contrasting two sites in Antarctica across the whole passage.

why.A: The only chronology mentioned is that the complication took some years to appreciate.
why.B: Correct — the bubbles are introduced as something nothing else offers, the firn complicates them, and the fourth paragraph gives the price.
why.C: No particular core is followed, and no laboratory work is described.
why.D: Two sites appear in one paragraph, to give the range of the offset.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that the alignment problem can be severe?

choices.text: A core can be counted downward like the rings of a tree.
The bubbles hold actual samples of the atmosphere rather than a proxy.
At a cold, dry interior site the difference can exceed two thousand years.
The top seventy to a hundred metres of an ice sheet are firn rather than ice.

why.A: Counting layers is what makes the record readable at all.
why.B: That is the record’s strength rather than evidence of the difficulty.
why.C: Correct — an offset of two thousand years is larger than most of the intervals such a record is used to argue about.
why.D: The thickness of the firn explains where the offset comes from without showing how large it can get.

context: The coastal site and the interior site are compared chiefly to show that:

choices.text: interior sites yield longer records than coastal ones.
coastal ice contains more air per unit volume.
only interior sites can be dated by counting annual layers.
the age offset depends on how quickly snow accumulates.

why.A: Record length is never compared, only the offset between the two clocks.
why.B: The amount of air in the ice is not discussed at either site.
why.C: Layer counting is described as a property of cores generally.
why.D: Correct — the sentence introducing them says the size of the offset depends on how fast snow piles up.

context: The narrative is best described as:

choices.text: a nephew’s account of an uncle whose position he can no longer read plainly.
an explanation of how a parish organist is chosen and replaced.
a record of a dispute between an organist and the parish that had employed him.
a description of the music played in a rural church across three decades.

why.A: Correct — the final paragraph says outright that he cannot decide between freedom and excuse, and has stopped believing the two can be told apart.
why.B: The parish’s procedures appear only as background to Peter’s thirty-one years.
why.C: Nobody quarrels; the parish offers him the post and he declines it.
why.D: Only one piece of playing is described, and it is there to show what the empty mornings allowed him.

context: According to the passage, when the parish offered Peter the post he:

choices.text: declined because the parish had already hired someone younger.
declined, and gave a reason everyone treated as a joke.
accepted, and held it until he was too old to play.
asked for time to consider and never answered.

why.A: The younger player is found afterward, not before.
why.B: Correct — he said no, cited the eleven hymns, and the passage notes that everyone took it as a joke.
why.C: He is never the organist; the first sentence establishes that.
why.D: His answer is immediate and is reported directly.

context: The detail that the canvas bag stayed packed most strongly suggests that Peter:

choices.text: kept his belongings separate from the rest of the household.
travelled often to parishes outside his own.
lived in permanent readiness to be called at short notice.
had stopped unpacking because he expected never to play again.

why.A: Only the shoes are in the bag, and no other household arrangement is described.
why.B: Athlone is where Mr Dolan went; Peter stays at St Brendan’s.
why.C: Correct — the bag sits beside the sentence listing the emergencies he was rung for, so it is a kit kept ready.
why.D: He plays throughout the thirty-one years the passage covers.

context: The list of mornings Peter was given — after a funeral, during the match, the cold eight o’clock — serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that the parish was steadily losing its congregation over time.
suggest that Mr Dolan avoided the least rewarding services.
explain why Peter eventually refused the organist’s post.
establish the conditions that left him unobserved, and so free.

why.A: Thin attendance is given for particular services rather than as a trend.
why.B: Mr Dolan’s absences are illness and travel, not selection.
why.C: His refusal is explained separately, and in a remark taken as a joke.
why.D: Correct — the sentence that follows says these were the mornings when nobody was listening closely, and so the ones where he could do as he liked.

context: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word "season" most nearly means:

choices.text: a stretch of the year that is his to plan.
a period of unusually warm weather.
a flavouring added to something plain.
a run of performances by a touring company.

why.A: Correct — it answers his own remark that the organist plays what the year requires, in the same eleven weeks.
why.B: The only weather in the passage is the February cold, which is incidental.
why.C: That sense belongs to cooking and has no place in the sentence.
why.D: No touring or programme of performances is mentioned.

context: The remark that a substitute plays "whatever the morning has left lying about" is used to convey that his repertoire was:

choices.text: borrowed, taken without permission from the organist’s own books.
unplanned, made from whatever the occasion happened to require.
old-fashioned, drawn from music the parish had discarded.
careless, assembled without any preparation at all.

why.A: No question of taking anyone else’s music arises.
why.B: Correct — it is set directly against the organist’s fixed eleven hymns in eleven fixed weeks.
why.C: Nothing suggests the music itself was out of date or cast off.
why.D: The passage shows him playing with great deliberation when given room.

context: The narrator’s tone in the final paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: reassured, having finally understood his uncle’s choice.
amused by the joke about the eleven hymns.
reflective and openly undecided.
resentful of the parish that overlooked his uncle.

why.A: The paragraph reports the opposite, that he stopped believing the two could be separated.
why.B: The joke belongs to an earlier paragraph and is not revisited.
why.C: Correct — he says he has never been able to decide, and ends on a doubt rather than a conclusion.
why.D: The parish is not blamed; it offered him the post and he refused it.

context: The passage is built by:

choices.text: alternating between Peter’s account and Mr Dolan’s.
moving backward from the clearing of the flat to Peter’s first Sunday.
setting out an argument and then supporting it with three examples.
stating the arrangement, illustrating it, ending it, then weighing it.

why.A: Mr Dolan never speaks and is described only from outside.
why.B: The flat is cleared at the end, and the narrative runs forward to reach it.
why.C: No thesis is proposed; the closing paragraph declines to reach one.
why.D: Correct — the thirty-one years are stated, the mornings illustrate them, Mr Dolan’s death ends them, and the last paragraph judges.

context: Which detail best supports the view that Peter valued what his position allowed him?

choices.text: He opened out a plain recessional until it did not want to end.
He kept his shoes in a canvas bag by the door of the flat.
He was rung whenever Mr Dolan had shingles or the flu.
He was sixty-four when the parish offered him the post.

why.A: Correct — it is the one moment the passage shows him using the freedom the empty mornings gave him.
why.B: The bag shows readiness to be called, not what he did once he arrived.
why.C: Mr Dolan’s illnesses explain how he got the work.
why.D: His age bears on the refusal rather than on what he valued.

context: The main point of the passage is that the familiar explanation for the milk’s position is:

choices.text: a recent invention of marketing writers with no factual basis at all.
largely wrong about the cause and misleading about the effect.
correct in outline but exaggerated in the size of its effect.
impossible to test, because shoppers cannot be tracked reliably.

why.A: The arrangement is said to be older than the marketing literature, and a small effect is conceded.
why.B: Correct — the layout is explained by the loading bay, and the selling is attributed instead to placement within reach.
why.C: The passage rejects the cause outright rather than merely scaling down the effect.
why.D: Tracking studies are cited as having produced usable findings.

context: According to the passage, the chillers are at the back of the shop because:

choices.text: the back of a building is naturally cooler than the front.
shoppers must be made to walk the full length of the aisles.
the loading bay is at the back, and the front faces the car park.
refrigeration equipment is too loud to place near the tills.

why.A: The passage makes no claim that one end of a building is cooler than the other.
why.B: That is the explanation the passage is arguing against.
why.C: Correct — the second paragraph gives exactly that chain, ending at the car park.
why.D: Noise from refrigeration equipment is never mentioned anywhere in the passage.

context: The passage implies that a shopper arriving with a written list would:

choices.text: spend longer in the shop than a shopper without one.
be more susceptible than most to displays placed beside the tills.
buy roughly the nine items of the familiar anecdote.
be among the least affected by the milk’s distance from the door.

why.A: A direct line through the shop implies less time, and duration is not measured anyway.
why.B: The till displays are offered as what works generally, not as something list-users are more prone to.
why.C: The nine items belong to the anecdote the passage says the research does not support.
why.D: Correct — the third paragraph calls planned shoppers extremely resistant, walking a direct line and buying what they came for.

context: The sentence about anyone who has worked in a shop naming the flaw serves to:

choices.text: introduce the practical objection that the rest of the paragraph develops.
suggest that academic researchers have overlooked obvious evidence.
establish the writer’s own experience of working in retail.
concede that the popular explanation is partly right.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph goes straight on to pallets, the lorry and the loading bay.
why.B: Researchers are credited later with careful findings and are not criticised.
why.C: The writer claims no such experience, attributing the knowledge to shop workers generally.
why.D: The concession comes in the third paragraph and concerns the effect, not the cause.

context: As it is used in the final paragraph, the word "flatters" most nearly means:

choices.text: smooths a surface by pressing it down.
tells each party something agreeable about itself.
praises someone insincerely in order to gain a favour.
makes something appear larger than it really is.

why.A: That is a sense of a different word and does not fit a story.
why.B: Correct — the two sentences after it say what the story tells the shopper and what it tells the retailer.
why.C: No one is seeking a favour; the story simply circulates.
why.D: Size is not what the story misrepresents in that paragraph.

context: In saying that the trap "is the last four feet of it," the writer means that unplanned buying is driven by:

choices.text: the short queue in which a shopper waits to pay.
the distance from the chillers to the checkouts.
what lies within arm’s reach at the moment of choosing.
the final aisle a shopper passes before the exit.

why.A: The queue is one of three positions listed, not the whole of the point.
why.B: That distance is the walked journey the passage has just dismissed.
why.C: Correct — the sentence before it says position within reach matters more than distance walked.
why.D: The claim covers eye-level ends of aisles and tills alike rather than one final aisle.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the popular explanation is best described as:

choices.text: hostile, treating those who repeat it as foolish.
neutral, presenting it beside the evidence without preference.
approving, finding it a useful simplification of the research.
sceptical, and interested in why it is so durable.

why.A: Nobody is mocked; the opening grants that everyone knows the explanation.
why.B: The writer calls it at best half true, which is a judgement.
why.C: It is treated as a distortion rather than a useful shorthand.
why.D: Correct — the last paragraph asks outright why the story survives and answers that it flatters everyone.

context: The passage proceeds by:

choices.text: stating a belief, refuting its cause, testing its effect, explaining its appeal.
comparing two supermarkets with different floor plans.
tracing the history of the supermarket layout from its origins to the present day.
presenting research findings and then drawing practical advice for shoppers.

why.A: Correct — the five paragraphs run in that order, ending with why the story flatters everyone.
why.B: Only one shop layout is described, and no second store is set beside it.
why.C: The only historical claim is that the layout predates the marketing literature.
why.D: No advice is offered to anyone.

context: Which finding best supports the claim that the walk itself does little selling?

choices.text: Shoppers without a list do buy a few per cent more.
Tracked shoppers on a planned trip look at almost nothing on the way.
Unplanned purchases cluster at eye level near the ends of aisles.
Milk arrives on pallets several times a week and must be chilled at once.

why.A: A measurable increase is evidence that the walk sells a little, not that it sells nothing.
why.B: Correct — if the walk sold, the people doing the most of it would not pass the shelves unseeing.
why.C: That shows where selling does happen, which is a different claim.
why.D: The pallets explain the layout rather than its effect on buying.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: the discovery that some beaches are far older than the coastlines beside them.
the difficulty of separating zircon from the other minerals in sand.
how dated zircon grains show where sand came from, and what they miss.
the process by which uranium decays into lead inside a crystal.

why.A: That is one striking result rather than the passage’s subject.
why.B: Separation is never described as difficult or described at all.
why.C: Correct — the middle paragraphs build the method and the last paragraph sets out its limits.
why.D: The decay is one sentence, included to explain why the grain carries a date.

context: According to the passage, when a zircon crystallises it:

choices.text: takes up lead and rejects uranium almost completely.
takes up equal amounts of uranium and lead.
takes up neither uranium nor lead until it is buried.
takes up uranium and rejects lead almost completely.

why.A: Reversing the two would destroy the dating method entirely.
why.B: Equal uptake would leave no way to tell decay from original content.
why.C: The uptake happens at crystallisation, not at burial.
why.D: Correct — the second paragraph states it in those words, which is why later lead must have grown there.

context: The passage suggests that a sand sample yielding only one sharp peak of ages would most likely indicate:

choices.text: a single dominant source region feeding the deposit.
a sample too small to be dated reliably.
a source rock that contained no zircon at all.
grains that had been recycled through many earlier cycles.

why.A: Correct — each peak is said to correspond to an episode of mountain building upstream, so one peak points to one such source.
why.B: Sample size is fixed at several hundred grains and is not tied to the shape of the spectrum.
why.C: A zircon-free source contributes no grains and so produces no peak.
why.D: Recycling is what makes a peak record an older rock, not what reduces the number of peaks.

context: The description of zircon as "stubborn" functions in the passage to:

choices.text: emphasise how rarely the mineral is found in ordinary sand.
explain why the grain’s date survives repeated transport and burial.
account for the hardness that makes the mineral so difficult to crush.
suggest that zircon resists the chemical treatment used to date it.

why.A: The same sentence calls the mineral common.
why.B: Correct — the sentence goes on to say it survives several cycles of mountain, river and seabed without being reset.
why.C: Hardness is listed separately, in the clause before it.
why.D: The dating is presented as straightforward once grains are picked out.

context: As it is used in the second paragraph, the word "reset" most nearly means:

choices.text: being remounted for laboratory examination.
having its shape worn down by transport.
having its internal clock returned to zero.
being moved to a new geological setting.

why.A: Laboratory handling is described in the next paragraph and is unrelated.
why.B: Wear would alter the grain’s shape without touching its age.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph is about the date locked into the grain, so what survives is the record of its crystallisation.
why.D: Moving between settings is exactly what the grain does while not being reset.

context: The statement that a beach "is the end of a queue" chiefly conveys that:

choices.text: its sand is deposited in an orderly sequence along the shore.
new grains must wait for older ones to be washed away.
coastlines form one after another in a predictable order.
its grains arrived after a long journey begun in distant places.

why.A: No ordering of grains along the shore is described.
why.B: Nothing in the passage has grains waiting for room.
why.C: The sequence being described belongs to the sediment, not to coastlines.
why.D: Correct — it follows the example of grains from rocks two thousand kilometres away and closes the paragraph denying that a beach is made by its own coastline.

context: The passage’s attitude toward the zircon method is best described as:

choices.text: enthusiastic about its reach and frank about what it cannot show.
doubtful that the ages obtained can be trusted.
detached, describing the procedure without appraising it.
critical, holding that its limits outweigh what it reveals.

why.A: Correct — results are called regularly startling, and the last paragraph names the biases plainly.
why.B: The dates themselves are never questioned; what is qualified is what a distribution represents.
why.C: Judgements run through the passage, from stubborn to startling.
why.D: The limits are called the ordinary ones, and the method is still evidence.

context: The passage develops by:

choices.text: recounting the history of the method in the order of its refinements.
naming the puzzle, the mineral that solves it, the method, the results, the limits.
weighing zircon dating against two rival techniques for the same job.
following a single sand sample from its collection through to its publication.

why.A: No chronology of the method is given.
why.B: Correct — the five paragraphs run in exactly that order, ending on what the distribution cannot say.
why.C: No dating technique other than the zircon method is mentioned at any point.
why.D: The sample in the third paragraph is generic, and no publication is described.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that a zircon spectrum can under-represent a real source?

choices.text: Grains may be eighteen hundred million years old.
Each peak corresponds to an episode of mountain building upstream.
A basalt province producing almost no zircon can be invisible in the distribution.
Several hundred grains are picked from a single sample and dated one by one.

why.A: An old age shows the method’s reach rather than a gap in it.
why.B: That is the claim about what the peaks do show.
why.C: Correct — a source that contributed sediment while leaving no grains is precisely a source the spectrum misses.
why.D: The sampling procedure says nothing about which sources are represented.

context: The passage distinguishes a distribution of ages from a single date mainly to show that:

choices.text: individual grains cannot be dated with useful precision.
averaging the grains would give the age of the beach itself.
older grains are more reliable than younger ones.
one sand sample records several separate sources at once.

why.A: Grains are dated individually, and their precision is never questioned.
why.B: No average is taken, and the beach is explicitly not made by its own coastline.
why.C: Reliability is never tied to a grain’s age.
why.D: Correct — the third paragraph says what comes back is not a number but a spectrum, whose peaks are close to a fingerprint of the sources.

context: The passage is best described as:

choices.text: a daughter’s portrait of her father’s craft, its limits, and what he left behind.
an argument that hand-painted signs are better than machine-cut lettering.
an account of how a family business was driven under by new technology.
a history of sign painting as a trade, from its origins to its slow decline in towns.

why.A: Correct — the passage moves from his work and his one skill, the edge, to what the machine did better, to his retirement and the emptied brushes she keeps.
why.B: The fourth paragraph grants that the vinyl letters were better on the bakery window, and the father himself scorned people who claimed handwork was better at everything.
why.C: He stops because his hand begins to shake, not because the work dried up; the jobs nobody had modernised kept coming to him.
why.D: Only one painter and one career are described, and no earlier history of the trade is given.

context: According to the passage, the father stopped working because:

choices.text: the bakery and the pharmacy had replaced their painted signs.
his daughter chose not to take over the business from him.
sentimental customers had begun to complain about his prices.
a slight shake in his hand had spoiled the stroke.

why.A: Those changes had already happened in his last ten years of work, and he kept working through them.
why.B: The narrator says she did not become a sign painter, but this is never given as a reason for his stopping.
why.C: Those complaints are mentioned as something he answered sharply, not as the reason he retired.
why.D: Correct — the sixth paragraph says his hand had begun to shake a little, enough that the stroke was no longer one stroke.

context: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word “outlast” most nearly means:

choices.text: move faster than.
sell better than.
last longer than.
look brighter than.

why.A: Speed plays no part in the sentence; the comparison is about how long each kind of lettering survives.
why.B: Nothing is said about sales. The point is durability in the sun.
why.C: Correct — the vinyl would stay on the window longer, because sunlight fades enamel and does very little to vinyl.
why.D: Brightness is not the comparison; fading is mentioned only as the reason painted letters would wear out first.

context: When the narrator says her father solved “a problem that did not exist on paper,” she means the problem:

choices.text: had never been written about by any other sign painter.
appeared only on a real curved hull seen from a particular spot.
was invented by the boat’s owner to test his skill.
could be solved only by working without any written plan or drawing at all.

why.A: The phrase is about where the problem arises, not about whether anyone had recorded it.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph explains that a hull curves in two directions and the name must read straight from the quay, so the difficulty exists only in the actual boat and viewpoint.
why.C: No owner sets him a test; the difficulty comes from the shape of the hull.
why.D: He does make a plan of sorts, a chalk line; the point is that a flat drawing could not show the problem at all.

context: In the fourth paragraph, the narrator’s attitude toward machine-cut lettering is best described as:

choices.text: fair-minded, granting that it had real advantages.
resentful, blaming it for taking her father’s best customers.
nostalgic, wishing the bakery had kept its painted sign.
contemptuous, treating vinyl as cheap and lifeless.

why.A: Correct — she says outright that the machine was not the enemy, and that the vinyl was perfectly straight and would outlast anything her father painted there.
why.B: The opening line of the paragraph refuses exactly this reading: she will not pretend the machine was the enemy.
why.C: She never regrets the bakery’s choice, and her father himself called the vinyl very good.
why.D: The only judgement given of the vinyl is praise, from the narrator and from her father.

context: The statement that the father “had no patience for people who pretended that handwork was better at everything” serves mainly to:

choices.text: explain why he charged sentimental customers more than others.
suggest that he resented the customers who kept him in work.
reveal that he privately preferred machine-cut signs to his own.
show that his praise of the vinyl letters was sincere, not merely polite.

why.A: Nothing suggests he set different prices; those customers complained about the ordinary price.
why.B: His impatience is with a particular claim, not with the people who hired him in general.
why.C: He thought the machine better at some things, not at everything; the boat shows what it could not do.
why.D: Correct — it follows “He meant it,” and explains why he could call a rival’s work very good without irony.

context: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.text: It alternates between the narrator’s childhood summer in the shop and the present-day job she holds now.
