It compares two sign painters who took opposite views of new technology and follows how each one fared.
It moves from the father’s trade and skill, to the machine’s strengths and limits, to his retirement.
It follows a single commission, the lettering of one boat, from the first request to the finished hull.

why.A: The present-day job appears once, in the final paragraph; there is no back-and-forth.
why.B: Only one sign painter appears, and his view of the machine is mixed rather than opposed to anyone’s.
why.C: Correct — the paragraphs run in that order, from the brushes and the edge, through the bakery and the boat, to the biscuit tin.
why.D: The boat is one episode among several; the passage covers his last ten years and beyond.

context: According to the passage, unlike the vinyl lettering, the father’s painting could:

choices.text: resist fading in strong sunlight.
be laid out to read straight on a curved hull.
be finished from start to end within a single afternoon.
keep its spacing perfectly even.

why.A: The passage says the opposite: sun fades enamel and does very little to vinyl.
why.B: Correct — the fifth paragraph opens by saying that what the machine could not do was the boat.
why.C: That is said of the bakery’s vinyl banner, cut by a machine in an afternoon.
why.D: Perfect spacing is credited to the vinyl letters on the bakery window.

context: Which detail best shows that the father’s rule about rinsing brushes twice had a practical purpose?

choices.text: A brush put away with paint in its heel will never again make a clean edge.
The narrator spent most of that July cleaning brushes.
His brushes were stored in a biscuit tin on a shelf in the garage.
The narrator first took it for a rule old men invent to keep children busy.

why.A: Correct — the second paragraph explains that the second rinse clears the heel, and that an uncleaned heel ruins the brush for the one thing he sold.
why.B: This shows how long the lesson took to learn, not why the rule mattered.
why.C: Where the brushes ended up says nothing about the reason for rinsing them.
why.D: That is the narrator’s mistaken early view, which the rest of the paragraph corrects.

context: The narrator’s uncertainty about why she keeps the tin suggests that she:

choices.text: intends one day to take up sign painting with the brushes.
regrets that her father never taught her how to lay down the stroke herself.
believes the brushes have been damaged by years of storage.
values the evidence of her father’s care as much as the brushes themselves.

why.A: She says she did not become a sign painter, and nothing suggests she plans to.
why.B: Regret about the lesson is a natural guess, but the passage never raises it; her question is about the tin.
why.C: She reports that the heel of a brush is still soft, which is the sign of a brush in good condition.
why.D: Correct — she wonders whether she keeps it for what it holds or for how carefully it was emptied, and the brushes are still soft because he cleaned them.

context: The passage is primarily about:

choices.text: a family story about a near-drowning that was retold, as a joke, every Christmas.
the methods a trained lifeguard uses to teach adults how to float.
a daughter learning that an old fear, not ignorance, held her mother back.
a friendship between an elderly swimmer and a woman learning to swim.

why.A: The lake story is central to one paragraph, but it matters as the key to the mother’s difficulty, not as the passage’s subject.
why.B: The methods are listed only to show that they did not work.
why.C: Correct — the closing paragraph says the true explanations missed the point, because the mother never doubted she would float; the lake memory was the real obstacle.
why.D: The old man makes one remark and demonstrates a breath; no friendship is described.

context: According to the passage, who first remarks on the way the mother holds her breath?

choices.text: the narrator, during their first lesson
an old man swimming in the next lane
the instructor of the aqua-aerobics class
the mother’s younger brother

why.A: The narrator tried many explanations, but breath was not among them; that is the point of the old man’s remark.
why.B: Correct — the fourth paragraph says an eight o’clock swimmer stopped at the wall and spoke to her.
why.C: The aqua-aerobics class is mentioned only as what came before their Tuesday sessions.
why.D: The brother appears only in the story of the lake, years before.

context: The comparison of the mother to “a dog carrying a stick” describes:

choices.text: the way she held her head up out of the water as she swam.
her eagerness to fetch the float board for each lesson.
how quickly she was able to cross the pool.
her habit of bringing things from home to the baths.

why.A: Correct — the same sentence says she swam with her chin held high, and the image pictures exactly that.
why.B: The image comes in the description of her swimming a length, not of any equipment.
why.C: The sentence says she swam badly; speed is not what the image describes.
why.D: Nothing she carries to the pool is mentioned.

context: The narrator’s remark that her mother found most explanations “correct and useless” anticipates the passage’s later point that:

choices.text: the mother distrusted her daughter’s training as a lifeguard.
a float board and a foam buoy are the wrong equipment for adult learners.
the old man’s advice was no more accurate than the narrator’s.
the facts about floating were true but did not touch the real difficulty.

why.A: The mother chose her daughter as teacher and never questions her training.
why.B: The equipment is one item in a list of attempts, and it is not singled out as the problem.
why.C: The old man’s remark is what finally helps, so the passage does not rank it with her explanations.
why.D: Correct — the final paragraph says everything the narrator told her was true and none of it was what she needed.

context: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: defensive, insisting that her methods would have worked in time.
bitter that a stranger succeeded where she had failed.
rueful, admitting that true advice had missed what mattered.
triumphant at her mother’s eventual success in the pool.

why.A: She makes no such claim; she says none of it was what her mother needed.
why.B: The old man is presented gratefully, and no resentment toward him appears.
why.C: Correct — she reflects on how little her explanations had to do with it, while standing by the fact that they were true.
why.D: The mother’s progress is reported in the paragraph before; the last paragraph is about the narrator’s mistake.

context: The description of the mother’s standing up as “quicker and quieter than panic” serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that the mother was not really afraid of the water at all.
suggest an old, automatic response rather than fear felt in the moment.
criticise the mother for refusing to try harder in the lessons her daughter gave.
contrast the mother with the lane swimmers who arrived at eight.

why.A: The sentence denies that it was panic, not that fear was involved; the lake memory shows fear lay underneath.
why.B: Correct — the narrator calls it a kind of reflex, as though her legs decided without consulting her, which prepares for the memory revealed later.
why.C: She did everything asked of her at the side; the narrator describes the reflex without blame.
why.D: The lane swimmers are mentioned in the first paragraph and are not compared with her here.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: Failed lessons, a stranger’s remark, a memory revealed, slow progress, and a reflection.
A childhood memory first, followed by the adult events it explains, in order.
A comparison of two methods of teaching swimming, ending with a verdict on which is better.
A single evening at the pool, told in the order in which it happened.

why.A: Correct — the paragraphs follow that order, from the first three weeks to the narrator’s closing thoughts.
why.B: The childhood memory appears in the fifth paragraph, after the lessons have already been described.
why.C: Only the narrator’s methods are described, and the old man offers a remark rather than a method.
why.D: The passage runs from January to the following summer.

context: The old man’s remark differs from the narrator’s explanations chiefly in that the remark:

choices.text: drew on formal training that the narrator did not have.
was spoken to the narrator rather than to her mother.
was repeated every Tuesday until the mother understood it.
was about what she did with her breath, not what her body would do.

why.A: Nothing is said about his training, while the narrator had been a lifeguard.
why.B: The passage stresses the reverse: he did not say anything to the narrator, and spoke to her mother.
why.C: He speaks once, in the fourth week, and she laughs at it at once.
why.D: Correct — the narrator explained that the body floats; the old man noticed that she was holding her breath as though saving it.

context: Which detail best supports the narrator’s conclusion that her mother’s difficulty was not doubt about floating?

choices.text: She could float face-down for a count of five with a hand under her.
She would do anything she was asked at the side of the pool.
She thought of her brother every time the water came up past her chin.
She refused every suggestion about the style of her stroke.

why.A: This shows she could float with support, but it does not show what stopped her once the hand moved away.
why.B: Her willingness shows she was cooperative, not what lay behind her standing up.
why.C: Correct — this ties her reflex to the lake, which is what the last paragraph means by nobody having to go in after her.
why.D: That comes after she could already swim and concerns her stroke, not her fear.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the family’s Christmas version of the lake story:

choices.text: was invented to amuse the younger children.
left out what the event had meant to the mother as a child.
was usually told by the mother herself.
exaggerated how badly the brother had been hurt.

why.A: The event happened; nobody was hurt, and it was retold, not invented.
why.B: Correct — it was told as a funny story about the man’s ruined shoes, while the mother still thought of it whenever water reached her chin.
why.C: Who told it at Christmas is not said, only that she had never told it any other way.
why.D: The passage says nobody was hurt, and the Christmas version dwelt on the shoes.

context: The central idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: a good method depends on knowing what kind of thing is being counted.
counting every single item is the only reliable way to take stock.
older workers are always more accurate than younger ones.
stocktaking is dull work that no one can ever do perfectly.

why.A: Correct — Mrs Okafor says the trick was knowing which kind of thing was in front of you, and the narrator ends by praising exactly that judgement.
why.B: The hinge box shows an exact count missing an error that weighing caught.
why.C: Mrs Okafor’s counts are admitted to be slightly wrong; the point is her judgement, not her age.
why.D: The narrator hoped it could be done perfectly, but the passage is about choosing a method, not about dullness.

context: According to the passage, Mrs Okafor counted boxes of screws by:

choices.text: moving them across the counter in fives with a ruler.
tipping each box out and counting the screws in tens.
copying the previous year’s figures onto the sheet.
weighing ten screws and then the box, and dividing.

why.A: That is the narrator’s method, described in the third paragraph.
why.B: She did not tip boxes out at all; she weighed them.
why.C: She consulted last year only in noting that she had marked the hinge box as light.
why.D: Correct — the fourth paragraph describes the brass scale and exactly this procedure.

context: As it is used in the second paragraph, the word “deferred” most nearly means:

choices.text: put off a decision about.
handed extra work to.
gave way to the judgement of.
paid a higher wage to.

why.A: That is the everyday sense of “defer,” but the sentence is about whom he yielded to, not what he postponed.
why.B: Nothing suggests he passed his duties to her; the sentence is about her authority.
why.C: Correct — Mrs Okafor was the only person whose view Mr Drummond accepted over his own.
why.D: Pay is never mentioned; the sentence describes respect for her judgement.

context: Mrs Okafor’s remark that the narrator was “going to be there until Wednesday” is a way of saying that:

choices.text: the stocktake had been scheduled to last until the middle of the next week.
counting every box by hand would take far longer than the day allowed.
the narrator would be kept late as a punishment.
she planned to check the narrator’s counts later in the week.

why.A: The stocktake took place on a single Sunday.
why.B: Correct — she says it after noting that she had done four shelves to the narrator’s one, with about three hundred boxes in the aisle.
why.C: She says it kindly, over a cup of tea, with no suggestion of blame.
why.D: She never proposes checking the narrator’s work.

context: The narrator says that the claim about Mrs Okafor’s numbers was made “more sharply than I meant to.” At that moment the narrator’s tone was:

choices.text: defensive and somewhat irritated.
amused by her method.
apologetic about the slow pace.
indifferent to the outcome.

why.A: Correct — “sharply” marks the remark as an edge of irritation at being outpaced.
why.B: Nothing is said lightly; the narrator is disputing her method.
why.C: The narrator goes on counting out of pride, which is the opposite of apology.
why.D: The narrator cares enough to argue and then to keep counting.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward Mrs Okafor in the final paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: resentful that she had been proved right about the hinges.
dismissive, treating her method as a shortcut the narrator has since outgrown.
neutral, reporting her habits without any judgement of them.
admiring of her judgement, which included knowing when to count one at a time.

why.A: The paragraph begins by saying she was not smug, and the narrator shows no grievance.
why.B: Weighing is presented as right for identical items, and the narrator praises her for knowing which items those were.
why.C: The final sentence is a strong judgement: very few people could have done what she did.
why.D: Correct — the narrator stresses that she counted the mixed hooks exactly as the narrator did, and ends by calling her rare.

context: The episode of the brass hinges mainly serves to:

choices.text: prove that Mrs Okafor’s counts were more precise than the narrator’s.
reveal that the shop’s labels were unreliable throughout.
show that an exact count can miss an error that weighing catches.
explain why Mr Drummond trusted Mrs Okafor above everyone.

why.A: She admits that her counts are off by a few; what she caught was the wrong metal, not a more precise number.
why.B: One box was mislabelled; nothing suggests the problem was widespread.
why.C: Correct — the narrator would have counted thirty correctly and never noticed the steel, while the box felt wrong in Mrs Okafor’s hand.
why.D: His trust is stated in the second paragraph, before the hinges appear, and is not tied to them.

context: The passage is organized mainly by:

choices.text: tracing the narrator’s career from the shop to later jobs in detail.
setting two methods side by side, testing them, and drawing a lesson.
describing the shop, the procedure, and then the year’s accounts.
presenting Mrs Okafor’s argument first and then the narrator’s rebuttal of it.

why.A: Later jobs are mentioned in one sentence at the end.
why.B: Correct — the narrator’s counting and Mrs Okafor’s weighing are described, the hinge box tests them, and the final paragraph draws the lesson.
why.C: The accounts are mentioned only in Mrs Okafor’s argument, never presented.
why.D: The narrator’s objection comes first and is answered by her, not the reverse.

context: According to Mrs Okafor, her count would differ from the narrator’s in that hers would be:

choices.text: roughly right for the whole aisle, where the narrator’s would cover only part.
exact for every box she counted, where the narrator’s would contain small errors.
quicker to check against the accounts afterward.
approved by Mr Drummond, where the narrator’s would not.

why.A: Correct — she says the narrator would have a perfect count of a third of the shop and she a decent count of all of it.
why.B: This reverses her claim; she admits her own counts are off by a few.
why.C: She says nobody could find the difference in the accounts, not that checking was quicker.
why.D: Mr Drummond’s approval is never discussed in the argument.

context: Which detail best supports Mrs Okafor’s claim that the errors in weighed counts do little harm?

choices.text: She weighed a box twice whenever it felt wrong in her hand.
By eleven o’clock she had done four shelves to the narrator’s one.
She had marked the box of hinges as light the year before.
Nobody had ever been able to find the difference in the accounts.

why.A: That shows her care in weighing, not that the leftover errors were harmless.
why.B: Speed is a separate advantage and says nothing about the cost of her errors.
why.C: This shows weighing catching a mistake, not that its own errors were small.
why.D: Correct — if the small errors cancelled so nearly that the accounts never showed them, they did no practical harm.

context: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.text: workers who do not join a pension have knowingly chosen the present over the future.
automatic enrolment is a costless way to steer people toward saving.
how a saving choice is framed shapes behaviour, and no framing of it is neutral.
most workers do not understand how pension contributions work.

why.A: This is the economists’ reading the passage sets out to undercut.
why.B: The sixth paragraph describes a cost, and the seventh says behaviour cannot be steered for free.
why.C: Correct — the passage builds from the switch to automatic enrolment to the conclusion that there is no neutral form.
why.D: Not understanding the options is one survey answer, and the passage does not endorse it as the explanation.

context: According to the passage, after firms switched to automatic enrolment, participation among new hires rose to about:

choices.text: one in two.
nine in ten.
three per cent.
one in three.

why.A: Around half is where participation had often been before the switch.
why.B: Correct — the third paragraph says it rose to something close to nine in ten and stayed there.
why.C: Three per cent is the example of a default contribution rate, not a participation figure.
why.D: No such figure appears in the passage.

context: The passage implies that the economists who read survey answers as preferences were mistaken because:

choices.text: the same kind of workers acted differently when only the ticked box changed.
the workers had lied to the surveyors about their finances.
the surveys had questioned workers at the wrong firms.
most of the workers could not in fact afford to save anything.

why.A: Correct — if non-joiners had truly preferred the present, they would have opted out in numbers; they did not, so the answers were not preferences.
why.B: The final paragraph says the surveys were not wrong about what people said.
why.C: The passage raises no problem with who was surveyed.
why.D: If they could not afford it, they would have opted out after automatic enrolment, and most did not.

context: The example of two workers hired in March and May at neighbouring desks serves to:

choices.text: show that the workers hired in May were better paid.
explain why some firms delayed switching to automatic enrolment.
suggest that workers at neighbouring desks compared their pensions with each other.
show that outcomes differed even though the workers themselves did not.

why.A: Their jobs are described as the same; pay is not compared.
why.B: The hiring date marks when the switch applied, not a delay.
why.C: No conversation between the two is described.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph ends by saying it is difficult to argue the May recruits cared more about their old age.

context: By calling “I meant to get round to it” “a precise description of a decision nobody had made,” the writer suggests that workers who did not join had:

choices.text: deliberately misled the surveyors about their intentions.
made a careful decision that they preferred not to explain.
never actually chosen against saving; they had simply not acted.
planned to join the pension as soon as their pay rose.

why.A: The writer says the surveys were not wrong about what people said.
why.B: The phrase says that no decision had been made at all.
why.C: Correct — the automatic-enrolment results show that no preference had been formed, so the survey answer was literally accurate: nothing had been decided.
why.D: Pay rises are never mentioned as part of their thinking.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the automatic-enrolment finding is best described as:

choices.text: dismissive, treating the finding as an overstated fashion.
appreciative of its importance but wary of how simply it is told.
wholly enthusiastic, seeing it as proof that defaults cost nobody anything.
neutral, reporting the results without judging them.

why.A: The writer credits it with millions of people saving who would not otherwise have been.
why.B: Correct — the writer says it is usually told too simply, describes its cost, and then insists that none of this makes it less important.
why.C: The sixth paragraph describes exactly such a cost.
why.D: The passage judges throughout, calling the popular version shaky and the finding important.

context: The passage is structured as:

choices.text: a reading, a change that undercuts it, a caution, a cost, and a return to the opening.
a history of workplace pensions from their origins in the last century to the present day.
two rival theories of why people save, weighed evenly side by side.
a problem, a list of possible solutions, and a recommendation addressed to employers.

why.A: Correct — it moves from the economists’ reading, through the switch and its results, to the simplified story and its cost, and ends back at the surveys.
why.B: The passage covers only the change from opting in to opting out.
why.C: The economists’ reading is overturned rather than weighed evenly.
why.D: No list of solutions and no recommendation to employers is offered.

context: The passage separates inertia from “the quiet message a default sends.” Unlike inertia, that message can explain why:

choices.text: workers who were enrolled automatically failed to return the opt-out form.
participation rose so sharply among new hires.
older workers were slower than younger ones to join.
some workers who would have saved more stayed at the default rate.

why.A: Not returning a form is what inertia alone would explain.
why.B: Both inertia and the message could produce this; it does not separate them.
why.C: Age is mentioned only in who gained most, not as a difference in speed.
why.D: Correct — the sixth paragraph ties those workers to the default being read as advice, which inertia alone would not predict.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that automatic enrolment helped those least likely to join on their own?

choices.text: Participation stayed close to nine in ten.
The default contribution rate was three per cent.
The gain is concentrated among younger and lower-paid workers.
The firms held no seminars on compound interest.

why.A: This shows the size of the gain, not who received it.
why.B: The rate is an example of the message a default sends, not evidence about who benefited.
why.C: Correct — the seventh paragraph says these were the workers least likely to fill in the form.
why.D: This shows how little else changed, not who gained.

context: Which finding best supports the writer’s claim that automatic enrolment has a cost?

choices.text: Workers who would not fill in a form to join did not fill one in to leave.
Many workers who would have chosen a higher rate stayed at the default.
Participation among new hires had often hovered around half.
The firms did not make their pensions any more generous.

why.A: This is the evidence that the switch worked, not that it cost anything.
why.B: Correct — the sixth paragraph says the box raised the number of savers and, for some of them, lowered the amount saved.
why.C: This is the starting point before the switch.
why.D: This shows the comparison was fair, not that the default had a cost.

context: The main idea of the passage is that overdue fines:

choices.text: mostly drove away poorer borrowers rather than speeding returns.
were abolished mainly out of sympathy for struggling borrowers.
must be kept, since without them borrowers hold on to books much longer.
raised money that libraries can no longer afford to lose.

why.A: Correct — the passage finds that fines sorted borrowers and mainly produced absence, and that returns held up when they were dropped.
why.B: The second paragraph says the libraries’ reasons were not sentimental.
why.C: Return rates held roughly steady; only a small rise in items a few days late is noted.
why.D: The money collected is described as small, often less than the cost of collecting it.

context: According to the passage, unpaid fines were found to cluster:

choices.text: among borrowers of popular new titles.
in libraries with the longest opening hours.
among adults who borrowed the most books.
among children and in the poorest neighbourhoods.

why.A: Popular titles appear only in the discussion of books kept a few days late.
why.B: Longer opening hours are mentioned as a separate change, not as where debts clustered.
why.C: Heavy borrowers are never identified as the ones who owed.
why.D: Correct — the second paragraph says exactly this.

context: As it is used in the final paragraph, the word “lenient” most nearly means:

choices.text: efficient.
wealthy.
forgiving.
popular.

why.A: The sentence contrasts “lenient” with “accurate,” not with “wasteful.”
why.B: Money is not the point of the closing sentence.
why.C: Correct — the sentence denies that the libraries simply became softer on borrowers.
why.D: The sentence is about how the libraries treat borrowers, not how they are regarded.

context: When the writer says that for some borrowers the fine “was a closed door,” the point is that the fine:

choices.text: was collected only when the library was closed.
kept them from using the library at all.
could be paid only in person at the desk.
was never properly explained to them.

why.A: The fine was collected at a desk during opening hours.
why.B: Correct — the sentences before it describe a child with a blocked card who is not brought back.
why.C: How the fine was paid is not the point of the image.
why.D: The problem described is the cost, not confusion about it.

context: The writer’s view of abolishing fines is best described as:

choices.text: supportive, while admitting costs and gaps in the evidence.
enthusiastic, seeing no drawbacks in it for libraries at all.
sceptical that return rates really held steady.
neutral, declining to draw any conclusion.

why.A: Correct — the sixth paragraph lists lost books, late popular titles and confounding changes, and the seventh still calls the direction of the evidence hard to miss.
why.B: The writer explicitly says it would be too neat to stop at the good news.
why.C: The steady returns are reported without doubt.
why.D: The closing paragraphs draw a firm conclusion about what fines were for.

context: The detail about books arriving “with notes of apology tucked inside” serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that the borrowers had deliberately stolen the books they kept.
suggest that the fines had been set too low to matter.
show that the returns chute was poorly supervised.
illustrate that shame over debts had kept borrowers and books away.

why.A: The books had been kept out of embarrassment, not stolen.
why.B: The shame described implies the sums mattered a great deal to those who owed them.
why.C: The chute is simply where the books arrived.
why.D: Correct — the sentence before describes borrowers ashamed of the sum who came back once it was forgiven.

context: The sixth paragraph functions mainly to:

choices.text: reverse the passage’s argument by showing that fines had worked after all.
propose charging fines only on popular new titles.
qualify the case against fines by noting costs and confounding changes.
explain why libraries no longer charge for lost books.

why.A: The next paragraph resumes the argument, calling the evidence hard to miss.
why.B: Popular titles are named as a case where lateness matters more, but no such policy is proposed.
why.C: Correct — it notes lost-book charges, late popular titles, and other changes introduced at the same time.
why.D: The paragraph says most libraries still do charge for lost books.

context: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.text: A history of one library system from its founding until the day it closed its doors.
The case for fines, evidence against it, their real role, caveats, and a conclusion.
A comparison of two cities that took opposite approaches to overdue fines.
A list of objections to abolishing fines, each answered in turn by the writer.

why.A: Many library systems are discussed, and none is followed from its founding.
why.B: Correct — the paragraphs run from the rationale for fines to what they turned out to do, then qualify and conclude.
why.C: Only one city is singled out, and no opposing city is described.
why.D: The objections come together in one paragraph and are conceded rather than answered.

context: According to the passage, fines were meant to prompt punctual returns but in practice mainly:

choices.text: sorted out those who could pay from those who stayed away.
raised money that paid for the libraries’ longer opening hours.
encouraged borrowers to renew their books online.
reduced the waiting lists for new titles.

why.A: Correct — the fifth paragraph says those who could pay kept borrowing and those who could not quietly left.
why.B: Longer hours are a separate change, and the money raised is called small.
why.C: Automatic renewals are another change, not an effect of fines.
why.D: Waiting lists are raised only as a caveat to abolishing fines.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that fines mainly produced absence?

choices.text: The money collected was often less than the cost of the staff time spent collecting it.
Some libraries saw more items returned a few days late.
Return rates held roughly steady after fines were abolished.
In one system, those owing most were the least likely to have visited that year.

why.A: This shows fines were a poor source of money, not that they kept people away.
why.B: This is a cost of abolishing fines, not evidence about what fines did.
why.C: Steady returns show abolition was safe, but not that fines had driven people off.
why.D: Correct — this links the debts directly to borrowers who had stopped coming.

context: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

choices.text: show that closing a street to cars usually fails in the long run.
defend shopkeepers who object to closures.
argue that the evidence for closures is weaker than it looks.
propose a plan for closing streets in poorer towns.

why.A: Passage B says plainly that none of this means closures fail.
why.B: Shopkeepers’ objections are raised in Passage A, not defended in Passage B.
why.C: Correct — Passage B says the evidence usually offered is weaker than its confidence suggests.
why.D: Passage B asks for better evidence, not a plan.

context: Passage A suggests that its writer would respond to a paint shop losing trade after a closure by:

choices.text: recommending that the street be reopened to traffic for the shop’s sake.
treating it as a sign of poor planning, not a reason to keep cars.
arguing that the shop should move out of the town.
doubting that the shop had really lost any of its customers at all.

why.A: Passage A says the answer is not to leave the street to traffic.
why.B: Correct — Passage A says a closure without loading bays or nearby parking is planned badly, and the answer is to plan it well.
why.C: Relocation is never suggested.
why.D: Passage A grants that heavy-goods shops can lose customers.

context: In Passage A, the remark that “complaints are what a shopkeeper hears” helps explain why shopkeepers:

choices.text: overestimate how many customers arrive by car.
dislike pedestrian streets in general.
raise their prices after a closure.
rarely answer the surveys taken about their trade.

why.A: Correct — the drivers are the ones who complain about parking, so they loom larger than they are.
why.B: The remark explains a mistaken estimate, not a general dislike.
why.C: Prices are never mentioned.
why.D: The surveys mentioned stop people on the pavement, not shopkeepers.

context: Passage B’s warning that a closed street “may simply be a quieter struggling street” suggests that:

choices.text: closures make streets less noisy and therefore more pleasant.
shopkeepers on such streets tend to complain less.
struggling streets lose visitors after a closure.
removing cars may leave a weak street’s real problems untouched.

why.A: Quiet is mentioned, but the point is that it does not cure the struggle.
why.B: Shopkeepers are not the subject of the image.
why.C: The image says the street stays as it was, not that it gets worse.
why.D: Correct — the image says the closure changes the noise, not the decline, for towns with half-empty streets and little money.

context: Passage B’s attitude toward street closures is best described as:

choices.text: hostile, treating closures as a mistake in most of the towns that try them.
enthusiastic about closures in towns with little money.
guarded, granting that some succeed but questioning the evidence.
indifferent to whether closures succeed or fail.

why.A: The writer denies that closures fail and praises some of them.
why.B: Those are the towns the writer says the evidence tells us least about.
why.C: Correct — the writer says some plainly succeed and would not want to drive through them again, but calls the evidence weaker than it looks.
why.D: The writer cares enough to say what evidence would be persuasive.

context: Passage A is organized mainly by:

choices.text: presenting research findings in the order in which they were first published.
answering an objection, describing a closure’s effects, and conceding a limit.
comparing two named towns that reached opposite decisions about closure.
following a single closure from the first proposal through to its completion.

why.A: No dates of publication are given.
why.B: Correct — the shopkeepers’ fear, the effects on footfall and rents, and the heavy-goods concession come in that order.
why.C: No particular towns are named or compared.
why.D: The passage speaks of closures in general.

context: Both writers would most likely agree that:

choices.text: some closures succeed.
shopkeepers are usually right that their customers drive.
the evidence for closures is fully convincing.
towns choose which streets to close more or less at random.

why.A: Correct — Passage A reports rising footfall and rents, and Passage B says some closures plainly succeed.
why.B: Passage A calls this fear mistaken, and Passage B does not take it up.
why.C: Passage B calls it weaker than its confidence suggests.
why.D: Passage B says towns do not choose at random.

context: The writer of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A’s point that rents on closed streets rose within two years by saying that:

choices.text: rents always rise over time, so a two-year rise in rents means nothing at all.
landlords are the best judges of whether trade on a street has really improved.
rising rents prove the shopkeepers were wrong to object in the first place.
the rise may reflect new paving and well-chosen streets, not the absence of cars.

why.A: Passage B makes no general claim about rents.
why.B: That is Passage A’s reasoning, not a response to it.
why.C: Passage B does not take sides with Passage A on the shopkeepers.
why.D: Correct — Passage B says closed streets are chosen because they already look promising, and that new paving and publicity may deserve the credit.

context: Passage A asks “whether the street as a whole will be more used.” Passage B would most likely object that this question:

choices.text: is impossible to answer without counting footfall.
matters less than whether shopkeepers approve.
ignores the streets and residents that the gains may come from.
favours the towns that have little money.

why.A: Passage B does not doubt that footfall can be counted.
why.B: Shopkeepers’ approval is not Passage B’s concern.
why.C: Correct — Passage B says footfall is drawn from surrounding streets and traffic moves to the road behind, and that counting the plaza alone counts the winners.
why.D: Passage B worries that those towns are the least studied, not the most favoured.

context: Which detail in Passage B best supports the claim that a council may be “counting the winners”?

choices.text: Towns close streets that already have heavy foot traffic.
Shops on the surrounding streets rarely feature in the evaluation.
Some closures plainly succeed.
Councils that close streets have money for benches.

why.A: This supports a different point, the selection problem.
why.B: Correct — if trade was drawn from nearby streets that are never measured, only the gains are counted.
why.C: This is a concession, not support for the charge.
why.D: This concerns why closed streets look good, not whom the count leaves out.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: What a recipe card leaves out, read closely, records what its writer could take for granted.
Printed recipes preserve a cook’s knowledge far better than handwritten cards do.
The grandmother kept careless records that her family can no longer use.
A family recipe can be fully recovered by testing it against printed versions.

why.A: Correct — the passage argues that the cards’ silences are information and ends by saying they show what one woman already knew.
why.B: The fourth paragraph calls the printed recipe a different achievement from the card’s, “and not simply a better one.”
why.C: The second paragraph says treating the cards as failed documents “gets them backward.”
why.D: The fifth paragraph says the added steps made the bread more reliable without making it any more hers.

context: According to the passage, the card headed “Sunday” contains:

choices.text: four ingredients and no quantities.
an oven temperature in an outdated unit.
a grocer’s name written in the margin in pencil.
one instruction and nothing more.

why.A: That describes the card for soda bread.
why.B: That describes the card for a lemon cake.
why.C: That is on the gingerbread card, next to the changed amounts of treacle.
why.D: Correct — the first paragraph says it holds the single instruction “start the night before,” and nothing else at all.

context: The narrator says that writing down what the body already knew “would have been like writing down how to hold a spoon.” The comparison suggests that those steps were:

choices.text: too complicated to explain in writing.
meant to be taught only to children.
too familiar to the cook to seem worth recording.
kept secret from anyone outside the immediate family circle.

why.A: The image points the other way; holding a spoon is the simplest thing a cook does.
why.B: The cards were written for the cook herself or someone who had stood beside her, not for children.
why.C: Correct — the same sentence gives the reason they were left out: the body already knew them.
why.D: Nothing in the passage suggests secrecy; the steps went unwritten because they were obvious to her.

context: The example of a card that gives the sugar “to the quarter ounce” but the flour only as “enough” serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that the grandmother was careless about measuring her flour.
illustrate the claim that what a card leaves unsaid is itself information.
suggest that sugar cost a good deal more than flour when the cards were written.
prove that the cards were written to be followed by a stranger.

why.A: This is the tempting reading, but the passage takes the vague “enough” as a sign that she never needed to measure it, not as carelessness.
why.B: Correct — it follows “Their silences are information,” and shows that the exact figure marks the ingredient she had once got wrong.
why.C: That may be true of the world, but the passage never mentions prices; it reads the precision as a record of a past mistake.
why.D: The second paragraph says the reverse: they were not written for a stranger.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It describes the cards, rereads them, sets them against printed recipes, admits a loss, and defends their worth.
It follows the grandmother’s life from her girlhood to her last years, using the cards as dates along the way.
It lists the faults of printed recipes and then proposes a new way of writing them that fixes each fault.
It argues that the cards are better than cookbooks and then withdraws that claim in the final paragraph.

why.A: Correct — the six paragraphs follow that order, from the index cards to the historians who read omission as carefully as statement.
why.B: None of the cards is dated, and the passage never narrates her life.
why.C: The passage praises printed recipes as a real achievement and proposes no new format.
why.D: The passage never ranks the cards above cookbooks, and the final paragraph strengthens its case rather than withdrawing it.

context: According to the fourth paragraph, a printed recipe differs from one of the grandmother’s cards in that the printed recipe:

choices.text: records a cook’s past mistakes more honestly.
is always more accurate than a handwritten card.
leaves out whatever the body already knows.
is written for any reader, so it can take nothing for granted.

why.A: The record of past mistakes belongs to the cards, in their crossings-out and exact figures.
why.B: The paragraph calls it a different achievement, “and not simply a better one.”
why.C: That is what the cards do; the printed recipe tries to put back what they leave out.
why.D: Correct — “The printed recipe addresses everyone and so must assume nothing,” while the card can assume almost everything.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward printed cookbooks in the fourth paragraph is best described as:

choices.text: dismissive, treating a printed cookbook as useless to any serious cook.
wholly admiring, preferring a good printed cookbook to the family cards.
respectful of their achievement, while denying it is simply a better one.
indifferent, since she has never cooked from a printed recipe.

why.A: A cookbook is called useless only if it assumed as much as the cards do; she praises the printed recipe for letting strangers cook your food.
why.B: She refuses to rank the two, and the passage ends by valuing what the cards alone can show.
why.C: Correct — she calls the printed recipe “a real achievement” she does not want to belittle, and then says it is a different achievement from the card’s.
why.D: She says she has tried adding what the printed recipes say to the soda bread.

context: Which detail best supports the narrator’s statement that “The crossings-out tell you more”?

choices.text: Several cards are so stained with butter that the writing shows through from the back.
The amount of treacle on the gingerbread card was changed three times, in different inks.
None of the cards is dated and none is signed, because it was clear whose they were.
The lemon cake card gives an oven temperature in a unit that is no longer used.

why.A: The stains show heavy use, but they are not crossings-out and reveal nothing about changes of mind.
why.B: Correct — the next sentences show the changes recording a search for the right treacle after a grocer closed.
why.C: This explains a missing signature, not what the corrections reveal.
why.D: This shows the card’s age, not anything learned from a correction.

context: It can reasonably be inferred from the third paragraph that after Harrison’s closed, the grandmother:

choices.text: never again found a treacle that fully satisfied her.
stopped making gingerbread and put the card away.
took up printed recipes in place of her own cards.
wrote the grocer’s name down so she would avoid the shop.

why.A: Correct — the three changes in different inks, with the grocer’s name in the margin, lead the narrator to conclude the treacle “was never quite right again.”
why.B: The card “records the search,” which means she kept adjusting the recipe rather than abandoning it.
why.C: Nothing links the grocer’s closing to cookbooks.
why.D: The shop had already closed; the name marks the treacle she had lost.

context: The final paragraph serves mainly to:

choices.text: introduce a new subject, the work of historians, for its own sake.
explain why the narrator’s soda bread never tastes like her grandmother’s.
recommend that families publish their recipe cards as cookbooks.
argue that the cards remain valuable in spite of the loss just described.

why.A: The historians are brought in only to support the point about the cards.
why.B: That is explained in the fifth paragraph, not the sixth.
why.C: No such recommendation is made, and the passage says a card would be useless to a general reader.
why.D: Correct — it opens “Yet the outline is not nothing” and ends on what the cards can tell that no cookbook can.

context: The main idea of the passage is that a rest in music:

choices.text: is the most important part of any piece of music.
cannot be practised and so is best left to chance on the night.
is charged attention whose power comes from the music around it.
sounds the same in a recording as it does in a hall.

why.A: This is the advice the fifth paragraph calls “a lovely thing to say” and “not quite true.”
why.B: The fourth paragraph says a rest cannot be practised the way a phrase can, but the passage asks for judgement and trust, not chance.
why.C: Correct — the passage says a rest leaves attention with nowhere to go and borrows all its meaning from the notes on either side.
why.D: The passage says recordings hide the difference, not that there is none.

context: According to the second paragraph, what does a rest remove?

choices.text: all sound from the concert hall
the performer’s next action
the listeners’ attention to the music
the composer’s control over the piece

why.A: The paragraph says a hall is almost never silent during a rest.
why.B: Correct — “What the rest removes is not sound but the performer’s next action.”
why.C: Attention is what the rest leaves behind, with nowhere to go.
why.D: Composers handing decisions to performers comes up in the third paragraph, through the pause sign.

context: The phrase “a kind of listening with the volume turned up” suggests that during a rest the audience:

choices.text: attends more intently than while notes are playing.
hears the last note more loudly than before.
begins to make noise because it is bored.
expects the next passage to be played louder than the last.

why.A: Correct — the phrase explains why a rest “can be the loudest moment in a piece”: everyone in the hall is waiting.
why.B: The dying note is fainter, not louder; the volume in the image belongs to the listening, not the sound.
why.C: Breathing and coughing are mentioned, but the image describes heightened attention, not restlessness.
why.D: Nothing in the image concerns how loudly the music will resume.

context: The third paragraph says that when a whole orchestra stops dead for a full bar, “the effect is not of a pause but of a floor giving way.” This image suggests that such a silence:

choices.text: makes the players lose their place in the music and stop.
reveals that the hall’s acoustics are poorly designed.
gives the players a welcome chance to breathe and reset.
comes as a shock, not as a rest.

why.A: The orchestra stops because the score tells it to; no one loses their place.
why.B: The acoustics of the room are raised in the fourth paragraph, and not as a fault.
why.C: The paragraph says a player who treats the bar as a chance to breathe has made the passage smaller.
why.D: Correct — a floor giving way is sudden and alarming, the opposite of the breather a pause implies.

context: The last sentence of the fourth paragraph, about silences on recordings, serves mainly to:

choices.text: argue that recordings are a poor way to learn music.
suggest that performers should practise rests with a recording.
explain why the difficulty of judging a rest is easy to overlook.
show that rests on recordings are usually a beat too long.

why.A: The sentence makes a narrower point about silences and does not judge recordings as teaching tools.
why.B: The paragraph says no tool can settle a rest in advance, since each room is different.
why.C: Correct — on a recording a silence is always the same length in the same room, so the night-to-night judgement the paragraph describes never shows.
why.D: The beat-too-long rest is a live one, on Wednesday; recordings are the same every time.

context: The author’s attitude toward the advice that “silence is the most important part of music” is best described as:

choices.text: scornful, treating it as the mistake of careless teachers.
sympathetic to its appeal but unwilling to accept it as true.
fully in agreement, having built the passage on it.
uncertain, unable to decide whether it is right.

why.A: Parting company with the advice is not scorn; the author credits its loveliness and never blames teachers.
why.B: Correct — the author calls it “a lovely thing to say” before saying it is not quite true, and replaces it with a more careful claim.
why.C: The fifth paragraph exists to correct this advice.
why.D: The author decides plainly: silence “is not the most important part of the music.”

context: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A common misunderstanding, what a rest does, why it is hard, a correction, and what it asks of players.
A history of how composers have written rests, from the earliest scores down to the orchestral works performed today.
A comparison of two famous performers, one who rushes rests and one who holds them, with a verdict on the better.
A set of practice exercises for rests, each followed by a note on the mistakes students commonly make with it.

why.A: Correct — the paragraphs move in that order, from students treating rests as waiting rooms to the trust the final paragraph describes.
why.B: The passage gives no history and names no period; it discusses rests as they are performed.
why.C: No performers are named, and young and older players are contrasted only in the final paragraph.
why.D: The passage says a rest cannot be practised the way a phrase can, and offers no exercises.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that a rest “has no meaning of its own”?

choices.text: A rest is written on the page with a shape, a place on the staff and a length in beats.
Young players rush rests because silence feels like exposure to them.
During a rest in a hall, a string is often still faintly ringing.
The same silence means little after one held note but can stop a room after a long build.

why.A: This describes how a rest is notated, not where its meaning comes from.
why.B: This explains a habit of players, not what gives a rest its meaning.
why.C: This shows a rest is not truly silent, which is a different point from the second paragraph.
why.D: Correct — the silence is identical in both cases; only the notes before it differ, so its meaning must come from them.

context: The author suggests that a player who “treats that bar as a chance to breathe” has:

choices.text: misread the score and come in a bar too early.
followed the composer’s pause sign exactly as it was written.
weakened the passage without a mistake anyone could name.
shown the trust that the final paragraph praises.

why.A: The player sits through the bar; nothing suggests a wrong entry.
why.B: The pause sign is a separate case, in which the performer decides how long to hold the silence.
why.C: Correct — the next words say the player “has not made a mistake that anyone could name, but has made the passage smaller.”
why.D: Trust means letting the silence work, not using it to rest.

context: According to the final paragraph, young players differ from older ones in that young players:

choices.text: hold rests too long because they are counting beats.
hurry through rests because the silence leaves them exposed.
play the notes around a rest more carefully.
rely on recordings to learn exactly how long each rest should be.

why.A: Counting is what students do in the first paragraph; the young players here rush.
why.B: Correct — “Young players rush rests because silence feels like exposure,” while older ones learn to let the silence work.
why.C: The paragraph compares how the two handle silence, not their care with notes.
why.D: Recordings appear in the fourth paragraph, not in this comparison.

context: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.text: argue that visitors should be able to handle objects, not only look.
call for glass cases to be removed from museums and galleries altogether.
defend the old museum rule that visitors may not touch anything at all.
describe how Bronze Age axe heads were made and used.

why.A: Correct — Passage A quarrels with the assumption that looking is the only way of knowing a thing and defends the handling table.
why.B: Passage A says it has no quarrel with the glass case for the objects that need it.
why.C: Passage A grants the rule was right for fragile objects but argues against looking as the only way in.
why.D: The axe head is an example of what handling teaches, not the subject of the passage.

context: According to Passage A, what should a museum do about the fact that a replica is not the real thing?

choices.text: Keep replicas behind glass beside the originals.
Offer replicas only to children.
Stop using replicas and let visitors handle originals.
Say so plainly on the label.

why.A: Passage A puts replicas on a handling table, in the hand, not behind glass.
why.B: Passage A says adults also ask better questions after handling objects.
why.C: Passage A accepts that fragile originals need protection; replicas are its answer to that.
why.D: Correct — Passage A grants the objection and says “the label should say so plainly.”

context: When Passage A says that a museum offering only the eye “is teaching one sense to do the work of five,” the point is that such a museum:

choices.text: overwhelms visitors by appealing to every sense at once.
employs too few guides to explain its objects.
relies on sight alone for knowledge the other senses could supply.
is designed mainly for visitors with poor eyesight.

why.A: This reverses the image; the complaint is that only one sense is used.
why.B: Staffing is never mentioned; the “work” is the work of knowing.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph has just listed what the hand learns about weight and balance that the eye cannot.
why.D: The image concerns which senses are used, not the eyesight of visitors.

context: As it is used in Passage B (“It frames”), the word “frames” most nearly means:

choices.text: falsely accuses.
sets apart for attention.
puts into words.
builds a structure for.

why.A: That is a real sense of “frame,” but nothing in Passage B involves blame.
why.B: Correct — the next sentences say the case removes an object from use and places it “in the world of attention.”
why.C: Framing a question is a real use, but the case is not phrasing anything.
why.D: The case does not construct the object; it changes how the object is seen.

context: In Passage B, the example of a spoon on a kitchen table and a spoon alone in a lit case serves mainly to:

choices.text: show how taking an object out of use invites us to see it as made.
argue that everyday objects do not belong in museums.
suggest that a replica spoon would teach visitors as much as the original.
explain why lighting matters more than the case itself.

why.A: Correct — the spoon in the case “asks to be looked at as something made, by someone, at a particular time.”
why.B: Passage B uses the spoon to show what a case adds, not to exclude such objects.
why.C: Replicas come up only in the final paragraph, and not with the spoon.
why.D: The light is part of the description; the point is the object’s removal from use.

context: The writer of Passage B regards handling tables with:

choices.text: hostility, since they put the objects in a museum’s care at risk.
unqualified enthusiasm, as the best way there is to teach visitors.
indifference, having never watched visitors use one.
approval of what they do, with doubt about one claim made for them.

why.A: A defence of the glass case can read as hostility to handling, but Passage B never says handling tables endanger anything, and its writer has set up several.
why.B: The writer says a case does something a handling table cannot.
why.C: The writer describes watching visitors at a handling table put objects down.
why.D: Correct — the writer has set up several and says children love them, but rejects the claim that touching a replica is a deeper kind of knowing.

context: Both writers would most likely agree that:

choices.text: a replica teaches as much as the original does.
glass cases should be taken out of most galleries.
handling tables can be of real value to visitors.
looking is the only real way of knowing an object.

why.A: Passage B denies that a replica can teach what the original alone carries.
why.B: Neither writer proposes removing cases; Passage A keeps them for objects that need them.
why.C: Correct — Passage A defends them, and Passage B says, “I do not object to handling tables” and that children love them.
why.D: Passage A argues against exactly this assumption.

context: Passage A says that “the real thing in a case is not fully present either.” The writer of Passage B would most likely respond that:

choices.text: the writer of Passage A is right, and cases should therefore be kept to a minimum.
the case gives the object a kind of presence, by making it something to look at.
visitors cannot tell a replica from an original, so presence does not matter.
touching an object is the only way to make it fully present to a visitor.

why.A: Passage B argues that a case is more than a regrettable necessity, which is the view it rejects.
why.B: Correct — Passage B says the case frames the object, and that this shift is where much of a museum’s meaning comes from.
why.C: Passage B stresses what only the original carries, so it would not say the difference is invisible.
why.D: This is closer to Passage A’s position than to Passage B’s.

context: The two passages disagree most directly about whether:

choices.text: the glass case mainly limits knowing or itself creates meaning.
fragile objects need to be protected from the hands of visitors.
children enjoy handling objects in museums.
a replica should be labelled as one.

why.A: Correct — Passage A treats the case as leaving the object present to one sense only; Passage B says the case frames the object and is where much of its meaning comes from.
why.B: Both writers accept that some objects need protection.
why.C: Both writers say that they do.
why.D: Passage B never raises labelling, so the two do not disagree about it.

context: Which detail from Passage B best supports its suggestion that a case can lengthen the time a visitor spends looking?

choices.text: Children love the handling tables that the writer has set up in the past.
The scratch along the axe blade was made before anyone we could name was born.
Proposals to bring visitors closer are generous in spirit.
An object in the hand is soon put down, but one behind glass cannot be.

why.A: This is a concession about handling tables, not evidence about looking time.
why.B: This shows what the original alone carries, not how long visitors look.
why.C: This is a courtesy to the other side, not evidence.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph concludes that an object behind glass, which cannot be put down, is sometimes looked at for longer.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Root pressure in spring supplies most of the water that reaches a tree’s leaves.
Scientists still cannot agree about how water reaches the top of a tall tree.
Evaporation at the leaves pulls a cohesive column of water up under tension.
Air bubbles regularly block the conduits of trees on hot, dry days.

why.A: The second paragraph says root pressure lifts water only a few metres and is often absent in summer.
why.B: The last paragraph grants that details about refilling are argued over, but it says the central idea has held.
why.C: Correct — the passage rules out pushing, explains the pull, and ends by saying the central idea has held.
why.D: This is the point of the fifth paragraph, a risk the system survives, not the passage’s main idea.

context: According to the passage, capillary action in tubes as wide as a tree’s can lift water:

choices.text: a few metres.
a metre or less.
about ten metres.
more than a hundred metres.

why.A: That is the limit the passage gives for root pressure.
why.B: Correct — the second paragraph says that in such tubes it “accounts for a metre or less.”
why.C: That is the limit for a suction pump at the top of a building.
why.D: That is the height of the tallest trees, which capillary action cannot explain.

context: The detail that a grapevine cut early in the season “will weep sap” serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that root pressure is real, even though it cannot explain the lift.
prove that grapevines lift water higher than other plants do.
suggest that cutting a plant is the best way to measure its water use.
introduce the idea that sap is pulled from the top of the plant.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph grants that water can be pushed from below “in some plants in spring,” then says root pressure lifts water only a few metres.
why.B: No comparison of heights is made; the vine illustrates pressure from the roots.
why.C: The measurements in the last paragraph use instruments clamped to branches and leaves.
why.D: Weeping sap is evidence of a push from below, the explanation the passage then sets aside.

context: The passage says that a column being pulled from above is “like a rope rather than a pile of bricks.” The comparison means that the water is:

choices.text: as heavy as a wall of the same height.
able to bend around corners in the wood.
stored in separate blocks stacked one above another up the trunk.
held under tension instead of being pushed up from below.

why.A: Weight is not the comparison; the image contrasts pulling with pushing.
why.B: Flexibility is not what the image describes.
why.C: The passage describes an unbroken column, not separate blocks.
why.D: Correct — the same sentence says the column is under tension, which is how a rope, and not a pile of bricks, bears a load.

context: Based on the passage, a tree whose leaf pores had all closed would most likely:

choices.text: draw up more water than usual, since none of it would then be escaping into the air.
lift water to its top by root pressure instead.
draw up very little water, since the pull depends on evaporation from the leaves.
develop more air bubbles in its conduits than on a dry day.

why.A: This sounds sensible, since less would be lost, but the passage makes evaporation the engine of the lift, not a leak.
why.B: Root pressure lifts water only a few metres and is often absent in summer.
why.C: Correct — water leaves through the pores, and each departing molecule tugs the column; with no evaporation there is nothing to pull.
why.D: Bubbles form when tension becomes too great, which happens on hot, dry days, not when the pull stops.

context: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A history of botany told through the lives of the scientists who first studied how trees drink water.
A puzzle, two failed answers, the accepted one, its strange consequences and risks, and how it won acceptance.
A comparison of how three kinds of tree move water, closing with the conclusion that one of them is the most efficient.
An experiment described step by step, followed by its results and an account of the errors in how it was run.

why.A: No scientist is named, and the passage explains a mechanism rather than telling lives.
why.B: Correct — the paragraphs move from the pumpless tree to root pressure and capillarity, to the pull, tension, failures, and the measurements that ended the doubt.
why.C: Trees are discussed in general; no kinds of tree are compared.
why.D: The passage reports several findings, and no single experiment is walked through.

context: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that the pull “tracks the drying power of the air”?

choices.text: Instruments on living trees showed tension rising by morning and easing at dusk.
Researchers listening to trees with sensitive instruments heard faint clicks on hot, dry days.
The conduits in the wood are dead cells whose contents are gone.
A grapevine cut early in spring will weep sap.

why.A: Correct — tension follows the sun’s course across the day, just as a pull driven by evaporation should.
why.B: The clicks are evidence of columns breaking, not of the pull following the weather through the day.
why.C: This explains why the lift costs the tree no energy, not what drives its rate.
why.D: This shows root pressure, the explanation the passage sets aside.

context: As it is used in the sentence “The system is not so much safe as forgiving,” the word “forgiving” most nearly means:

choices.text: willing to pardon those who have done wrong.
free from any risk of breaking down.
easily persuaded to change its course.
able to survive failures without collapsing.

why.A: That is the everyday sense of the word, but the sentence describes a plumbing system, not a person pardoning anyone.
why.B: That is what “safe” would mean, and the sentence sets “forgiving” against “safe.”
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph concerns persuasion or change of direction.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph says trees survive blocked conduits through redundancy, detours and refilling.

context: The author presents the physicists’ long scepticism about the explanation as:

choices.text: foolish, because the answer should have been obvious to them from the start.
justified, since the theory has since been abandoned in favour of root pressure.
understandable, since water had rarely been seen to behave that way in experiments.
puzzling, since no one has yet measured tension inside a living tree.

why.A: The first paragraph says the answer still strikes many people as too strange to be true.
why.B: The passage says the central idea has held.
why.C: Correct — the last paragraph gives exactly that reason for the doubt, and describes the careful measurements that eventually answered it.
why.D: Tension was measured with instruments clamped to branches and leaves.

context: According to the passage, compared with a suction pump at the top of a tall building, a tree:

choices.text: uses far more energy to lift the same water.
lifts water many times higher.
works only when the air is still and humid.
pushes water up from below instead of pulling it.

why.A: The passage says the tree spends no energy on the lift; the sun does the work.
why.B: Correct — the pump cannot draw water up more than about ten metres, and a tree does many times better.
why.C: Trees draw the most water on sunny, breezy days and the least on still, humid nights.
why.D: The passage says the water is pulled from the top, not pushed.

context: The main point of the passage is that old window panes are uneven because:

choices.text: of how they were made and fitted, not because glass slowly flows.
glass is a liquid that sags over centuries under its own weight.
glass has no crystal structure and so resists simple classification.
impurities in older glass let it flow faster than modern glass.

why.A: Correct — the passage rules out flow on the numbers and traces the thickness to spinning, cylinders and glaziers’ choices.
why.B: This is the church guide’s story, which the passage sets out to refute.
why.C: This is true according to the second paragraph, but it is that paragraph’s point, not the cause of uneven panes.
why.D: The third paragraph says impurities help, “but not by nearly enough to close the gap.”

context: According to the passage, surveys of old windows found panes installed with the thick edge:

choices.text: always at the bottom, as the church guides claim.
only in windows made from cylinder glass.
in the middle of the pane rather than at an edge.
at the top and at the sides, as well as at the bottom.

why.A: The surveys found exceptions, which is why they matter.
why.B: The passage does not tie the exceptions to one method of manufacture.
why.C: The passage speaks only of edges.
why.D: Correct — the fourth paragraph says most glaziers put the heavier edge at the bottom, “But not all,” and names the top and sides.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that glass does not flow visibly over many centuries?

choices.text: Old glass contains more impurities than modern glass and flows somewhat more readily.
Spun discs of glass were never even, so panes cut from them varied in thickness.
Roman glass vessels nearly two thousand years old show no sign of having slumped.
Physicists argue with some heat about what to call the state glass is in.

why.A: This concedes a small difference in flow; it does not show that flow is invisible.
why.B: This explains where the thickness came from, not whether glass flows.
why.C: Correct — if glass sagged at the rate the story needs, walls this old would show it.
why.D: This shows glass is odd, not that it holds its shape.

context: The second paragraph serves mainly to:

choices.text: prove that glass is in fact a liquid rather than a solid.
grant what is true in the popular story before challenging its explanation.
describe the several methods once used to make and fit window glass in earlier centuries.
explain why church guides are unreliable sources of information.

why.A: The paragraph says physicists argue about what to call glass; it proves nothing about its being a liquid.
why.B: Correct — it admits that many panes are uneven and glass is strange, and the next paragraph opens, “The explanation, though, does not survive.”
why.C: Manufacture is the subject of the fourth paragraph.
why.D: The paragraph credits the guide’s observation as often correct.

context: In the first paragraph, the comparison to “honey sliding down the inside of a jar” is used to describe:

choices.text: how glass supposedly sags over the centuries under its own weight.
the colour that very old window glass has taken on.
the way molten glass was spun into a disc.
the sweetness of a story that listeners enjoy hearing and repeating.

why.A: Correct — the same sentence says the glass has sagged under its own weight, “like honey sliding down the inside of a jar.”
why.B: Colour is never mentioned; the image is about slow movement.
why.C: Spinning comes up in the fourth paragraph, not in the guide’s story.
why.D: The appeal of the story is discussed later, and not through this image.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the church guide’s story is best described as:

choices.text: contemptuous, treating it as a foolish tale for tourists.
approving, since the story gets visitors and students interested in science.
undecided about whether the story is true.
corrective but not scornful, since it credits what is true in the story.

why.A: Rejecting the explanation is not contempt; the writer grants the story a real basis in fact.
why.B: The writer explains why the story persists but does not approve of repeating it.
why.C: The writer decides plainly: “The sag is in the story, not in the pane.”
why.D: Correct — the writer calls the observation often correct and the story “not entirely false,” while showing its explanation fails.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: A step-by-step account of how window glass was made, from the earliest spun discs to the float glass of today.
A debate between two named scientists over the nature of glass, followed by the writer’s verdict on it.
A popular claim, what is right about it, why its explanation fails, the real cause, why it lasts, and a lesson.
A list of common myths about everyday materials, each answered in turn with the evidence against it.

why.A: Methods of manufacture fill one paragraph; modern methods are not described.
why.B: No scientists are named, and the passage does not stage a debate.
why.C: Correct — the six paragraphs follow that order, ending on the general shape of a durable error.
why.D: The passage deals with a single myth about glass.

context: The passage suggests that if glaziers had always set the heavier edge at the bottom, then:

choices.text: the flowing-glass story would have been proved correct.
the surveys could not have told the two explanations apart as clearly.
old panes would have been perfectly even in thickness from top to bottom.
the glass would have flowed faster because of the added weight.

why.A: Bottom-heavy panes would fit the story without proving it; the viscosity figures would still rule flow out.
why.B: Correct — panes with the thick edge at the top or sides are “exactly what the flowing-glass story cannot explain”; without them, both stories would predict the same windows.
why.C: The unevenness came from manufacture, so it would remain whichever way the panes were set.
why.D: The passage says glass does not flow at any visible rate, whichever way up it is set.

context: According to the final paragraph, how does “A pure invention” differ from an error that “leans on something true”?

choices.text: The first is easily dislodged; the second borrows credibility from its true part.
The first spreads faster than the truth; the second is repeated only by experts.
The first is harmless to believe; the second misleads the public about glass.
The first rests on some evidence; the second rests on no evidence at all.

why.A: Correct — nothing props up an invention, while the leaning error borrows credibility each time the true part holds.
why.B: The paragraph says nothing about speed of spread or who repeats either kind.
why.C: Both are errors; the difference is how hard each is to dislodge.
why.D: The paragraph says the reverse: the invention has nothing propping it up.

context: As it is used in the sentence “The explanation, though, does not survive a look at the numbers,” the word “survive” most nearly means:

choices.text: stay alive through.
last longer than.
escape notice during.
hold up under.

why.A: This is the literal sense, but an explanation is not a living thing.
why.B: The sentence is not about duration; the numbers expose the explanation at once.
why.C: The point is that the explanation is examined and fails, not that it goes unseen.
why.D: Correct — the explanation fails once the viscosity figures are examined.

context: The main idea of the passage is that honeybees:

choices.text: measure distance by how much energy the flight to the food has cost them.
cannot find their way over open water.
judge distance by optic flow, which works because recruits fly the same route.
learn the location of food by following the scent the dancer leaves on the comb.

why.A: The second paragraph describes experiments that cast doubt on exactly this.
why.B: Open water is one limit, noted in the last paragraph, and even there the bees report a distance.
why.C: Correct — the tunnel experiments show the bees measure optic flow, and the fifth paragraph explains why that error does not matter.
why.D: Scent is never mentioned; recruits read the angle and length of the dance.

context: According to the passage, the angle of the dancer’s straight run tells other bees:

choices.text: how far away the food is.
the direction of the food relative to the sun.
how much food the flower patch still holds.
how many recruits should fly out to the patch.

why.A: The length of the waggle gives the distance.
why.B: Correct — the first paragraph says exactly this.
why.C: The quantity of food is not something the passage says the dance reports.
why.D: The passage does not say the dance sets a number of recruits.

context: Which result described in the second paragraph most directly shows that a bee’s reported distance can fall even as the effort of the trip rises?

choices.text: Bees trained to a high feeder reported shorter distances.
Bees made to carry small weights did not report longer distances.
Bees flying into a headwind seemed to report longer trips.
Bees that flew further burned more fuel on the journey.

why.A: Correct — the climb cost them more, yet they reported less, so the report cannot simply track effort.
why.B: This shows added effort without a longer report, but the reported distance did not fall.
why.C: This is the early observation that appeared to support the energy idea.
why.D: This is the premise of the energy guess, not a result that tests it.

context: When the passage says that “The dance, in other words, was reporting scenery,” it means that the dance:

choices.text: described the flowers and landmarks along the route.
was performed only when the view from the hive was clear.
showed recruits which patterns to look for on the tunnel walls.
conveyed how much of the view had streamed past the bee.

why.A: The dance reports a quantity of flow, not a description of particular sights.
why.B: The passage gives no such condition for dancing.
why.C: The patterns were set by researchers; recruits are not taught them.
why.D: Correct — the sentence before says the bees “were measuring how much the world had streamed past their eyes.”

context: The reference to looking out of a train window serves mainly to:

choices.text: show that bees see much as people do on long journeys.
suggest that bees fly as fast as trains over open ground.
relate optic flow to an experience familiar to most readers.
explain why bees avoid flying close to walls.

why.A: The comparison is about how motion appears, not about the eyesight of bees.
why.B: Speed is not compared.
why.C: Correct — fence posts racing past and distant hills barely moving illustrate the quantity just named.
why.D: Bees in the tunnel flew close to the walls, and nothing says they avoid them.

context: Based on the passage, which recruit would be most likely to land well short of or beyond the food?

choices.text: One who flies the dancer’s exact route but into a stronger headwind.
One who flies high over open fields where the dancer flew low by a hedge.
One who flies the dancer’s route on a later day of the same week, in fine weather.
One who watches the dance several times before leaving the hive.
