why.A: A headwind adds effort, but the passage shows the bee’s odometer measures flow, not effort, so the same route gives the same reading.
why.B: Correct — the different path gives a different amount of optic flow for the same distance, and the last paragraph says such a recruit may land short or long.
why.C: The fifth paragraph says bees flying the same route see the same flow, so the error cancels.
why.D: Watching more often would not change the distance the dance encodes.

context: The author treats the idea that bees measured distance by energy as:

choices.text: reasonable and partly supported, though mistaken.
a careless guess that no evidence ever supported.
still the leading explanation among researchers.
correct for bees flying over open water.

why.A: Correct — after reporting the experiments against it, the author adds that the idea “had been sensible” and that early observations appeared to support it.
why.B: The author grants that headwind observations once appeared to support it.
why.C: The tunnel experiments replaced it with optic flow.
why.D: Open water is where the odometer under-reports, and energy is not mentioned there.

context: The fifth paragraph is structured as:

choices.text: a new experiment, followed by its surprising result.
a list of the odometer’s limits, from least to most serious.
a question, followed by the admission that nobody knows.
an apparent weakness, followed by the reason it does no harm.

why.A: No experiment is described in the fifth paragraph.
why.B: The limits are the subject of the sixth paragraph.
why.C: The paragraph answers its own doubt rather than leaving it open.
why.D: Correct — it opens “At first this looks like a flaw” and ends “The measurement is wrong in a way that does not matter.”

context: According to the passage, compared with a bee flying close to a patterned wall, a bee flying high across an open field for the same distance sees:

choices.text: much more optic flow.
the same amount of optic flow.
much less optic flow.
no optic flow at all.

why.A: This reverses the paragraph; it is the bee near the wall that sees an enormous amount.
why.B: The paragraph contrasts the two cases precisely because the flow differs.
why.C: Correct — the fourth paragraph says exactly this.
why.D: The field bee sees less flow, not none.

context: As it is used in the sentence “the bee’s odometer had read it faithfully,” the word “faithfully” most nearly means:

choices.text: loyally.
accurately.
hopefully.
reluctantly.

why.A: This is the everyday sense of “faithful,” but the sentence is about how exactly the instrument recorded the flow.
why.B: Correct — the odometer recorded the exaggerated flow exactly as it was; the error lay in the tunnel, not the reading.
why.C: Nothing in the sentence expresses hope.
why.D: The reading is not described as grudging.

context: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.text: A teenager staying with his great-aunt learns from her to write down only what he has actually measured.
A teenager staying with his great-aunt discovers a love of weather that shapes the rest of his career.
A great-aunt persuades a university to take over the rainfall record she has kept for decades.
A great-aunt teaches her great-nephew to forecast rain more accurately than radar can.

why.A: Correct — the last paragraph says he has never since been able to round an uncertain number, and it traces the habit to Ruth and the gauge.
why.B: The last paragraph says the story does not end with him falling in love with weather; he became an accountant.
why.C: The hydrologist only comes to check that the post is level; nothing is handed over.
why.D: Ruth grants that radar is better at telling where rain is going; her gauge measures rain, it does not forecast it.

context: According to Ruth, the weakness of radar is that it:

choices.text: cannot tell anyone where the rain is heading next.
is less useful than a gauge for someone planning a picnic.
reports rainfall only for large regions and never for any single place such as Ruth’s garden.
estimates what reaches the ground from signals reflected back from the sky.

why.A: Ruth says the reverse: radar is very good at telling you where rain is going.
why.B: Ruth says she would not trade radar for anything if she were planning a picnic.
why.C: The narrator says radar covers any square mile; Ruth’s objection is that it guesses, not that it is coarse.
why.D: Correct — the third paragraph says radar measured “something bouncing back from the sky” and made a guess about what would reach the ground.

context: The passage most strongly suggests that the hydrologist valued Ruth’s records mainly because they:

choices.text: were more precise, reading by reading, than any figure that radar could supply.
recorded the storms of one unusually wild year in great detail.
formed a long series taken the same way in one place, which lets slow change be seen.
had not been interrupted once in forty-one years of daily readings.

why.A: This is Ruth’s point about the gauge, and it is tempting, but the hydrologist’s reason is length and consistency: one year on its own, however exact, “tells you almost nothing.”
why.B: He says single years are wild and tell you almost nothing, which is why one year would not interest him.
why.C: Correct — he says a single year tells almost nothing and that only forty years taken the same way let slow changes show through the noise.
why.D: The fourth paragraph says there was exactly one gap, the morning in March marked “no reading.”

context: As used in paragraph 3, the word “considered” most nearly means:

choices.text: regarded as.
thought about.
treated with respect.
added up.

why.A: That sense needs a description after it, as when a plan is thought foolish; here Ruth simply ponders the question.
why.B: Correct — Ruth thinks over the narrator’s question while she pours out the water, then answers it.
why.C: Nothing suggests she is showing the question respect; she is thinking before she answers.
why.D: She adds nothing up; the word describes her pausing to think.

context: The narrator’s statement that “I became an accountant” (paragraph 7) mainly serves to:

choices.text: make clear that what he kept from that summer was a habit of care with numbers, not a love of weather.
suggest that the summer at Ruth’s house left no lasting mark on him at all.
express his regret that he did not follow the hydrologist into scientific work, as Ruth had quietly hoped he might.
explain why he found the hydrologist’s visit so hard to follow at the time.

why.A: Correct — it corrects listeners who expect a weather story, and the next sentence names what he did keep: he cannot round a number he is unsure of.
why.B: The next sentence says the reverse: he still cannot round an uncertain number without seeing the funnel.
why.C: He voices no regret; he treats the career as beside the point of the story.
why.D: His career is not connected to the visit; the visit is how he learned who used the record.

context: The hydrologist says slow changes show through the noise the way “a face shows through a crowd” (paragraph 5). The comparison suggests that:

choices.text: a single year of rainfall shows a clear trend if it is read carefully.
rainfall records are mostly errors that must be removed before use.
the hydrologist recalls the observers he visits better than their data.
a pattern emerges only from long, patient attention to a mass of varied data.

why.A: He says the opposite: a single year “tells you almost nothing.”
why.B: The noise is the natural wildness of single years, not mistakes in the record.
why.C: This takes the face in the crowd literally; the image is about seeing a pattern in data.
why.D: Correct — the image follows the claim that only forty years of readings let the changes show; “if you look long enough” carries the idea of patience.

context: Ruth’s attitude toward radar is best described as:

choices.text: scornful, since she thinks it is useless beside her brass gauge and its cards.
envious, since it has made her decades of work unnecessary.
appreciative of what it does well but unwilling to treat it as a measurement.
uncertain, since she does not understand how it works.

why.A: Her line that radar “did not measure rain” invites this reading, but she opens by praising it for telling where rain is going.
why.B: Nothing suggests envy, and the hydrologist’s visit shows her work is still needed.
why.C: Correct — she would not trade it for anything when planning a picnic, yet insists that it “did not measure rain.”
why.D: She explains exactly how it works: it measures a signal and guesses at the rain.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It opens with the narrator as an adult, flashes back to a single summer, and closes on the day he finally left Ruth’s house.
It moves from the narrator’s arrival, to Ruth’s routine and reasons, to a morning he took the reading himself, and then to what he kept from it.
It gives Ruth’s case for rain gauges, then the hydrologist’s case against them, then the narrator’s own verdict on the dispute.
It follows Ruth’s forty-one years of record keeping in order, from her first card to her last.

why.A: It opens in the summer itself, and it never describes his departure.
why.B: Correct — paragraphs 1–5 cover the arrival, the gauge and Ruth’s reasons, paragraph 6 the morning he reads it, and paragraph 7 its lasting effect.
why.C: The hydrologist supports Ruth’s record; there is no case against gauges.
why.D: The passage covers one June; the forty-one years are summed up in a single paragraph.

context: According to Ruth, an “honest gap” in the record differs from a guess in that the gap:

choices.text: tells the people using the record what they do not know, while a guess misleads them.
can be filled in later from a neighbour’s gauge, while a guess cannot be corrected.
is allowed by the weather service’s rules, while a guess is forbidden by them.
happens only when the observer is ill, while a guess happens when she is careless.

why.A: Correct — the fourth paragraph: the gap told users “exactly what they did not know,” and a guess told them “something false.”
why.B: Filling it from a neighbour’s gauge is the narrator’s suggestion, and Ruth rejects it.
why.C: The passage never mentions any rules; Ruth’s reason is about honesty, not regulation.
why.D: That is not the distinction she draws; she contrasts what each tells the users.

context: Which quotation best shows that the narrator came to hold himself to Ruth’s standard?

choices.text: “I went out in my socks.”
“She looked at me as though I had suggested forging a signature.”
“I have told it, over the years, to people who expected it to end with me falling in love with weather”
“Then I counted the small lines again, got the same awkward number, and wrote that.”

why.A: This shows that he hurried, not what he did at the gauge.
why.B: This is tempting because it states the standard vividly, but it is Ruth’s reaction; at this point the narrator is the one proposing to estimate.
why.C: This tells what the story is not about; it shows nothing of his own conduct.
why.D: Correct — alone and unobserved, he records the exact awkward figure rather than the convenient mark.

context: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: A girl lost a spelling bee because she had never properly learned the word she was given.
A father who could not spell pushed his daughter to succeed where he had failed.
A lost spelling bee revealed that a father and daughter had each kept up the practice for the other’s sake.
Spelling bees are unfair because a single slip of the tongue can end a contest that a child has spent years preparing for.

why.A: She insists she knew the word: “the story is not that I did not know it.”
why.B: He was not pushing her; he had hoped for a year that she would lose so they could stop.
why.C: Correct — the loss leads to the conversation in the car, where each learns the other had been “enduring something for the other’s sake.”
why.D: The last paragraph says she cannot tell the story as one about “the unfairness of a silent letter.”

context: According to the passage, the narrator was eliminated because she:

choices.text: tried to take back a letter after she had already said it.
began the word with a letter she knew did not come first.
took too long to answer after asking for the language of origin.
had never practised that particular word before the bee.

why.A: The rules forbid taking a letter back, and she “could not take it back,” but she never tried to.
why.B: Correct — she said “n,” and the silent letter she had drilled “had simply not come out first,” though she knew the word.
why.C: She asked for the origin to gain a few seconds, but no time limit is mentioned and that is not why the bell rang.
why.D: The card for “mnemonic” had gone soft at the corners from practice.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the father laughed in the car (paragraph 5) mainly because he was:

choices.text: relieved that practice he had kept up for her sake could finally end.
amused by how nervous his daughter had looked on the stage.
trying to hide from her how disappointed he was by her early loss.
pleased that she had lasted longer than he had expected.

why.A: Correct — he tells her he had hoped for a year that she would lose early “so that we could stop.”
why.B: Nothing in his words concerns how she looked; he talks about ending the cards.
why.C: She had prepared for disappointment, but what he says shows there was none to hide.
why.D: He does not mention how long she lasted; he had hoped she would lose early.

context: As used in paragraph 3, the word “merciless” most nearly means:

choices.text: cruel in intent.
impossible to learn.
rarely enforced.
allowing no second chance.

why.A: The rules are described as strict, not as meant to hurt anyone.
why.B: The paragraph calls the rules “simple.”
why.C: The bell shows the rules were enforced every time.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph explains it at once: a speller has “no chance to take a letter back.”

context: The narrator mentions that her father “could not spell them himself” (paragraph 2) mainly to explain why he:

choices.text: left school at fifteen to work in a print shop.
had hoped for a year that she would lose.
checked each letter she said against the card.
used a formal voice when reading the words.

why.A: The print shop explains how he came to spell poorly, not the reverse.
why.B: That hope comes from thinking she loved the cards, as paragraph 5 explains.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph goes on: “So he held each card close to his face, checked every letter I said against it with his finger.”
why.D: The voice is the one he used on the telephone; spelling has nothing to do with it.

context: The narrator says she regarded her spelling “the way I regarded my brown eyes” (paragraph 1). She means that she saw her spelling as:

choices.text: a gift she had inherited from her father along with his careful habits.
a fact about herself rather than something she had achieved.
something other children envied her for.
the feature that made her stand out on stage.

why.A: Her father could not spell, so the talent did not come from him.
why.B: Correct — the same sentence glosses the image: “not an accomplishment, exactly, but a fact about me.”
why.C: She says adults found it important; envy is never mentioned.
why.D: The image is about how she thought of the skill, not how she looked on stage.

context: The narrator’s tone in describing the bell (“It was not a loud bell. It did not need to be.”) is best described as:

choices.text: dry, conveying how much a small sound could mean.
angry, blaming the organisers for a cruel signal.
fond, recalling the bell with nostalgia.
puzzled, unsure why a bell was used at all.

why.A: Correct — the flat, clipped sentences understate the bell to show its weight: a quiet sound that ended a child’s bee.
why.B: She blames no one; the last paragraph rejects a story about unfairness.
why.C: Nothing in the lines is warm; the bell signals failure.
why.D: She explains exactly what the bell was for.

context: In the structure of the passage, the account of the narrator’s mistake in paragraph 4 leads directly into:

choices.text: the defence she had prepared, which her father accepts without argument.
an explanation of the nerves that made her start with the wrong letter.
a description of the child who went on to win the regional bee.
a conversation in the car that changes what the mistake meant to her.

why.A: This borrows words from paragraph 5, but she says “I did not get to use it”; he starts laughing instead.
why.B: The last paragraph says she cannot tell the story as one about nerves.
why.C: The winner is never mentioned.
why.D: Correct — paragraphs 5 and 6 turn from the mistake to the discovery that each had kept the cards going for the other.

context: According to paragraphs 5 and 6, the narrator and her father had both:

choices.text: hoped for a year that she would lose early so they could stop.
prepared a defence of her mistake before reaching the car.
kept up the practice because each thought the other wanted it.
considered the cards the best part of their evenings.

why.A: Only the father says this; she had been afraid to stop winning.
why.B: Only the narrator prepared a defence.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 6 says they were “two people who had each been generously enduring something for the other’s sake.”
why.D: Each was enduring the cards, not enjoying them.

context: Which detail from the passage best supports the narrator’s claim that she knew the word she misspelled?

choices.text: She asked for the definition of the word before spelling it.
The card for “mnemonic” had gone soft at the corners from practice.
Her father began to laugh once they were in the car.
She now has a sharper eye for a misplaced letter than many editors.

why.A: She asked for the language of origin, and the passage says she did not need it.
why.B: Correct — the worn card shows how often she had practised that exact word.
why.C: His laughter concerns ending the practice, not her knowledge of the word.
why.D: This describes her skill decades later, not what she knew that afternoon.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A father passes a driving test and then gives up driving, having needed to make that choice himself.
A daughter learns that her father’s driving is safer than she had feared.
Road tests for older drivers are too lenient to catch the real problems that their families can see every day.
A daughter at last finds the courage to tell her father he should stop driving.

why.A: Correct — he hands over the keys because he had wanted to find out for himself before anyone told him he couldn’t.
why.B: He passes, which invites this reading, but he stops driving at once, and she never says she was wrong about his driving.
why.C: The examiner’s leniency is one detail of paragraph 5, not the point of the passage.
why.D: She never tells him; he makes the decision himself.

context: According to the passage, what fault did the examiner report in the father’s driving?

choices.text: He drifted toward the centre line on a bend.
He parked poorly beside the kerb during the test.
He used his indicator far too often.
He took one turn too wide.

why.A: That is the narrator’s complaint from paragraph 2, not the examiner’s finding.
why.B: His parallel parking is described only in his practice sessions.
why.C: The indicator comes up on the drive home, when he criticises the narrator’s use of it.
why.D: Correct — the examiner mentions “a couple of points off for a wide turn.”

context: It can reasonably be inferred from paragraph 2 that the narrator and her brother had:

choices.text: already reported their father’s driving to the licensing office.
caused the dent in the rear bumper themselves.
avoided telling their father outright that his driving was unsafe.
persuaded their father to take the road test early.

why.A: The letter was a form letter sent to every driver his age.
why.B: The narrator implies her father caused the dent and blamed someone else.
why.C: Correct — they had been “failing to say” it for two years and wanted a stranger to say it for them.
why.D: The test was required at his age, not arranged by them.

context: In paragraph 2, the narrator admits that her hope “does me no credit.” As used here, the word “credit” most nearly means:

choices.text: belief.
honour.
a loan.
a listing among the makers.

why.A: In some phrases “credit” means belief, but she is not saying she will be disbelieved; she is judging her own hope.
why.B: Correct — she means the hope reflects badly on her; it earns her no esteem.
why.C: The financial sense is the everyday one, but nothing here is borrowed or owed.
why.D: That is the sense of film credits, which has no place in the sentence.

context: The detail that the father once complained that a newspaper’s “crossword was getting easier” (paragraph 1) mainly serves to:

choices.text: show him as proud and quick to take a general matter personally.
suggest that his mind was declining along with his driving.
explain why the licensing office sent him a form letter.
show that he spent more of his time on puzzles than on driving.

why.A: Correct — it follows “He took it personally anyway,” as an example of the kind of man who would.
why.B: A man who finds the crossword too easy is being shown as sharp, not declining.
why.C: The letter went to every driver his age; the crossword has nothing to do with it.
why.D: The detail is about his character, not how he spent his time.

context: The narrator describes her father holding the printed result “like a diploma” (paragraph 5). The comparison suggests that he:

choices.text: meant to frame the result and hang it at home.
was surprised to receive a certificate instead of a licence.
was embarrassed by the examiner’s remark about his turn.
regarded passing as an achievement worth showing off.

why.A: This takes the comparison literally; nothing is said about framing it.
why.B: The examiner explains that the licence will follow; he shows no surprise.
why.C: Holding the result in both hands suggests pride, not embarrassment.
why.D: Correct — a diploma is proof of something earned, and paragraph 6 explains that proving he could still pass was what he wanted.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward her own hope that her father would fail (paragraph 2) is best described as:

choices.text: defiantly proud.
coldly indifferent.
candidly ashamed.
openly amused.

why.A: She admits the hope reflects badly on her.
why.B: Her rehearsing of kind words later shows she cares a great deal.
why.C: Correct — she says “plainly” that the hope “does me no credit.”
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph treats the hope as a joke.

context: Paragraphs 3 through 5 are mainly organized to:

choices.text: compare the father’s driving in 1961, when he first learned, with the way he drives today.
build toward the failure the narrator expects and then deliver a pass instead.
explain the rules of the road test in the order they are applied.
describe the examiner’s career and her view of older drivers.

why.A: 1961 dates the handbook he learned from; his driving then is never described.
why.B: Correct — the practice, the wait, and her rehearsed kind words lead up to “He passed.”
why.C: No rules of the test are described.
why.D: The examiner is described in two sentences, and her views are never given.

context: How does the narrator’s view in the final paragraph differ from what she wanted in paragraph 2?

choices.text: At first she wanted someone else to settle the matter for him; by the end she sees he needed to settle it himself.
At first she thought he drove badly; by the end she believes he still drives well.
At first she wanted him to keep driving; by the end she wants him to stop.
At first she blamed the licensing office; by the end she blames herself for the test.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 2 wants “the state to do my job for me”; the last paragraph says a handed decision “would not have been the same thing.”
why.B: His passing invites this, but she never says his driving is good, and he stops driving at once.
why.C: This reverses her view; she hoped from the start that he would stop.
why.D: She never blames the office, and the test was required, not her doing.

context: Which quotation best supports the idea that the father had privately decided to stop driving before the test?

choices.text: “He was, I noticed, getting better”
“He took it personally anyway”
“commenting on my following distance”
“he had not wanted to for some time”

why.A: This describes his parking practice, which points toward driving on, not stopping.
why.B: This concerns the letter, not any decision about driving.
why.C: This happens after the test and shows only his habit of criticism.
why.D: Correct — his wish to stop predates the test.

context: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.text: argue that forecasters should give up numbers and describe rain in words instead.
show that most forecasts of rain turn out to be wrong.
explain what a rain probability means and why listeners so often misread it.
describe how weather services use radar to predict rain.

why.A: Paragraph 4 argues that words are “not a cure.”
why.B: The passage is about understanding forecasts, not about their accuracy.
why.C: Correct — the passage defines the number, traces the confusion to how it was presented, and proposes saying what it refers to.
why.D: Radar is never discussed.

context: According to the passage, which of the following does a rain probability tell a listener?

choices.text: How heavy the rain is likely to be if any falls at the place named in the forecast.
How often rain falls at that place on days that resemble the one forecast.
How much of the day is likely to be wet.
How many of the forecasters expect rain.

why.A: Paragraph 2 says the number “says nothing about how hard the rain will be.”
why.B: Correct — paragraph 2: rain falls at the location “on about three days in ten” on days like tomorrow.
why.C: “Thirty percent of the day” is one of the misreadings listed in paragraph 1.
why.D: This too is one of the misreadings in paragraph 1.

context: Based on paragraph 3, the psychologists’ findings suggest that listeners’ confusion comes mainly from:

choices.text: how, and for how long, forecasters in each place had presented the numbers.
a general weakness in arithmetic that schooling has failed to correct.
differences in how often it actually rains in the cities surveyed.
forecasters’ use of words like “likely” in place of numbers.

why.A: Correct — the pattern “tracked how long each city’s forecasters had been broadcasting probabilities and how they had explained them.”
why.B: A common belief, but the paragraph says “People were not failing at arithmetic.”
why.C: Cities do differ in rainfall, but the paragraph ties the pattern to forecasting practice, not climate.
why.D: Vague words are the subject of paragraph 4, not the cause identified here.

context: As used in paragraph 5, the word “quieter” most nearly means:

choices.text: softer in sound.
calmer in manner.
smaller in size.
less noticed.

why.A: Nothing about the problem makes a sound; the word is used in a narrowed sense.
why.B: The word describes a problem, which has no manner.
why.C: The paragraph goes on to show the problem can empty a number of meaning; it is not small.
why.D: Correct — the problem is one that draws less attention than the listener’s confusion.

context: The example of a five percent chance becoming a twenty percent chance on the evening broadcast (paragraph 5) serves mainly to:

choices.text: prove that commercial forecasters set out to deceive their listeners.
illustrate how quickly the weather can change between morning and evening.
show how a well-meant lean toward warning can empty the number of meaning.
show that listeners generally prefer larger numbers to smaller ones.

why.A: Inflating a number sounds like deception, but the paragraph says “Nobody is lying, exactly.”
why.B: The weather does not change; the same model figure is presented differently.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph ends by saying listeners learn to ignore the inflated figure “and the number stops carrying information.”
why.D: The paragraph says nothing about listeners’ preferences.

context: The claim that words “hide the disagreement about it” (paragraph 4) suggests that:

choices.text: forecasters choose vague words on purpose so that their own mistakes are harder to catch.
people who hear the same word may hold very different estimates without knowing it.
words reduce the uncertainty in a forecast.
people argue more about words than about numbers.

why.A: The disagreement is among listeners, not something forecasters hide.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph says two listeners hearing the same word may act on estimates “that differ by half.”
why.C: The sentence before says “Words do not remove the uncertainty.”
why.D: The point is that disagreement is concealed, not that people argue.

context: The author’s attitude toward the fix described in paragraph 6 is best described as:

choices.text: approving, precisely because it asks so little.
disappointed that it does not go further.
doubtful that it has ever been tried.
eager to turn every listener into a statistician.

why.A: Correct — the author calls it “modest” and adds that it need not make listeners statisticians: “It does not need to.”
why.B: Calling the fix “modest” might suggest this, but the author treats its modesty as a strength.
why.C: The author says it has been tried and describes services that use it.
why.D: The author says the fix does not need to do that.

context: The passage opens with:

choices.text: a report of the psychologists’ study.
a brief history of weather forecasting.
an argument about the side effects of medication.
a familiar forecast and several common misreadings of it.

why.A: The study appears in paragraph 3.
why.B: No history of forecasting is given.
why.C: Medication is mentioned only in the last paragraph.
why.D: Correct — the first paragraph quotes the forecast and lists three incompatible readings.

context: According to paragraph 5, how do listeners treat unforecast rain compared with sunshine that arrives despite a warning?

choices.text: They forget the rain but complain about the sunshine.
They blame the forecaster just as much for the sunshine as for the rain.
They remember the rain but forget the sunshine, or recall it fondly.
They pay no attention to either one.

why.A: This reverses the paragraph.
why.B: The forecaster is blamed “only for the first kind of error.”
why.C: Correct — the paragraph says exactly this.
why.D: The unforecast rain is remembered.

context: Which statement from the passage best supports the claim that confusion about rain probabilities can be reduced?

choices.text: “Some weather services now attach a sentence to their forecasts”
“The pattern tracked how long each city’s forecasters had been broadcasting probabilities and how they had explained them”
“Numbers invite a false precision”
“Nobody is lying, exactly.”

why.A: This is tempting, but it shows only that the fix exists; it gives no evidence that it reduces confusion.
why.B: Correct — if understanding varies with how the numbers were explained, then better explanation can change it.
why.C: This describes a drawback of numbers, not a way to lessen confusion.
why.D: This concerns inflated figures, not whether confusion can be reduced.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Since tips track service only weakly, the real question is who should bear the risk of an unsteady income.
Tipping should be abolished because it began as an undemocratic foreign custom that critics once called a form of bribery.
Diners tip generously mainly because they want to reward good service.
Servers earn more under tipping than they would under any fixed wage.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 6 says arguments should stop pretending tips reward service and names “the honest question.”
why.B: The author says “None of this means tipping should, or will, disappear”; the history is one paragraph.
why.C: This is the belief the passage calls “mostly wrong.”
why.D: Paragraph 4 says a skilled server in a busy restaurant can earn more, not every server.

context: According to the passage, which factor raises the size of a tip?

choices.text: The server standing beside the table.
The diner’s rating of the service, above all.
The number of diners at the table.
The size of the bill.

why.A: Paragraph 2 names the reverse: tips rise when she crouches rather than standing over it.
why.B: The connection to service ratings is “real but remarkably weak,” not the main factor.
why.C: Party size is never mentioned.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 2 says tips rise with the bill, and paragraph 5 repeats that tips depend on “the bill and the sunshine.”

context: The passage suggests that the restaurants that “have quietly gone back” to tipping most likely did so because:

choices.text: the laws against tipping had all been repealed.
their prices had fallen too low to pay the fixed wage they had promised their staff.
servers or diners, or both, missed something tipping gave them.
diners began to rate their service more highly.

why.A: Those laws were repealed in the 1920s; this concerns modern restaurants.
why.B: Abolition meant raising prices, not lowering them.
why.C: Correct — the same paragraph says abolition asks both groups “to give up something they value.”
why.D: Nothing connects ratings to the return to tipping.

context: As used in paragraph 3, the word “inevitable” most nearly means:

choices.text: widely admired.
bound to exist.
easy to enforce.
foreign in origin.

why.A: Nothing in the paragraph concerns admiration.
why.B: Correct — the custom did not always seem certain to be here; it was once “argued about rather than assumed.”
why.C: Enforcement is discussed for the laws against tipping, not for tipping itself.
why.D: The paragraph says tipping was seen as foreign, but that is not what the word means.

context: The author mentions the state laws against tipping (paragraph 3) mainly to show that:

choices.text: tipping was once argued about rather than taken for granted.
tipping remains illegal in several states, though the laws are rarely enforced.
laws against tipping were easy to enforce.
tipping first began in the United States.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph ends by saying the laws are a reminder that “the practice was once argued about rather than assumed.”
why.B: Every one of the laws was repealed by the late 1920s.
why.C: They were “almost impossible to enforce.”
why.D: It was regarded as a European import.

context: The author says a diner who tips is “taking part in a ritual” (paragraph 5). The word “ritual” suggests that tipping:

choices.text: is a religious custom that has lost its first meaning.
gives the diner real control over how a server behaves.
is carried out in exactly the same way in every restaurant, whatever its size or price.
is done for the satisfaction of doing it more than for the effect it claims.

why.A: This takes “ritual” literally; nothing religious is discussed.
why.B: This is what the diner believes, but the sentence before says she is “not steering the server’s behaviour in any meaningful way.”
why.C: Rituals can be uniform, but the passage never claims tipping is; the word points to belief, not sameness.
why.D: Correct — the ritual “allows her to believe” she steers the server when, the paragraph argues, she does not.

context: The author’s treatment of the defenders of tipping in paragraph 4 is best described as:

choices.text: dismissive, treating their arguments as excuses.
admiring, adopting their view as the author’s own.
fair-minded, granting that their case has real force.
sarcastic, mocking servers who prefer tips.

why.A: The author puts their case at length and without mockery.
why.B: The next paragraph begins “But,” and argues the case is weakest where it concerns service.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph opens “Defenders of tipping have a real case, and it deserves to be put fairly.”
why.D: The final paragraph says such servers “are not fools.”

context: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: It traces the history of tipping from its origins to the present in strict order of time.
It challenges a common belief, gives evidence and history, grants the other side its case, and then recasts the question.
It compares tipping customs in several countries and ranks them from best to worst.
It describes one restaurant’s trial of fixed wages and then reports the results.

why.A: The history occupies only paragraph 3.
why.B: Correct — paragraphs 1–3 challenge the belief, paragraph 4 concedes, and paragraphs 5–7 reframe the issue as one of risk.
why.C: Only the United States is discussed, apart from the reference to Europe.
why.D: No single restaurant’s trial is described.

context: The author contrasts a server in “a busy, expensive restaurant” with one in “a quiet diner across town” (paragraph 5) in order to show that:

choices.text: what a server earns from tips depends more on where she works than on skill.
servers in expensive restaurants are more skilled than those in diners.
diners in quiet places tend to tip more generously.
a fixed wage would pay both servers exactly the same.

why.A: Correct — the first does well “mainly because she works in a busy, expensive restaurant, not because she is better at her job.”
why.B: The paragraph denies this.
why.C: Nothing is said about how diners in quiet places tip.
why.D: The paragraph does not discuss fixed wages.

context: Which detail does the author offer as evidence that tips depend on things other than service?

choices.text: Several states once passed laws against tipping.
Servers are divided about working for a fixed wage.
Diners mention the service when asked about tips.
Tips rise when the weather outside is sunny.

why.A: This is history of the custom, not evidence about what drives tips.
why.B: This concerns servers’ preferences, not what tips depend on.
why.C: This shows what diners believe, which the passage says is mistaken.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 2 lists sunny weather among cues unrelated to service.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: House numbers were invented mainly so that governments could tax and conscript people.
Landmark directions serve most neighbourhoods better than numbered addresses do.
Whether people accept an address depends less on how it works than on what it arrives with.
Codes for small squares of the earth will soon replace street addresses.

why.A: This is the point of paragraph 3, which paragraph 4 calls “not the whole truth.”
why.B: Paragraph 2 says landmarks succeed only for those who already belong.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 6 says the technical problem “was always the easier half” and ties acceptance to whether an address came with something residents wanted.
why.D: The author says only that the codes are clever and that trust is a separate question.

context: According to the passage, eighteenth-century governments introduced house numbers in order to:

choices.text: help letters, doctors, and ambulances find homes quickly in narrow, crowded streets.
locate households for taxes, conscription, and the lodging of soldiers.
answer residents’ requests for them.
settle disputes over who owned the land.

why.A: These are benefits named in paragraph 4, not the reasons governments gave numbers.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 lists these reasons.
why.C: Paragraph 3 says numbers “did not come because residents asked for them.”
why.D: Land titles come up only in paragraph 6, in a modern context.

context: The passage suggests that an addressing scheme is most likely to be accepted by residents when it:

choices.text: arrives together with a service or right the residents themselves wanted.
has a clever technical design that can locate every house precisely.
is carried out quickly by officials before residents can object.
replaces landmarks that people from outside cannot recognize.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 6 says such addresses have “usually been welcomed,” sometimes painted by residents themselves.
why.B: Precision sounds like a selling point, but paragraph 5 says trust “is not one that cleverness answers.”
why.C: Imposed addresses were resisted, so speed would not help.
why.D: That is a real advantage of addresses, but the passage ties acceptance to what residents want, not to outsiders’ convenience.

context: As used in paragraph 4, the word “exclusion” most nearly means:

choices.text: deliberate privacy.
official punishment.
a legal exemption.
being shut out.

why.A: The sentence contrasts exclusion with freedom; it is a loss, not a chosen privacy.
why.B: No one is being punished; the lack of an address simply bars access.
why.C: An exemption would be a benefit; here the word names a cost.
why.D: Correct — people without addresses are shut out of bank accounts, voting, and more.

context: The examples of the ambulance, the letter, and the bank account in paragraph 4 mainly serve to:

choices.text: prove that addresses were first invented to deliver mail.
illustrate how governments used numbers to tax households.
show what an address makes possible, balancing the account of addresses as tools of control.
suggest that most people would rather remain hard to find.

why.A: Paragraph 3 says numbers came so governments could find people.
why.B: Taxation is paragraph 3; these examples show benefits to residents.
why.C: Correct — they follow “it is not the whole truth” and show the other half of the story.
why.D: The paragraph argues the reverse: being hard to find is a cost, usually paid by the poor.

context: The phrase “the state closing its fist” (paragraph 4) refers to:

choices.text: governments shutting their offices to the public once the numbering was complete.
governments tightening their hold on the people they could now locate.
the state running short of money.
officials refusing to number houses at all.

why.A: This takes the image literally.
why.B: Correct — it sums up paragraph 3, where numbers let officials tax, conscript, and lodge soldiers.
why.C: Nothing in the passage concerns state finances.
why.D: The paragraph before describes officials numbering houses, not refusing to.

context: The author’s attitude toward the schemes that give each small square of the earth a code (paragraph 5) is best described as:

choices.text: impressed by their design but unsure that design alone will earn trust.
dismissive, since the author regards them as a gimmick.
enthusiastic, seeing them as the answer to the problem of trust.
indifferent, treating them as a minor detail.

why.A: Correct — “These systems are clever,” the author says, before adding that trust “is not one that cleverness answers.”
why.B: The closing doubt invites this, but the author plainly calls the systems clever.
why.C: The author says cleverness does not answer the question of trust.
why.D: The author weighs them with care, noting who likes and distrusts them.

context: Paragraph 4 differs from paragraph 3 in that paragraph 4:

choices.text: rejects outright the claim that governments numbered houses in order to find the people living in them.
continues the history of numbering into the nineteenth century.
offers evidence that residents never resisted house numbers.
complicates the account of addresses as tools of control by describing what their absence costs.

why.A: It says that account is “not the whole truth,” which qualifies it rather than rejecting it.
why.B: Paragraph 4 turns to the present, not the next century.
why.C: Paragraph 3 says numbers were smeared with mud, and paragraph 4 does not dispute it.
why.D: Correct — it grants “there is truth in that telling” and then adds what addresses make possible.

context: According to paragraph 2, directions given by landmarks work well for neighbours but badly for:

choices.text: people who share the landmarks.
the woman who sells eggs.
anyone arriving from outside.
the residents who have lived there longest.

why.A: Those are the neighbours, for whom the system works.
why.B: She is one of the landmarks, not someone the system fails.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph says so directly.
why.D: Long residents share the landmarks, so the system works for them.

context: Which detail best supports the author’s claim that eighteenth-century residents understood why their houses were being numbered?

choices.text: Some cities now let residents name their own streets.
Newly painted numbers were smeared with mud or scraped away.
Rural houses were known by family or farm names.
An ambulance can find a numbered house in the dark.

why.A: This is a recent practice, not evidence about the eighteenth century.
why.B: Correct — residents resisted the numbers because they grasped what they were for.
why.C: This concerns naming in wealthy countries, not residents’ grasp of numbering.
why.D: This is a modern benefit of addresses.

context: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.text: defend footnotes as the place where an argument shows what it depends on.
urge publishers to move every note to a website.
describe the life and work of Edward Gibbon.
show that most footnotes are written to display the writer’s learning rather than to support a claim.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 2 states the thesis: the footnote “is the place where the argument admits what it depends on.”
why.B: The author criticises that practice.
why.C: Gibbon is one example in paragraph 4.
why.D: Paragraph 5 grants that notes are sometimes abused, but that is not the passage’s point.

context: According to the passage, what happens to a sentence in a history book when its note is removed?

choices.text: It becomes cleaner and easier to follow.
It becomes more honest, since nothing is hidden in small type.
It becomes longer, since the note’s qualifications move into it.
It becomes an assertion the reader must take on trust.

why.A: This is the view the author argues against: the sentence “does not become cleaner.”
why.B: Paragraph 6 says such a book “has not become more honest by becoming less cluttered.”
why.C: Paragraph 4 mentions qualifications that would clutter a sentence, but never says they move into it when a note is cut.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 2 says this directly, and paragraph 6 agrees that removing sources makes a book’s debts “harder to inspect.”

context: The passage suggests that a writer whose sources are hard to find may be:

choices.text: more honest than a writer who uses footnotes.
more likely to be praised by scholars.
less careful, knowing that fewer readers will check.
required by publishers to list sources online.

why.A: Paragraph 6 denies that such a book has become more honest.
why.B: The praise in paragraph 3 is for readability, not from scholars.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 6 says such a book gains “a writer who knows that fewer readers will check.”
why.D: The passage describes a trend among publishers, not a requirement placed on writers.

context: As used in paragraph 6, the word “debts” most nearly means:

choices.text: money owed to its publisher.
the sources it relies on.
its errors of fact.
its promises to its readers.

why.A: This is the everyday sense, but the paragraph is about sources, not money.
why.B: Correct — a book owes its claims to its sources, and hiding them makes those debts “harder to inspect.”
why.C: The paragraph concerns where claims come from, not whether they are mistaken.
why.D: The book owes its claims to sources; nothing is said about promises to readers.

context: The author mentions Edward Gibbon (paragraph 4) mainly as an example of:

choices.text: a writer whose notes were full of life and personality.
a writer who used notes only to show off his reading.
a scholar who opposed the use of footnotes.
a publisher who moved notes to the back of the book.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph opens by calling the footnote “a place of unexpected life” and then describes Gibbon’s arguments, doubts, and jokes.
why.B: That abuse is described in paragraph 5, not linked to Gibbon.
why.C: Gibbon used them richly.
why.D: Gibbon was a historian, not a publisher.

context: The statement that notes “let a second voice speak underneath it” (paragraph 4) suggests that footnotes:

choices.text: are usually written by a different author.
exist mainly to contradict the main text.
are meant to be read aloud.
let a writer add doubts, jokes, and qualifications beside the main argument.

why.A: This takes “second voice” literally; the voice is the same writer’s.
why.B: Notes can hold qualifications and counterexamples, but they support the text rather than oppose it.
why.C: The image is about the writer’s voice on the page, not reading aloud.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph lists exactly these as what notes can hold.

context: The author’s attitude toward writers who use notes “as a display case” (paragraph 5) is best described as:

choices.text: admiring.
indifferent.
critical.
envious.

why.A: The author treats this use as an abuse of the form.
why.B: The author warns readers to be suspicious of such notes, which is not indifference.
why.C: Correct — the author calls such notes “a performance” of care rather than evidence of it.
why.D: Nothing suggests the author wishes to write that way.

context: Which choice best describes how paragraphs 5 and 6 relate to each other?

choices.text: Paragraph 5 praises footnotes for their liveliness; paragraph 6 turns to criticising the ways they are abused.
Paragraph 5 admits that notes are abused; paragraph 6 argues that this does not count against notes.
Paragraph 5 describes Gibbon’s notes; paragraph 6 describes a modern writer’s.
Paragraph 5 proposes moving notes online; paragraph 6 reports the results.

why.A: The order is the reverse: paragraph 5 criticises abuses, and paragraph 6 defends the form.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 6 opens “But the case against bad footnotes is not a case against footnotes.”
why.C: Gibbon is discussed in paragraph 4.
why.D: The author opposes moving notes online.

context: According to paragraph 2, how does a footnote differ from the sentence it supports in a history book?

choices.text: The sentence says that something happened; the note says how the writer knows.
The sentence gives the evidence; the note draws the conclusion.
The sentence is written for scholars; the note is written for general readers.
The sentence can be checked; the note must simply be trusted.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 2 draws exactly this contrast.
why.B: This reverses the roles.
why.C: The paragraph distinguishes them by what they say, not by audience.
why.D: This reverses the point: the note is what allows checking.

context: Which quotation best supports the author’s claim that footnotes serve a reader who may want to disagree?

choices.text: “A reader is right to be suspicious of notes that run longer than the text they support.”
“The main text speaks in one voice.”
“Few readers seem to miss them.”
“a writer telling you exactly where to push if you think the argument will not hold”

why.A: This mentions a sceptical reader, which is tempting, but it warns against bad notes rather than showing what notes offer.
why.B: This contrasts text and notes but says nothing about disagreement.
why.C: This describes readers’ indifference, not what notes offer them.
why.D: Correct — the note points the doubtful reader to the exact place to test the argument.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Palace staircases were designed for display rather than for everyday use.
Modern building codes have made stairs safer than they have ever been in the long history of architecture.
A stair succeeds by fitting the body so consistently that we never have to think about it.
Architects should build staircases in place of lifts in tall buildings.

why.A: This is paragraph 4’s point, and paragraph 5 shows those stairs obeyed the same principle as ordinary ones.
why.B: Codes are mentioned once, as evidence of how sensitive walkers are to uneven steps.
why.C: Correct — the passage opens and closes on this point, and paragraph 5 shows that even the grand stair depended on it.
why.D: The author would not want to climb forty floors and grants there are good reasons for lifts.

context: According to the passage, why must a steeper step be shallower?

choices.text: Steep steps need less stone and timber to build.
The leg that climbs it has only one natural stride length.
Building codes limit the total height of a single flight.
Shallow steps are easier for the eye to judge.

why.A: Paragraph 2 says the rule is about the body “rather than about stone or timber.”
why.B: Correct — paragraph 2 gives this reason: “the leg that climbs it has one natural length of stride.”
why.C: The codes mentioned in paragraph 3 limit variation between steps, not total height.
why.D: The passage says walkers stop looking at steps, so the eye is not the reason.

context: It can reasonably be inferred from paragraph 3 that a person is most likely to trip on a step that:

choices.text: differs slightly in height from the steps before it.
is much steeper than the others and plainly visible.
is the very first step in a flight.
is made of marble rather than of wood.

why.A: Correct — the body lifts the foot to a learned height, so a step that is off by “less than the thickness of a finger” catches it.
why.B: A visible difference would be seen; the danger is a step nobody is watching.
why.C: Walkers do look at the first few steps, so those are the ones they see.
why.D: The paragraph says nothing about materials.

context: As used in paragraph 1, the word “intimately” most nearly means:

choices.text: secretly.
romantically.
rarely.
closely.

why.A: Nothing about using stairs is hidden.
why.B: That sense has no place in a sentence about stairs.
why.C: The sentence says we use stairs a great deal while noticing them little.
why.D: Correct — we use stairs with our bodies, in direct contact, as the next sentences explain.

context: The statement that the grand staircase’s “effect depended entirely on the climber not having to think” (paragraph 5) serves mainly to:

choices.text: explain why grand staircases were built with deliberately low steps that slowed every climber down.
argue that grand staircases were more dangerous than ordinary ones.
show that the theatrical stair relied on the same consistency as the humble one.
suggest that palace guests were careless about where they stepped.

why.A: The low steps were explained in paragraph 4 as slowing the climber; this sentence concerns consistency, not height.
why.B: Nothing suggests palace stairs were more dangerous.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph argues the two traditions share a principle, and this is the point where they meet.
why.D: The point is that a good stair freed guests from watching their feet, not that they were careless.

context: The author calls a staircase “less a structure than a promise” (paragraph 4). The image suggests that a stair:

choices.text: should be built to outlast every other part of the building.
must keep the pattern its first steps set for the body.
stands for the architect’s commitment to the owner.
can be altered later if it does not suit its users.

why.A: The promise concerns consistency, not durability.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 explains that the body assumes every step will be like the ones before; the stair must keep that promise.
why.C: The promise is made to the climber’s body, not to an owner.
why.D: Nothing in the image concerns changing a stair.

context: In paragraph 6, the author’s attitude toward modern buildings that hide their stairs is best described as:

choices.text: regretful.
approving.
outraged.
amused.

why.A: Correct — the author grants the good reasons but says plainly, “something has been lost.”
why.B: The author accepts the reasons but laments the loss.
why.C: The author concedes “There are good reasons for this,” which is not outrage.
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph is played for humour.

context: How does paragraph 5 relate to paragraph 4?

choices.text: It rejects the claim in paragraph 4 that consistency is a stair’s chief virtue.
It gives a second example of a staircase built for display.
It explains how grand staircases gave way to modern stairwells.
It shows that the two kinds of stair contrasted in paragraph 4 rest on one principle.

why.A: Paragraph 4 calls that claim strange for a stage, which invites this reading, but paragraph 5 confirms it.
why.B: No new staircase is introduced.
why.C: Modern stairwells are the subject of paragraph 6.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 5 declines to set the traditions “against each other” and shows both depend on consistency.

context: According to the passage, how did the steps of palace staircases differ from ordinary steps?

choices.text: They were uneven, so that guests would watch their feet.
They were steeper, so that hosts could make an entrance.
They were lower and deeper, suiting a slower stride.
They ignored the relation between height and stride.

why.A: Paragraph 5 says a guest who had to watch her feet “could not make an entrance.”
why.B: They were low and shallow, not steep.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 4 calls them deliberately low, and paragraph 5 says they “simply chose a slower stride.”
why.D: Paragraph 5 says they “obeyed the same relation.”

context: Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that walkers rely on a stair’s regularity rather than on watching it?

choices.text: Blondel’s rule is still written into building codes.
Walkers glance at the first few steps and then look away.
Palace stairs were built to be watched from the landings.
Modern stairs are placed in fire-resistant shafts.

why.A: This shows the rule has lasted, not how walkers use their eyes.
why.B: Correct — after the first few steps, the body moves on what it has learned rather than what it sees.
why.C: This concerns onlookers, not the climber’s own attention.
why.D: This concerns where stairs are put, not how people climb them.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Folk songs lived by changing, and the fixed versions that recording allowed have largely ended that life.
Collectors who saw variation as decay were wrong, because every change to a song is an improvement.
Cecil Sharp found English ballads surviving unchanged in the Appalachian mountains.
Recording has done nothing but good for folk music by preserving it.

why.A: Correct — the passage defends variation as the life of the songs and ends by saying recording has stopped them changing.
why.B: The first half is the passage’s view, but paragraph 5 calls the claim that every variant improves a song “sentimental.”
why.C: Paragraph 3 says “The songs had changed.”
why.D: Paragraph 7 says recording is “not entirely to be regretted,” and then names its price.

context: According to paragraph 1, why did Child often print more than one text of a ballad?

choices.text: He could not decide which version was the original.
Printers had made errors in the earlier editions.
Each text came from a different country.
Singers sang it differently.

why.A: The idea of recovering an original belongs to paragraph 2, not to Child’s reason for printing variants.
why.B: No printing errors are mentioned.
why.C: Different singers, not countries, account for the versions.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph gives exactly this reason.

context: The passage suggests that the collectors who quietly improved the texts they printed were, in effect:

choices.text: recovering the songs as their first poets had actually written them.
recording the songs exactly as the singers had performed them.
changing the songs themselves while believing they were undoing change.
following the method later recommended by Cecil Sharp.

why.A: This is what the collectors believed, but the passage treats the supposed original as an assumption, not something they recovered.
why.B: Smoothing and restoring lines is the opposite of exact recording.
why.C: Correct — they thought they were “repairing the damage rather than adding to it,” yet smoothing lines is itself a change.
why.D: Sharp is presented as undermining the collectors’ view, not endorsing their method.

context: As used in paragraph 6, the word “faithfully” most nearly means:

choices.text: loyally.
accurately.
religiously.
hopefully.

why.A: Loyalty to a person is the everyday sense, but here the word describes exact copying.
why.B: Correct — a singer learning from a record reproduces that one version exactly.
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph concerns religion or devotion.
why.D: The word describes how closely she copies, not her hopes.

context: The account of Cecil Sharp’s travels in paragraph 3 mainly serves to:

choices.text: provide evidence against the view that variation meant decay.
show that the ballads were first composed in America.
explain how Child gathered his 305 ballads.
describe the recording equipment Sharp carried.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph opens “That view did not survive contact with the singers,” and Sharp found changed songs that were “more alive.”
why.B: The ballads had been carried from Britain.
why.C: Sharp’s travels came later and are separate from Child’s collection.
why.D: No equipment is mentioned; recording enters only in paragraph 6.

context: The image of songs worn down “like a coin passed from hand to hand” (paragraph 2) expresses:

choices.text: the author’s own view that ballads lose a little of their value each time they are sung.
the idea that ballads were once sold for money.
the speed with which ballads spread between countries.
the early collectors’ belief that each singing wore away part of an original.

why.A: The image is vivid enough to seem like the author’s claim, but paragraph 3 says the view “did not survive contact with the singers.”
why.B: This takes the coin literally.
why.C: The image is about wear, not speed.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 2 reports what collectors “assumed,” and the coin image belongs to that view.

context: The author’s attitude toward the claim that “every variant is an improvement” (paragraph 5) is best described as:

choices.text: approving, since it is the author’s own view.
undecided, since the evidence is mixed.
sceptical, treating it as sentimental.
indifferent, since it concerns only collectors.

why.A: The author rejects it: “Change is not always growth.”
why.B: The author states a clear position on the claim.
why.C: Correct — the author says whoever claims it “is being as sentimental as the collector” who called every variant a ruin.
why.D: The claim is attributed to defenders of the folk process, and the author engages it directly.

context: Paragraph 1 mainly introduces:

choices.text: Cecil Sharp’s journey through the Appalachians.
the variation Child met in collecting ballads.
the effect of recording on folk songs.
the author’s own experience as a singer.

why.A: Sharp appears in paragraph 3.
why.B: Correct — “The ballads would not hold still.”
why.C: Recording is the subject of paragraph 6.
why.D: The author never describes singing.

context: How does the author’s view of variation in paragraph 5 differ from the early collectors’ view in paragraph 2?

choices.text: The author grants that some changes are losses but denies that change is decay in itself.
The author holds that every change improves a song, where the collectors held that every change ruined one.
The author agrees with the collectors but thinks recording has made the damage worse.
The author believes the originals can still be recovered, while the collectors did not.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 5 admits mishearings and dropped verses, yet says change “is simply what happens to a song that is still in use.”
why.B: This pits two extremes against each other, but paragraph 5 rejects both of them.
why.C: The author disagrees with the collectors, and recording is said to have slowed change.
why.D: It was the collectors who hoped to recover originals.

context: Which quotation best supports the claim that recording made variation sound like error?

choices.text: “The songs had changed.”
“Change is not always growth.”
“the recordings preserve voices and styles that would otherwise have vanished”
“A version that departed from the record began to sound less like a variant and more like a mistake.”

why.A: This describes the Appalachian songs, before recording.
why.B: This concerns losses in oral change, not recording.
why.C: This names a benefit of recording, not its effect on how variants sound.
why.D: Correct — this states the shift directly.

context: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.text: argue that Celsius was a careless scientist.
show that global sea level is falling rather than rising.
explain why land once under ice sheets is still rising.
describe the history of Swedish harbour towns.

why.A: Paragraph 2 says Celsius “was right about the measurement.”
why.B: Paragraph 6 says the oceans “grow higher”; only the sea measured against rising land falls.
why.C: Correct — the passage explains rebound, extends it to other regions and the sinking bulges, and draws out its effect on planning.
why.D: Harbours are one clue in paragraph 1.

context: According to the passage, the land of Scandinavia sank during the ice age because:

choices.text: rising seas covered the land and slowly wore it down over many thousands of years.
the weight of the ice pressed the crust down into mantle rock that slowly flows.
earthquakes cracked the crust beneath the ice.
the melting ice carried the soil away with it.

why.A: The passage attributes the sinking to the ice’s weight, not the sea.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 explains that the crust sank because the mantle beneath it flows under steady pressure.
why.C: Earthquakes are never mentioned.
why.D: The land sank under the ice and rose when it melted.

context: The passage suggests that a harbour built centuries ago on the northern Gulf of Bothnia would today most likely be:

choices.text: too shallow, or too far from the water, to serve boats.
under deeper water than when it was first built.
unchanged, since the rise is too slow to notice.
sinking along with the bulge around the old ice sheet.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 1 describes harbours “growing too shallow,” and paragraph 2 explains that the land there is still rising.
why.B: Rising land means the water there is getting shallower, not deeper.
why.C: Paragraph 2 says the shoreline moves within a single lifetime.
why.D: The sinking bulges lie at the edges of the old ice, not in the Gulf of Bothnia.

context: As used in paragraph 4, the word “rebound” most nearly means:

choices.text: break apart into pieces.
sink further into the mantle.
freeze over again as it cools.
spring back up.

why.A: The land rises; it does not break.
why.B: This is the opposite of what the land does after the ice melts.
why.C: Nothing refreezes; the ice is gone.
why.D: Correct — the land rises again once the weight is gone.

context: The reference to “cold pitch or glacier ice” in paragraph 3 serves mainly to:

choices.text: suggest that the mantle is made of a tar-like substance.
explain why the Scandinavian ice sheet melted.
help readers picture how a solid can flow if given enough time.
show that the mantle is a liquid.

why.A: The comparison concerns how the rock behaves, not what it is made of.
why.B: The melting is not explained by this comparison.
why.C: Correct — the mantle is solid yet flows “very slowly,” as these familiar materials do.
why.D: The paragraph says the mantle is “solid.”

context: The statement that the ground of northern Sweden and Finland “still remembers the ice” (paragraph 4) suggests that:

choices.text: ice from the last ice age lies buried under the ground.
the land is still responding to a weight removed long ago.
people there still tell stories about the ice age.
the region will soon be covered by ice again.

why.A: This takes “remembers” literally; the ice has melted.
why.B: Correct — the sentence restates that the land “is still recovering” from the ice.
why.C: The sentence concerns the ground, not the people.
why.D: Nothing suggests the ice will return.

context: The author’s attitude toward Celsius is best described as:

choices.text: respectful of his measurement while noting that his explanation was wrong.
dismissive, treating his conclusion as a foolish mistake that no careful scholar would make.
reverent, presenting him as never having been mistaken.
indifferent, mentioning him only in passing.

why.A: Correct — “He was right about the measurement and wrong about the cause,” and his mark closes the passage as a lasting record.
why.B: “Wrong about the cause” could suggest this, but the author also notes that most scholars of his day agreed and that his measurement was right.
why.C: The author says plainly that he was wrong about the cause.
why.D: Celsius opens and closes the passage.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It lists regions of the world from the fastest rising to the fastest sinking.
It describes a series of experiments in the order they were run.
It argues that the ice age never reached Scandinavia.
It opens with a puzzle from 1731, explains its cause, extends the process to other regions, and returns to the rock.

why.A: No such ranking is given.
why.B: No experiments are described, only a measurement and later observations.
why.C: The passage says an ice sheet more than two kilometres thick covered Scandinavia.
why.D: Correct — Celsius’s mark begins and ends the passage, with the explanation and its wider effects between.

context: According to the passage, how does rebound affect coasts on land that bore the ice compared with coasts at the ice sheets’ former edges?

choices.text: Where the ice lay, the land is sinking; at the edges, it is rising.
Where the ice lay, the sea is rising faster; at the edges, it is falling.
Where the ice lay, rising land offsets the rising sea; at the edges, sinking land adds to it.
Both kinds of coast are rising, though the edges rise more slowly, just as Scotland does compared with Sweden.

why.A: This reverses the pattern; the edges were pushed up during the ice age but are subsiding now.
why.B: This reverses the effect on relative sea level.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 6 says the ground is “winning the race” in the Gulf of Bothnia, while on the sinking bulges “the two effects add together.”
why.D: Scotland lay under the ice; the edges are sinking, not rising.

context: Which detail from the passage shows that the land around Hudson Bay has risen?

choices.text: Celsius cut a line into a rock to mark the sea level.
Old beaches stand in staircases far above the present shore.
Parts of the Netherlands are sinking.
Satellites track the rise from year to year.

why.A: That rock is in the Gulf of Bothnia, not Hudson Bay.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 5 gives this as the sign of rebound there.
why.C: This concerns the edge of the old ice sheet in Europe.
why.D: Paragraph 4 describes satellite tracking of the Scandinavian rise.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A specialised memory lets the nutcracker recover its caches, and the surplus it buries plants the pines it relies on.
Whitebark pine forests grew from the seeds that forgetful nutcrackers failed to recover.
The nutcracker finds its buried seeds mainly by smell and by disturbed soil.
Birds that store food have better memories of every kind than other birds.

why.A: Correct — the passage moves from the bird’s memory to the pine that grows from its surplus caches.
why.B: Paragraph 6 says this “gets the story backward”: the forest grows from surplus, not forgetting.
why.C: Paragraph 2 says these explanations were tested and failed.
why.D: Paragraph 4 says nutcrackers do not stand out in other kinds of memory.

context: According to the passage, when researchers moved the landmarks in the test room, the nutcrackers searched:

choices.text: in the exact spots where they had buried their seeds, ignoring the moved landmarks.
near the caches that other birds had made.
at random until they found the seeds by smell.
in spots shifted by the same amount the landmarks had been moved.

why.A: This is where the seeds were, but the birds searched relative to the moved landmarks, not the original spots.
why.B: Paragraph 2 says they found other birds’ caches no better than chance.
why.C: Paragraph 2 says they were “not smelling seeds.”
why.D: Correct — paragraph 3 says they searched “shifted by just the amount the landmarks had been shifted.”

context: It can reasonably be inferred from paragraph 3 that relying on nearby landmarks helps a nutcracker in winter because:

choices.text: snow makes buried seeds easier to smell.
caches near trees are always dug more shallowly.
boulders and trees stay visible above the snow.
squirrels avoid caches placed near boulders.

why.A: The birds do not find seeds by smell.
why.B: Cache depth is not discussed in relation to landmarks.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph says snow “can bury the ground but not the boulders and trees.”
why.D: Squirrels appear only in paragraph 6, as raiders of caches.

context: As used in paragraph 6, the word “insurance” most nearly means:

choices.text: an unnecessary extra.
a reserve kept against possible loss.
a contract paid for in advance.
a guarantee that the bird will survive.

why.A: The surplus is more than the bird will usually eat, which invites this reading, but the paragraph says it is there for a reason.
why.B: Correct — the extra seed covers a long winter and caches lost to squirrels or mishaps.
why.C: That is the everyday sense of an insurance policy, but no contract or payment is involved.
why.D: Insurance reduces risk; nothing here guarantees survival.

context: The author mentions squirrels in paragraph 6 mainly as one reason that:

choices.text: a nutcracker buries more seed than it will need.
whitebark pine is declining across its range.
nutcrackers forget where their caches are.
buried seeds fail to grow in shallow soil.

why.A: Correct — some caches “will be raided by squirrels,” so the bird buries extra.
why.B: The decline in paragraph 7 is blamed on disease, beetles, and warming.
why.C: The paragraph says “The nutcracker does not forget much.”
why.D: Paragraph 5 says shallow soil is what a seedling needs.

context: The statement that the whitebark pine has “staked its future on the bird” (paragraph 5) suggests that the pine:

choices.text: was planted by people long ago to give the birds a steady supply of food.
produces seeds that harm birds that eat too many.
competes with the bird for space on the slopes.
depends on the nutcracker, having no other good way to spread its seeds.

why.A: People planting seedlings appears only in paragraph 7, as a recent response to decline.
why.B: Nothing suggests the seeds harm the birds.
why.C: The pine competes with other trees, not with the bird.
why.D: Correct — its seeds are wingless, the wind cannot spread them, and the bird is “close to the only disperser that matters.”

context: The author’s attitude toward the early scepticism about nutcracker memory (paragraph 2) is best described as:

choices.text: scornful, since the author treats the sceptics as foolish.
approving, since the author agrees with the sceptics that the birds rely mainly on smell.
understanding, since the author calls it reasonable before showing it was wrong.
puzzled, since the author cannot see why anyone doubted.

why.A: The author calls the scepticism reasonable.
why.B: The author reports that the smell explanation failed.
why.C: Correct — “the scepticism was reasonable,” the author says, and then describes the tests that answered it.
why.D: The author explains exactly why the doubt made sense.

context: Paragraph 4 mainly shifts the discussion from the nutcracker’s behaviour to:

choices.text: the trees it feeds on.
the structure of its brain.
the threats to its survival.
the design of laboratory tests.

why.A: The trees are the subject of paragraph 5.
why.B: Correct — it opens “The nutcracker’s brain reflects the demand” and discusses the hippocampus.
why.C: Threats are discussed in paragraph 7.
why.D: The tests were described in paragraphs 2 and 3.

context: According to paragraph 4, how do nutcrackers compare with related birds that do not store food?

choices.text: They have a larger hippocampus but do not stand out in other kinds of memory.
They have a better memory of every kind.
They have a smaller hippocampus but a much keener sense of smell than those birds.
They store less food but remember it for longer.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph says both things.
why.B: The paragraph calls this “too simple.”
why.C: Their hippocampus is larger, and smell was ruled out.
why.D: Nutcrackers are the ones that store food.

context: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that the forest grows from the bird’s success rather than its forgetfulness?

choices.text: “the forgotten seeds become the next generation of trees”
“a good number of them grow”
“They were remembering where they had put them.”
“It caches more seed than it will need”

why.A: This is the “happy accident” account that the author says “gets the story backward.”
why.B: This shows that unrecovered seeds grow, but not why they were left unrecovered.
why.C: This shows the bird’s memory, but says nothing about where the forest comes from.
why.D: Correct — the surplus comes from planning for loss, and paragraph 6 says the forest “grows from the insurance.”

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Every fever should be left untreated so the body can fight infection.
Fever is a malfunction of the brain’s thermostat caused by infection.
Fever is a costly defence the body chooses, so it should be weighed rather than reflexively suppressed.
Lizards and people fight infection in entirely different ways.

why.A: Paragraph 5 opens “None of this means that every fever should be left alone.”
why.B: Paragraph 2 says the shivering is “the thermostat working.”
why.C: Correct — the passage explains what fever does, grants when treating it makes sense, and rejects the reflex that treats it as the enemy.
why.D: The last paragraph says the lizard does “the same thing” our bodies do.

context: According to the passage, a person with a rising fever shivers because:

choices.text: the thermostat in the brain has stopped working properly because the infection has damaged it.
the brain’s temperature setting has been raised, so the body acts as if it were cold.
the infection has lowered the body’s temperature.
immune cells draw energy from muscle movement.

why.A: Paragraph 2 says the thermostat is working, at a new setting.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 2 says the body “behaves as it would in a cold room.”
why.C: The temperature is climbing, not falling.
why.D: No such link is described.

context: Based on the passage, which is the most reasonable conclusion about the lizard experiments?

choices.text: They suggest that raising body temperature helps an animal survive infection.
They prove that fever medicine is harmful to people.
They show that lizards produce fevers internally, as people do.
They show that warmth kills bacteria directly, whatever the animal’s condition.

why.A: Correct — infected lizards kept from warmer spots died more often.
