why.B: Many readers would draw this conclusion, but paragraph 6 says the human evidence is mixed and “the question remains open.”
why.C: Paragraph 4 says lizards raise their temperature “through behaviour alone.”
why.D: The passage says some microbes reproduce less well when warm, not that warmth kills them outright.

context: As used in paragraph 6, the word “reflex” most nearly means:

choices.text: a twitch of a muscle.
a careful decision.
a medical test.
an automatic habit.

why.A: That is the physical sense; here the word describes a habit of mind.
why.B: A reflex is the opposite of a considered choice.
why.C: Nothing in the sentence concerns testing.
why.D: Correct — the author objects to treating fever as the enemy without thinking.

context: The final sentence of the passage, about the lizard crawling toward a warm rock, mainly serves to:

choices.text: recommend treating a fever by lying in the sun.
show that lizards suffer far more from infection than people do, since they have no medicine.
suggest that human fever is the same defence the lizard achieves by behaviour.
admit that the lizard experiments may not apply to people.

why.A: This takes the image literally; the passage makes no such recommendation.
why.B: The sentence draws a likeness, not a contrast in suffering.
why.C: Correct — the lizard does “the same thing our own bodies were doing all along.”
why.D: The sentence claims the reverse, that the two are the same.

context: The author compares the part of the brain that controls temperature to “the thermostat in a house” (paragraph 2). The comparison suggests that this region:

choices.text: produces the body’s heat the way a furnace heats a house.
holds a setting that can be changed.
breaks down easily whenever the body falls ill.
lies close to the surface of the skin, where heat escapes.

why.A: The region sets the temperature; shivering and narrowed vessels produce and keep the heat.
why.B: Correct — the next sentence says signals during an infection “change its setting.”
why.C: Paragraph 2 says the thermostat keeps working.
why.D: The region is in the brain.

context: The author’s attitude toward doctors who recommend treating a fever for comfort (paragraph 5) is best described as:

choices.text: approving.
disapproving.
mocking.
puzzled.

why.A: Correct — the author says such doctors “are not ignoring the science. They are weighing it.”
why.B: The author defends them.
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph is scornful.
why.D: The author explains their reasons clearly.

context: Which choice best describes the role of paragraph 5 in the passage?

choices.text: It gives further laboratory evidence that fever helps.
It abandons the argument made in the earlier paragraphs and argues that every fever should be treated.
It describes how fever medicine acts in the body.
It qualifies the case for fever by granting when treatment makes sense.

why.A: The evidence ends in paragraph 4; paragraph 5 turns to exceptions.
why.B: Paragraph 6 continues the argument against treating fever as the enemy.
why.C: Only its effects on aches and temperature are noted.
why.D: Correct — it opens “None of this means that every fever should be left alone” and lists good reasons to treat one.

context: According to paragraph 7, how are the fever and the infection related?

choices.text: The fever is a poison made by the infection.
They are the same thing seen in two ways.
They arrive together but are on opposite sides.
The fever makes the infection stronger.

why.A: The fever is the body’s response, not the infection’s product.
why.B: The paragraph separates them onto opposite sides.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph says exactly this.
why.D: The passage argues that fever works against infection.

context: Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that fever is costly to the body?

choices.text: Lizards warm themselves by moving into the sun.
Each degree raises the rate at which energy is burned by about ten percent.
Some bacteria and viruses reproduce less well when the body around them is warmer.
A fever often ends in sweating.

why.A: This concerns how lizards raise their temperature, not its cost.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 gives this as the reason fever is “expensive.”
why.C: This is a benefit of fever, not a cost.
why.D: This explains how fever ends, not what it costs.

context: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

choices.text: question how much of Yellowstone’s change can be credited to the wolves.
argue that the wolves have had no real effect on the park’s elk, trees, or streams.
explain why beavers disappeared from Yellowstone’s streams.
call for wolves to be removed from the park again.

why.A: Correct — Passage B weighs other causes and patchy recovery, then says the wolves “are not the whole of it.”
why.B: Its doubts might suggest this, but the last paragraph says “None of this means the wolves have done nothing.”
why.C: That is the point of one paragraph, offered as a reason the willows have not recovered.
why.D: Passage B never suggests removing the wolves.

context: According to Passage A, how did the elk change after wolves returned?

choices.text: They moved outside the park, where hunters killed many of them.
They grew more numerous as their rivals declined.
They began to eat aspen instead of willow.
They grew fewer and warier and browsed less along the streams.

why.A: Hunting outside the park is a point made in Passage B, not A.
why.B: Passage A says they grew fewer.
why.C: Passage A says they browsed less on both.
why.D: Correct — Passage A says the elk “grew fewer and warier” and spent less time browsing streamside trees.

context: It can be inferred that the author of Passage B would regard the fall in elk numbers after 1995, taken alone, as:

choices.text: strong proof that fear of wolves drove the elk out of the valleys where they had crowded.
evidence that hunting outside the park had stopped.
weak evidence of the wolves’ influence, since other causes were at work.
a sign that the years of drought had ended.

why.A: This is close to Passage A’s account; Passage B says the fear claim “has proved harder still to confirm.”
why.B: Passage B says hunting was heavy in those years.
why.C: Correct — Passage B lists hunting, drought, bears, and cougars, and says untangling the wolves’ share is difficult.
why.D: Passage B names drought as a cause of the decline, not a sign of its end.

context: As used in the first paragraph of Passage B, the word “parable” most nearly means:

choices.text: a law of science that has been tested.
a teaching story.
a false rumour spread by visitors.
a long poem about nature.

why.A: The author contrasts the parable with the evidence.
why.B: Correct — the wolf story has become a tale with a moral, which “parables are hard to argue with” reflects.
why.C: The author doubts parts of the story but does not call it false; a parable is a teaching story.
why.D: Nothing about the story is in verse.

context: In Passage B, the contrast between wolves chasing elk and “a table of hunting permits” mainly serves to:

choices.text: suggest that dull evidence of other causes matters as much as the vivid story.
prove that hunters outside the park killed more elk in those years than the wolves did.
argue that hunting should be banned near the park.
show that the author prefers office data to fieldwork.

why.A: Correct — the table “is not” a vivid image, “and the table matters too.”
why.B: Passage B says untangling the shares is difficult; it proves no such ranking.
why.C: No policy on hunting is proposed.
why.D: The contrast is between vivid and dull evidence, not between methods.

context: The phrase “rewinding a clock” in the last paragraph of Passage B refers to:

choices.text: measuring how long the park went without wolves.
starting the wolf release programme over again.
repeating an old experiment in order to check whether its results still hold.
returning an ecosystem to exactly the state it was in before a change.

why.A: This takes the clock literally.
why.B: Nothing suggests repeating the release.
why.C: The image concerns reversing change, not replicating studies.
why.D: Correct — the previous paragraph says the park “changed into something else” and that removing the cause “has not undone all of the effects.”

context: The tone of the first paragraph of Passage A is best described as:

choices.text: doubtful, as though unsure of its facts.
angry, as though assigning blame.
vivid and confident.
dry and technical, like a report.

why.A: Doubts appear in Passage B; this paragraph states each result plainly.
why.B: Nothing in the paragraph blames anyone.
why.C: Correct — it tells the story as a sequence of clear results: trees grow tall, songbirds return, beavers come back.
why.D: The paragraph tells a story; the technical term comes in the next paragraph.

context: Which choice best describes how the last paragraph of Passage B relates to the rest of that passage?

choices.text: It reverses the passage’s argument and accepts Passage A’s account in full.
It limits the passage’s doubts, granting the wolves a role while denying they explain everything.
It introduces new evidence about the beavers.
It reports the elk-collar studies in more detail.

why.A: Granting the wolves a role might look like agreement, but the paragraph still rejects a story that makes them “the whole of it.”
why.B: Correct — “None of this means the wolves have done nothing,” but they are “not the whole of it.”
why.C: The beavers were discussed in the paragraph before.
why.D: The collar studies appear earlier and are not revisited.

context: Both passages agree that:

choices.text: the popular story of the wolves has been told more simply than the evidence supports.
the elk began avoiding the valleys and streams out of fear of the returning wolves.
the wolves had no effect on the streamside trees.
the beavers disappeared because the wolves returned.

why.A: Correct — Passage A says it “has sometimes been told too neatly,” and Passage B that recovery was “patchier than popular accounts suggest.”
why.B: Passage A describes warier elk, but Passage B says collared elk did not shun those places.
why.C: Passage A says the trees recovered; Passage B allows that fewer elk may explain some recovery.
why.D: Passage B says the beavers disappeared during the decades without wolves.

context: Which detail from Passage B most directly challenges Passage A’s claim that the elk grew “warier”?

choices.text: A run of droughts during those same years reduced the forage available to the elk in the park.
Grizzly bears and cougars took many elk calves.
Some researchers have begun building beaver dams by hand.
Collared elk did not, on the whole, avoid the places where wolves hunted.

why.A: This concerns elk numbers, not their behaviour toward wolves.
why.B: This is another cause of decline, not evidence about wariness.
why.C: This concerns stream restoration, not elk behaviour.
why.D: Correct — if the elk had grown wary of wolves, they would have shunned those places.

context: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.text: argue that unfinished novels should be sealed away in archives.
explain how Dickens meant to end The Mystery of Edwin Drood.
defend the practice of other writers completing unfinished novels.
criticise the completions of Edwin Drood as clumsy.

why.A: Passage A compares that treatment to a sealed tomb, “read about as often.”
why.B: Passage A says nobody knew what had become of Edwin.
why.C: Correct — Passage A calls completion a “conversation,” answers the objection about consent, and ends by calling a fragment an invitation.
why.D: The author finds some clumsy but regrets none of them.

context: According to Passage B, what did Max Brod do with Kafka’s unfinished manuscripts?

choices.text: He published them exactly as Kafka left them, making no choices of his own.
He published and arranged them but did not write the missing parts.
He completed The Castle from notes that Kafka had left.
He burned them as Kafka had asked.

why.A: This sounds like the preservation Passage B praises, but Brod “made editorial choices that scholars still dispute.”
why.B: Correct — Passage B says Brod published them, “arranged what Kafka had left,” and “did not write the missing chapters.”
why.C: The Castle “breaks off in the middle of a sentence.”
why.D: Brod refused to burn them.

context: The author of Passage A would most likely say that a completion sold in place of the original fragment is:

choices.text: a misuse, since a completion should stand beside the fragment, not replace it.
the best way to honour the dead author, since it gives readers the ending the author never wrote.
a forgery that fools its readers.
no different from a translation.

why.A: Correct — Passage A says, “I would not want a completion to replace the fragment on the shelf.”
why.B: Passage A never says completion should crowd out the fragment.
why.C: Passage A says a completion “is not a forgery.”
why.D: Translation is mentioned only in the list of what happens to books.

context: In the second paragraph of Passage A, the word “reading” in “What the completion offers is a reading” most nearly means:

choices.text: a session spent reading a book.
a performance aloud.
a figure shown on an instrument.
an interpretation.

why.A: This is the everyday sense, but the completion offers a view of the story, not time spent with it.
why.B: Nothing concerns reading to an audience.
why.C: That sense, as in a meter reading, does not fit.
why.D: Correct — the sentence goes on to call it “one writer’s best guess” about where the story was going, like a critic’s.

context: In Passage A, the list “edited, abridged, translated, adapted for the stage, taught badly in schools” serves mainly to:

choices.text: complain about how books are taught in schools.
show that completions are rarer than translations.
show that a dead writer consents to almost nothing that happens to a book.
argue that editing and abridging harm a book far more than any completion could.

why.A: Teaching is one item in a list that makes a larger point.
why.B: The list does not compare how common each is.
why.C: Correct — it supports the point that lack of consent is “true of almost everything that happens to a book.”
why.D: No ranking of harms is made.

context: Passage A says an untouched unfinished novel is “honoured in the way a sealed tomb is honoured.” The comparison suggests that such a novel is:

choices.text: protected in the only way that is truly respectful to a writer who has died.
respected in principle but, in practice, cut off from readers.
likely to be damaged by time and neglect.
valued mainly for the fame of its author.

why.A: Honouring a tomb sounds respectful, but the author uses the image to criticise leaving the book untouched.
why.B: Correct — the sentence ends “and read about as often,” and the paragraph says books are “kept alive by being used.”
why.C: The image concerns being unread, not physical decay.
why.D: The image says nothing about fame.

context: The author of Passage B regards Max Brod’s decision to publish Kafka’s manuscripts with:

choices.text: approval, while stressing what Brod chose not to do.
disapproval, since Brod ignored Kafka’s wishes.
indifference, since the author cares only about Dickens.
suspicion of Brod’s motives.

why.A: Correct — “It is hard to wish he had obeyed,” the author says, then notes that Brod “did not write the missing chapters.”
why.B: Brod did defy Kafka, but the author says “It is hard to wish he had obeyed.”
why.C: Brod’s choice is the passage’s central example.
why.D: The author never questions why Brod acted.

context: Passage B is organized mainly by:

choices.text: tracing the history of completed novels in order of time, from Dickens to Kafka.
comparing several completions of Edwin Drood.
listing reasons to burn unfinished manuscripts.
using an example to draw a distinction, then answering an objection to it.

why.A: Passage B discusses only two cases and follows an argument, not a chronology.
why.B: No completion is examined.
why.C: Passage B is glad Brod did not burn them.
why.D: Correct — Brod’s example leads to the distinction between preservation and replacement, and a later paragraph answers the defenders of completion.

context: Both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.text: completing an unfinished novel is a kind of forgery.
the ending of Edwin Drood is best left unwritten.
the fragment an author left should remain available to readers.
Kafka’s wish to have his work burned should have been obeyed.

why.A: Passage A says completion “is not a forgery.”
why.B: Passage A has read a dozen endings and regrets none.
why.C: Correct — Passage A does not want a completion to replace the fragment, and Passage B calls publishing it “an act of preservation.”
why.D: Passage B says “It is hard to wish he had obeyed.”

context: Which statement from Passage B most directly responds to Passage A’s hope that a completion will not “replace the fragment on the shelf”?

choices.text: “Publishing an unfinished work is an act of preservation”
“In practice, the completed version is the one that gets printed in paperback, adapted for television, and remembered.”
“It is hard to wish he had obeyed.”
“Readers of The Castle know that it breaks off in the middle of a sentence”

why.A: Both authors would grant this; it does not address whether a completion displaces the fragment.
why.B: Correct — it answers that, whatever the intention, the completion does in practice replace the fragment.
why.C: This concerns Brod and Kafka, not completions.
why.D: This describes an uncompleted book, not what happens when a completion exists.

context: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.text: A teenager working in a clock shop learns that a stopped clock she took for a memorial is really a practical tool of the trade.
A teenager working in a clock shop is taught the craft of repair by an old man who can diagnose a failing clock by its sound alone.
A watchmaker refuses to repair the clock in his window because it stopped at the moment his wife died.
A watchmaker loses customers because the stopped clock in his window makes his shop look careless.

why.A: Correct — the narrator imagines a tragedy behind the window clock (paragraph 3), learns it brings in repairs (paragraph 5), and carries the lesson into later life (paragraph 7).
why.B: He can hear a tired clock, and he teaches some repair late in August, but the narrator says she “was not especially good at it”; the story turns on the window clock.
why.C: That is the story the narrator invents in paragraph 3; paragraph 6 says “There had been no wife.”
why.D: A customer does tease him, but he says “Half of my repairs come in through that window.”

context: According to paragraph 1, what did the narrator mostly learn during the first three weeks of the job?

choices.text: How to open a case back and lift a balance wheel with a pair of tweezers
How to tell by ear which clocks in the shop needed attention
How to use a jeweller’s loupe
How to sweep, how to wrap a mantel clock, and how far to fill the kettle

why.A: Those skills come “toward the end of August,” in paragraph 7, not in the first three weeks.
why.B: That is Mr. Havel’s skill; the narrator never says she learned it.
why.C: The loupe is part of the picture she imagined; nothing says she was taught to use one.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 1 lists the broom, wrapping a mantel clock in newspaper, and not filling the kettle above the line.

context: When the narrator asks whether the clock is “hard to talk about,” Mr. Havel looks at her “with great interest” (paragraph 4). This reaction most strongly suggests that he:

choices.text: was moved that she had guessed a painful memory he usually kept to himself, and was deciding whether to share it.
was pleased that she had finally noticed the clock needed to be repaired.
had never imagined a sad story behind the clock.
suspected that she was mocking him, just as the customer had done.

why.A: This is the reading the narrator’s own story invites, but paragraph 6 says there was no tragedy of any kind in his life beyond a dispute about the drains.
why.B: He does not want it repaired; he explains why it is useful stopped.
why.C: Correct — he treats the question as telling him “something surprising” about her, and his answer in paragraph 5 is entirely practical; there was no sad story to touch.
why.D: The customer spoke “not unkindly,” and he answers the narrator openly rather than defensively.

context: In paragraph 2, when Mr. Havel says of the walnut clock, “That one is tired,” the word “tired” most nearly means:

choices.text: in need of sleep.
close to wearing out.
boring to listen to.
out of fashion.

why.A: That is the everyday sense; a clock does not sleep, and the next sentence shows he meant a part near failure.
why.B: Correct — the owner is later told that “the mainspring had been about to go.”
why.C: He is listening for a fault, not judging whether the clock is interesting.
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph concerns the clock’s style.

context: The sentence “I had been sentimental on his behalf, and he had been, the whole time, running a business” (paragraph 6) mainly serves to:

choices.text: sum up the gap between her invented story and the truth.
criticize Mr. Havel for caring more about his profits than about his customers or the narrator.
reveal that Mr. Havel had in fact lost his wife some years earlier.
explain why the narrator decided to leave the job at the end of the summer.

why.A: Correct — it sets her imagined grief (“sentimental on his behalf”) against his real purpose for the clock (“running a business”).
why.B: “Running a business” could sound like a complaint, but the narrator’s annoyance is at herself; she is “a little embarrassed,” not critical of him.
why.C: The same paragraph says “There had been no wife.”
why.D: The narrator says nothing about deciding to leave; paragraph 7 says she stayed through August.

context: In paragraph 2, the narrator says that on the hour the room “went off like a slow, uneven round of applause.” This comparison describes:

choices.text: customers clapping when a repair was finished.
the narrator’s admiration for Mr. Havel’s skill in the shop.
the noise of the street outside the shop window.
clocks striking at slightly different moments.

why.A: This takes the applause literally; no one claps in the passage.
why.B: The image describes sound in the room, not the narrator’s feelings.
why.C: The sound comes from the clocks lining the room.
why.D: Correct — the clocks “did not agree,” running a minute fast or slow, so the chiming took “most of a minute to die away.”

context: In paragraph 3, the narrator describes her younger self’s theory about the window clock in a tone that is best described as:

choices.text: sorrowful, as if still grieving the loss she imagined in Mr. Havel’s life.
angry at Mr. Havel for letting her believe something false.
gently mocking.
admiring of her own powers of observation and insight.

why.A: The adult narrator knows there was no loss; she is amused at her younger self, not grieving.
why.B: He never encouraged the story; she “built the whole story in an afternoon” herself.
why.C: Correct — “in the way a sixteen-year-old decides things” and “A wife, probably” poke fun at how quickly she built the story, without scorn.
why.D: The paragraph laughs at her conclusion rather than praising it.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It narrates the narrator’s summer in the shop day by day, from her first morning to her last.
It introduces the shop and a puzzle, offers the narrator’s mistaken explanation, reveals the real one, and then shows its lasting effect.
It contrasts two customers’ opinions of the window clock before giving the narrator’s own view.
It begins with the narrator’s adult career in several offices and then goes back to the one summer that she believes explains it.

why.A: The passage skips weeks at a time and never describes a last day.
why.B: Correct — paragraphs 1–3 set up the shop and her theory, paragraphs 4–5 reveal the truth, paragraph 6 gives her reaction, and paragraph 7 the lasting lesson.
why.C: Only one customer comments on the window clock.
why.D: The adult career appears only at the end, not at the start.

context: According to Mr. Havel, how does a clock that is right differ from a clock that is wrong?

choices.text: People ignore the right one but check their own watches against the wrong one.
The right one needs no repair, while the wrong one always has a broken mainspring.
The right one brings in repairs, while the wrong one drives customers away.
The right one is cheaper to make.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 5: “A clock that is right, nobody looks at twice. A clock that is wrong, everybody checks against.”
why.B: The broken mainspring belongs to the walnut clock, not to the stopped window clock.
why.C: He says the reverse: the wrong one brings in half his repairs.
why.D: He says nothing about cost.

context: Which quotation best supports the idea that the narrator carried Mr. Havel’s method into her own adult life?

choices.text: “He did teach me some repair work, eventually, toward the end of August”
“Half of my repairs come in through that window.”
“for several days I was careful never to dust that clock”
“I have occasionally, I admit, left an obvious mistake in a draft on purpose”

why.A: This is tempting because it names something she took from him, but she says she was not good at repair and that “What stayed with me instead was the window.”
why.B: This is Mr. Havel describing his own shop, not the narrator’s later life.
why.C: This shows her mistaken sympathy at the time, not a method she later used.
why.D: Correct — like the stopped clock, a deliberate obvious error makes people “stop and check their watch.”

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A sister repaints the family house mainly to win her father’s approval before she leaves home.
A near accident on a ladder convinces a brother and sister to hire professional painters.
A boy who resents helping his sister paint the house comes to take the work seriously and later adopts her standards.
A boy’s careless mistake ends his sister’s trust in him.

why.A: The father’s silent walk is praise, but paragraph 6 says the finished house “mattered to her less than the way it had been done.”
why.B: They finish the house themselves on the twenty-ninth of August.
why.C: Correct — he starts out insulted by the ladder job, changes after it slips, and two summers later paints the shed exactly as Maren would.
why.D: She goes on climbing with him holding the ladder, and later takes his advice on a stroke.

context: Why did Maren refuse to paint in direct sun?

choices.text: She did not want to be seen working by the neighbours, who would comment.
The paint dried too fast and left lap marks.
The ladder was unsafe on the sunny side of the house.
The heat made brush hairs come loose.

why.A: The neighbours are mentioned only when the house is finished.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 gives exactly this reason.
why.C: The ladder slips on damp grass on the west side, which has nothing to do with sun.
why.D: Loose brush hairs are mentioned, but not as the reason for avoiding sun.

context: In paragraph 4, Maren “did not say anything at all” after the ladder slipped. It can most reasonably be inferred that her silence showed that she:

choices.text: had been badly frightened and that the narrator’s lapse was serious.
had not noticed the slip, because all of her attention was on the paint.
had decided never to speak to her brother again for the rest of the summer.
blamed herself for setting the ladder on the slope.

why.A: Correct — the narrator calls her silence “the loudest thing possible,” and afterward he holds the ladder “as though it were the whole job.”
why.B: Silence can mean not noticing, but she caught the gutter and looked straight down at him; she noticed.
why.C: She keeps working with him and later responds when he points out a stroke.
why.D: Nothing suggests self-blame; the narrator took his foot off the rung.

context: In paragraph 3, Maren scraped every board “even where the old paint was sound.” As used here, “sound” most nearly means:

choices.text: noisy.
sensible.
deep.
in good condition.

why.A: This is the everyday sense of the noun, and it does not fit a description of paint.
why.B: Paint cannot be sensible; the word describes its condition.
why.C: As in the phrase a sound sleep, but the sentence contrasts sound paint with flaking paint, not with shallow paint.
why.D: Correct — she scraped even paint that was not flaking, because new paint was “only as good as the old paint.”

context: The final paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.text: suggest that the narrator painted the shed badly because Maren was not there to direct him.
reveal that the narrator’s mother disapproved of the way Maren had painted the house.
show that Maren’s standards have become the narrator’s own.
explain why the narrator never again needed anyone to hold a ladder for him.

why.A: He paints it with all of her care.
why.B: His mother’s question is about his effort on the shed, not about Maren’s work.
why.C: Correct — alone on the shed, he scrapes sound paint, follows the shade, and fetches a pin, then gives “exactly the answer Maren would have given.”
why.D: He needs no ladder only because the shed is eight feet tall; that is not the paragraph’s point.

context: When the narrator says in paragraph 2 that “A fence post could hold a ladder,” he means that:

choices.text: the ladder should have been tied to a post for safety.
the job he had been given needed no skill.
Maren thought her brother was stubborn.
the ground around the house was too soft.

why.A: This reads the image literally; he is complaining, not proposing a safer method.
why.B: Correct — the line follows “Anyone could hold a ladder,” and he says he took the job as “an insult.”
why.C: Maren’s reply is about his talking, not his stubbornness.
why.D: Soft, damp ground matters later, but this line is about the job.

context: In paragraph 3, the narrator’s description of Maren’s methods is best described as:

choices.text: exasperated, though so detailed that it shows how closely he was watching.
openly admiring, with no hint of complaint.
bitter and hostile.
uninterested.

why.A: Correct — “She was unbearable about the work” is exasperated, yet he records her reasons for scraping, the shade, and the pin.
why.B: He calls her “unbearable” and jokes that they will finish when she graduates.
why.C: His complaints are comic; nothing in the paragraph is hostile.
why.D: An uninterested observer would not record every one of her methods and reasons.

context: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

choices.text: It describes the painting of each wall in turn, following the order in which the siblings worked their way around the house.
It presents Maren’s view of the project and then the narrator’s opposing view.
It opens with the shed and flashes back to the house.
It moves from the narrator’s reluctance, through a turning point, to a change in him, and ends with proof that the change lasted.

why.A: The walls are mentioned only in passing; the passage is organized around the narrator’s change.
why.B: Their views converge; the passage does not set them out as a debate.
why.C: The shed comes last.
why.D: Correct — reluctance (paragraphs 1–3), the slip (paragraph 4), his new attention (paragraph 5), the finish (paragraph 6), the shed two summers later (paragraph 7).

context: According to the narrator, how did Maren’s interest in the finished house compare with her interest in the work itself?

choices.text: She cared about the finished house far more, and she photographed it again and again from every side.
She cared about both equally and said so to the neighbours.
She cared less about the finished house than about how the work had been done.
She lost interest in both once her father praised the house.

why.A: She took “one photograph” and did not seem interested in looking at it after that.
why.B: The neighbours speak; Maren says nothing about it.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 6: she took one photograph and “the finished house mattered to her less than the way it had been done.”
why.D: The narrator never ties her attitude to the father’s reaction.

context: Which quotation best supports the claim that the narrator had begun to share Maren’s standards before that summer was over?

choices.text: “I scraped it down to bare wood, all of it, including the boards where the old paint was perfectly sound.”
“I started, without meaning to, to watch what she was doing up there”
“I learned to test the ground before she climbed”
“my father walked all the way around it twice without speaking”

why.A: This shows he shares her standards, but it happens “Two summers later,” not before that summer ended.
why.B: Correct — during the summer he begins noticing thin strokes and crooked edges, and even points one out.
why.C: This shows care about the ladder, not about the quality of the painting.
why.D: This is the father’s approval, not evidence about the narrator.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: On the lake, the narrator learns that silence need not mean trouble.
The narrator learns why a frozen lake makes loud noises as the air around it grows colder.
The narrator discovers a lasting love of fishing during a week with her uncle.
An uncle helps the narrator’s parents settle the problems they were having at home.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 6 contrasts silence at home, which “meant that something was wrong,” with the restful silence of the lake, and the ending returns to “which kind of quiet it was.”
why.B: Ansel does explain the sounds, but that is the point of paragraph 4; the passage uses the ice to reach a larger point about silence.
why.C: She says she “would not describe any of it as exciting.”
why.D: Ansel has no part in the parents’ affairs, which they “did sort” out on their own.

context: According to Ansel, which ice should a person worry about?

choices.text: Ice that makes loud cracking noises on cold, clear afternoons as the air temperature falls
Ice near the shore where people drill holes
Ice under a heated shelter
Quiet ice in spring that has gone soft

why.A: He says the opposite: “Loud ice is thick ice.”
why.B: He never mentions the shore or the holes as dangerous.
why.C: The heater is mentioned, but not as a danger.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 4: “the ice that doesn’t say anything, in spring, when it’s gone soft.”

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the narrator was sent to stay with Ansel because:

choices.text: she had asked to learn ice fishing from an experienced relative in the north.
Ansel needed help running his fishing business.
her parents were having difficulties at home and wanted her out of the way.
she had been ill and needed cold, fresh air.

why.A: She kept a list of forty-one things she would rather be doing.
why.B: Nothing suggests Ansel fishes for a living, and they kept only four fish.
why.C: Correct — they were “sorting some things out” (paragraph 1), and at home that winter “silence had meant that something was wrong” (paragraph 6).
why.D: No illness is mentioned.

context: In paragraph 4, the ice “cracks and shifts to take up the strain.” As used here, “strain” most nearly means:

choices.text: an injured muscle.
stress.
an effort to hear.
a strand of music.

why.A: That is a common sense of the word, but it applies to bodies, not to a sheet of ice.
why.B: Correct — the shrinking surface puts the sheet under pressure it has “nowhere to go” to relieve, so it cracks.
why.C: The narrator listens, but the ice is not trying to hear anything.
why.D: The ice is said to sing, but this sentence is about physical forces.

context: The narrator’s list of “forty-one items,” mentioned in paragraph 2 and again in paragraph 6, mainly serves to:

choices.text: mark how much her attitude toward the week changed.
show that she never stopped wishing she were somewhere else, even at the end of the week on the lake.
suggest that Ansel’s home offered many more activities than the lake did.
explain why she agreed to go to the dentist when she returned.

why.A: Correct — in paragraph 2 the list measures her boredom; by paragraph 6 she is “a little ashamed” of it because the quiet turned out to be restful.
why.B: Paragraph 2 alone supports this, but paragraph 6 says she was ashamed of the list, which reverses it.
why.C: The list is of things she would rather be doing anywhere, not things at Ansel’s home.
why.D: The dentist is a joke about how bored she was, not a real plan.

context: The comparison to “someone running a wet finger around the rim of an enormous glass” (paragraph 3) describes:

choices.text: the narrator’s hand slipping on Ansel’s sleeve.
water filling the hole they had drilled.
the heater in the shelter.
a deep, rising, ringing sound from the ice.

why.A: She grabs his arm after the sound, and the image describes the sound.
why.B: The image is of a sound travelling across the lake, not of water.
why.C: The heater hums; the image describes the lake.
why.D: Correct — the same sentence calls it “a deep, rising note.”

context: In paragraph 6, the narrator’s attitude toward the week of fishing is best described as:

choices.text: bored, since nothing that happened during the week was at all exciting to her.
proud of the number of fish they caught.
unimpressed by the fishing but grateful for the quiet it brought.
anxious about the silence she found there.

why.A: “I would not describe any of it as exciting” invites this one-word reading, but the paragraph turns to what she valued: silence that “did not feel like an argument.”
why.B: Eleven perch in five days, four kept, is reported flatly, not proudly.
why.C: Correct — she would not call it exciting, yet she found the long silences “restful.”
why.D: She says the lake’s silence was restful, unlike the silence at home.

context: How does paragraph 4 relate to paragraph 3?

choices.text: It describes a second, even louder sound heard later that afternoon on the lake.
It explains the cause of the frightening sound that paragraph 3 describes.
It shows the narrator arguing with Ansel about whether to leave the ice.
It jumps forward to the end of the week.

why.A: The second, “shorter note” comes in paragraph 5.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 gives the noise and the narrator’s fright; paragraph 4 gives Ansel’s account of why the ice makes it.
why.C: She does not argue; she sits down again.
why.D: The end of the week comes in paragraphs 5 and 6.

context: According to paragraph 6, how did silence at home differ from silence on the lake?

choices.text: At home it meant that something was wrong; on the lake it meant nobody had anything to add.
At home it was restful; on the lake it was frightening.
At home it lasted longer than on the lake.
At home it was broken by arguments; on the lake it was broken by the ice.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph states both halves directly.
why.B: This reverses the paragraph.
why.C: The narrator compares what silence meant, not how long it lasted.
why.D: The lake does make sounds, but the paragraph contrasts what silence meant in each place.

context: Which quotation best shows that the narrator grew used to the sounds of the lake?

choices.text: “I believe I grabbed Ansel’s arm.”
“I did not believe him, exactly, but I noticed that he had not moved”
“He said all this the way other people say it looks like rain.”
“By the end of the afternoon I had stopped jumping.”

why.A: This is her first, frightened reaction, not evidence that she grew used to the sounds.
why.B: This shows her beginning to be reassured, not yet that she had grown used to the sounds.
why.C: This shows Ansel’s calm, not the narrator’s.
why.D: Correct — the fright of paragraph 3 fades within the same afternoon.

context: Which choice best states the main claim of the passage?

choices.text: The tradition that Cornish died in 1777 with Dolly Pentreath is inaccurate.
The alarm about the loss of the world’s languages has been greatly overstated.
Counting only fluent speakers misrepresents language loss, because what survives in partial forms can shape a language’s future.
Revived languages are the same as the languages they bring back.

why.A: The author does doubt it, but that is the point of paragraph 2, used as an example for the larger claim.
why.B: Paragraph 5 says the reverse: “None of this means that the alarm about language loss is overstated.”
why.C: Correct — the author argues the fluent-speaker count “is not telling us much” and asks instead “what is left of it, held by whom, and in what form.”
why.D: Paragraph 5 says a revived language “is also not the same thing as an unbroken one.”

context: According to the passage, semi-speakers are people who:

choices.text: learned the language fully at home as young children and go on using it for everything in daily life.
understand a great deal of a language and speak some, having heard it growing up but answered in another.
know only songs, prayers, and names of plants.
learned the language in classrooms as adults.

why.A: That describes fluent speakers, the first group on the spectrum.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 defines them this way.
why.C: Those are the people beyond the semi-speakers.
why.D: That describes learners of revived Cornish, in paragraph 5.

context: Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree that a language with no remaining fluent speakers:

choices.text: may still leave material from which it could be taught again.
is regarded by linguists as extinct and therefore beyond any possibility of revival.
should no longer receive money for teaching it.
will certainly be revived within a generation.

why.A: Correct — the author says revivals have been built from fragments like place names, songs, and scattered words, as with Cornish.
why.B: Some classification schemes do treat such languages as extinct, but the passage argues the opposite: Cornish was revived after its fluent speakers were gone.
why.C: The author presents the drying up of money as a harm that can “bring about the thing it describes.”
why.D: The author says some languages “will be” lost for good; nothing is certain.

context: In paragraph 2, the author says the Dolly Pentreath tradition is “almost certainly too tidy.” As used here, “tidy” most nearly means:

choices.text: clean.
considerable in size.
polite.
neat and simple.

why.A: That is the everyday household sense, and it does not describe a story.
why.B: As in the phrase a tidy sum, but the author is objecting to the story’s simplicity, not its size.
why.C: The tradition says she cursed at people; politeness is not the issue.
why.D: Correct — a single last speaker on a single date is simpler than the evidence that others spoke some Cornish after her.

context: Paragraph 5 mainly serves to:

choices.text: argue that the revival of Cornish has been a failure and that no other language should attempt one.
introduce the spectrum of speakers that linguists use.
acknowledge limits to the author’s argument without abandoning it.
give the evidence against the Dolly Pentreath tradition.

why.A: The paragraph notes how revived Cornish differs; it does not call the revival a failure.
why.B: The spectrum is introduced in paragraph 3.
why.C: Correct — it grants that the alarm is justified and that revived Cornish differs from the old language, before paragraph 6 opens with “But.”
why.D: That evidence appears in paragraph 2.

context: In paragraph 1, the author says last-speaker stories “get the arithmetic of language loss slightly wrong.” The phrase “arithmetic of language loss” refers to:

choices.text: the cost of teaching endangered languages in schools.
the way the loss of a language is counted.
the number of years since a language was last spoken at home.
the mathematics that linguists use to date old texts.

why.A: Money comes up in paragraph 4, but the “arithmetic” is about who gets counted.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 3 explains that a census counting only fluent speakers misses everyone else.
why.C: The passage never measures loss in years.
why.D: Nothing in the passage concerns dating texts.

context: The author’s attitude toward newspaper stories about last speakers is best described as:

choices.text: sympathetic to their emotional power but critical of what they imply.
dismissive, since the author regards them as sentimental inventions that should not be printed.
uncritical, since the author accepts their account of how languages die.
amused by their exaggerations.

why.A: Correct — the stories are “moving, and they are meant to be,” but they get “the arithmetic of language loss slightly wrong.”
why.B: The author criticizes the stories, which invites this reading, but calls them moving and never says they should not be printed or that they are invented.
why.C: The whole passage questions their account.
why.D: Nothing in the passage treats the stories as funny.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It traces the history of the Cornish language from its origins to the present day.
It compares the histories of two endangered languages in detail and then judges which of them has the better chance of surviving.
It reports a survey of endangered languages.
It presents a familiar story, tests it against an example, explains what it leaves out, concedes limits, and proposes a better question.

why.A: Cornish is an example; the passage gives no history of its origins.
why.B: Only Cornish is discussed in detail.
why.C: No survey is reported; the seven thousand figure is an estimate given in passing.
why.D: Correct — the newspaper story (1), Cornish (2), the spectrum and its stakes (3–4), the concession (5), the better question (6), and a closing point (7).

context: According to paragraph 5, how does the Cornish learned today differ from the Cornish of its earlier speakers?

choices.text: It is spoken today by far more people than spoke Cornish in the years before Dolly Pentreath died in 1777.
It has no written records to draw on.
It is learned in classrooms by teenagers and adults, with modern words and an accent shaped by English.
It is learned first, as a child’s home language.

why.A: The passage says it is spoken by “a small number of enthusiasts.”
why.B: It was reconstructed partly “from old texts.”
why.C: Correct — paragraph 5 states each of these differences.
why.D: That describes the old fluent speakers, not today’s learners.

context: Which quotation best supports the claim that declaring a language dead can hasten its loss?

choices.text: “Next come what are sometimes called semi-speakers”
“families who have kept fragments of it may stop passing them on”
“Cornish itself is now taught in some schools”
“a large share of the world’s roughly seven thousand languages are no longer being learned by children”

why.A: This introduces a kind of speaker; it says nothing about the effects of a declaration.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 4 says families reason that a dead language is not worth the trouble, so the declaration “can bring about the thing it describes.”
why.C: This shows a revival, the opposite of hastened loss.
why.D: This supports the general alarm, not the effect of declaring a language dead.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Trust in measurement rests on constant checking, a system people notice only when it fails.
The metric system swept away local units that had served people well for many generations.
Medieval bakers invented the baker’s dozen to avoid fines.
Weights-and-measures inspections are a waste because most scales turn out to be accurate.

why.A: Correct — the passage opens with the invisible checking behind every purchase and closes with a system whose “success looks like nothing at all.”
why.B: That is a cost the author concedes in paragraph 5, not the passage’s main point.
why.C: The author treats this as a story that “may be only partly true,” used as one example.
why.D: The author rejects this argument: the finding “is better read the other way.”

context: According to the passage, what happened to the kilogram in 2019?

choices.text: It was defined for the first time as the mass of a metal cylinder kept near Paris.
Its official copies were found to weigh exactly the same as the original.
It was replaced by the pound.
It was redefined in terms of a constant of nature.

why.A: That was the old definition, used “For more than a century” before 2019.
why.B: The copies and the original had drifted apart.
why.C: Nothing in the passage suggests this.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 6 states this directly.

context: Suppose an inspection finds that 98 percent of a city’s taxi meters are accurate. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that this result:

choices.text: shows that the inspections are a waste of money, since hardly any meters in the city were found to be wrong.
proves that most of the city’s drivers cheat whenever they can.
probably reflects the effect of inspecting meters, not evidence that inspections are unneeded.
means that meters should be redefined in terms of a constant of nature.

why.A: Paragraph 4 mentions exactly this argument, then rejects it: the finding “is better read the other way.”
why.B: A 98 percent accuracy rate would suggest the opposite.
why.C: Correct — the author says scales “are accurate largely because they are inspected.”
why.D: That idea belongs to the kilogram, not to taxi meters.

context: In paragraph 4, the inspector is described as “a figure so obscure that most people do not know the job exists.” As used here, “obscure” most nearly means:

choices.text: difficult to understand.
little known.
dimly lit.
deliberately hidden.

why.A: The job is not described as confusing, only as unknown.
why.B: Correct — the rest of the sentence explains it: most people do not know the job exists.
why.C: That is a literal sense that does not apply to a person’s job.
why.D: Nothing suggests the job is kept secret; people simply do not think about it.

context: In paragraph 4, the reference to a police car that “might be waiting around the next bend” mainly serves to:

choices.text: illustrate how the chance of being checked keeps people honest.
suggest that weights-and-measures inspectors should have the powers of the police.
show that taxi meters are the least reliable of all the measuring devices inspected.
argue that roads are more dangerous than they appear.

why.A: Correct — drivers keep to the limit because a check is possible, just as scales stay accurate “because they are inspected.”
why.B: The comparison concerns why checking works, not what powers inspectors should have.
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph ranks devices by reliability.
why.D: The road is only the second half of an analogy.

context: In paragraph 2, the author says that “a standard that nobody inspects is only a suggestion.” This statement suggests that:

choices.text: rulers should have asked merchants for their suggestions before issuing standards.
medieval standards were too vague to be followed.
a trader could never profit from differences in units.
rules about measures change behaviour only if they are enforced.

why.A: The word “suggestion” is not meant literally; nobody is being consulted.
why.B: The problem was not vagueness but the lack of anyone to check.
why.C: The same paragraph says traders did profit from them.
why.D: Correct — it explains why rulers’ orders to copy standards “were widely ignored.”

context: The author’s attitude toward standardized measurement is best described as:

choices.text: enthusiastic, treating it as a pure gain without any drawbacks for the people who had to accept it.
hostile, since it destroyed local customs.
supportive, while recognizing that it carries real costs.
indifferent to whether measures are accurate.

why.A: The author does champion measurement, but paragraph 5 states plainly that “Standardization has its costs.”
why.B: Paragraph 5 notes the loss, but the rest of the passage defends the system.
why.C: Correct — the author praises the checking that makes trust possible but concedes in paragraph 5 that standardization can “flatten real differences.”
why.D: The whole passage is concerned with accuracy.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It follows one inspector’s career from the first day to the last, drawing a lesson about trust from each stage of the work.
It makes a claim, traces its history, turns to modern practice, concedes costs, and adds an ironic case before concluding.
It compares the metric and imperial systems and argues for the second.
It moves from the present day backward to ancient times.

why.A: No individual inspector appears in the passage.
why.B: Correct — the claim (1), history (2–3), modern inspectors (4), costs (5), the drifting kilogram (6), and the conclusion (7).
why.C: The imperial system is never compared or defended.
why.D: The history runs roughly forward, from “most of history” to 2019.

context: According to paragraph 2, how did units of weight or volume for most of history differ from those that customers rely on today?

choices.text: They meant whatever a particular town, market, or merchant said they meant.
They were defined by a single cylinder kept in a vault.
They were checked far more often than today’s units.
They were based on constants of nature.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 2 says this, and gives the example of bushels differing between counties.
why.B: That is the kilogram of the last century, not the units of most of history.
why.C: The paragraph says orders about standards “were widely ignored.”
why.D: That describes the kilogram since 2019.

context: Which piece of evidence does the author explicitly treat as possibly unreliable?

choices.text: The finding that most scales, pumps, meters, and packages that inspectors test turn out to be accurate
The drift between the kilogram and its copies
The resistance to the metric system in France
The usual explanation of the “baker’s dozen”

why.A: The author reinterprets what this finding means, but does not doubt that it is accurate.
why.B: The author reports the drift without doubting it; the uncertainty was only about which had changed.
why.C: The author calls the resistance “considerable” and does not question it.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 3 says the story “may be only partly true,” though it captures something real.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Studies that line up hours of homework against grades can mistake struggling students for proof that homework fails.
Homework should be abolished because it widens the gaps between students from different homes.
The homework debate should ask what an assignment is meant to do rather than how long it takes.
Each student should do ten minutes of homework a night for each grade.

why.A: This is true to paragraph 3, but it is one step in the argument, not the passage’s main point.
why.B: The author grants the gap but says “the answer to that objection is not obviously to abolish homework.”
why.C: Correct — the author calls the public argument one “about the wrong thing” and ends by urging people to ask of each assignment “what it is supposed to do.”
why.D: The author doubts how much evidence supports “the exact figure.”

context: According to paragraph 2, reviews of the research have found that the link between homework and achievement is:

choices.text: strong for students of every age.
modest for older students and weak or absent for young children.
stronger for young children than for older students.
negative for students in the later years of secondary school.

why.A: The paragraph says it “depends, and especially on age.”
why.B: Correct — paragraph 2 states this directly.
why.C: This reverses the finding.
why.D: The paragraph calls it a “modest positive association” for them.

context: Based on paragraph 3, a student who spends two hours on a problem set that a classmate finishes in twenty minutes is most likely:

choices.text: finding the material harder than the classmate does.
learning more from the problem set than the classmate learned, because the extra time spent is itself useful practice.
copying answers from someone else.
being given more homework than the classmate.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph says the students reporting the most time “are the ones who find the material hardest.”
why.B: The passage says the slower student “still gets half of it wrong,” which is the opposite of learning more.
why.C: Copying is mentioned in paragraph 1 as a complaint, but not as the reason for slow work.
why.D: The two students do the same problem set.

context: In paragraph 5, the author says that any defence of homework “has to reckon with this rather than wave it away.” As used here, “reckon with” most nearly means:

choices.text: calculate.
suppose.
agree with.
deal seriously with.

why.A: “Reckon” can mean calculate, but nothing is being counted here.
why.B: In casual speech reckon can mean suppose, but that sense does not fit a defence that must address an objection.
why.C: The author faces the objection but does not simply agree with its conclusion.
why.D: Correct — the contrast with “wave it away” shows that the objection must be faced.

context: The example of two students doing the same chemistry problem set (paragraph 3) mainly serves to:

choices.text: show that homework does harm to students who find the subject difficult and should be cut back.
prove that chemistry homework is more useful than homework in other subjects.
show why simply comparing hours with grades can mislead.
illustrate the ten-minute rule.

why.A: The paragraph says such studies can make homework “look” harmful; the example explains that appearance, not a real harm.
why.B: Chemistry is just an example; no subjects are ranked.
why.C: Correct — the slow student’s two hours reflect struggle, so a study lining up hours against grades may measure “who was struggling.”
why.D: The rule is in paragraph 2 and is not what the example tests.

context: When the author says that “An hour of the first kind and an hour of the second kind are not the same hour” (paragraph 4), the point is that:

choices.text: some students work more slowly than others do.
time spent is a poor measure, since different kinds of homework differ in value.
homework should be measured in minutes rather than hours.
students often misreport the time they spend on homework in surveys.

why.A: That is the point of paragraph 3, not this sentence.
why.B: Correct — the sentence sums up the paragraph’s contrast between useful spaced practice and doubtful self-teaching.
why.C: The author objects to measuring by time at all.
why.D: Misreporting is not discussed.

context: The author’s response to critics who say homework widens gaps between students is best described as:

choices.text: granting that they are right about the problem while rejecting abolition as the remedy.
dismissive, since the author treats the objection as a distraction from the real question.
wholly persuaded, so that the author ends by calling for homework to be abolished.
confused about what the critics mean.

why.A: Correct — the author says “they are right that it can,” then that the answer “is not obviously to abolish homework.”
why.B: The author calls the objection “fair” and says it must not be waved away.
why.C: Agreeing that homework “can” widen gaps invites this reading, but the next paragraph opens “But the answer to that objection is not obviously to abolish homework.”
why.D: The author restates the critics’ point clearly.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It describes one school district’s decision to abolish homework, then reports what happened to its students’ grades in later years.
It lists the complaints of parents, teachers, and students in turn.
It presents two research studies and asks the reader to choose between them.
It frames a debate, reviews evidence, exposes a measurement problem, proposes a better question, answers an objection, and concludes.

why.A: Districts are mentioned only in passing in paragraph 1.
why.B: The complaints fill part of paragraph 1; the rest is argument.
why.C: No individual studies are presented.
why.D: Correct — the debate (1), evidence (2), the measurement problem (3), the better question (4), the objection and answer (5–6), and the conclusion (7).

context: In paragraph 4, homework that practises a skill already begun differs from homework that asks students to teach themselves something new in that the first:

choices.text: takes longer to complete than the second does.
requires a parent’s help, while the second can be done alone.
seems to help, while the second, done without feedback, is more doubtful.
must be done in a single sitting, while the second can be spread over several days.

why.A: The paragraph says nothing about which takes longer.
why.B: Paragraph 6 says focused practice can be done alone, “without special equipment or a parent’s help.”
why.C: Correct — spaced practice “seems to do real good,” while self-teaching with no one to correct mistakes “is much more doubtful.”
why.D: The paragraph says the practice works best “spread over several days.”

context: Which quotation best shows that the author doubts how firmly the ten-minute rule is supported?

choices.text: “a first-grader does ten minutes and a senior perhaps two hours”
“How much evidence stands behind the exact figure is less clear.”
“Reviews of the studies, of which there are now a great many”
“that kind of spaced practice is among the more reliable findings in the study of memory”

why.A: This explains how the rule works, not whether it is well supported.
why.B: Correct — it questions the evidence for the rule directly.
why.C: This describes the size of the research, not doubt about the rule.
why.D: This concerns spaced practice, not the ten-minute rule.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A good typeface for reading should go unnoticed, though its invisibility depends partly on readers’ habits.
German readers once read most of their books in blackletter rather than roman type.
Posters and shop fronts need lettering that catches the eye.
Warde was wrong to argue that type should be invisible.

why.A: Correct — the author mostly agrees with Warde but concludes that “the glass is only clear to eyes that have learned to see through it.”
why.B: That is a supporting example in paragraph 5, not the main idea.
why.C: That is the limit the author concedes in paragraph 4.
why.D: The author says “she was mostly right.”

context: According to paragraph 1, the printer said that the narrator’s essay looked like:

choices.text: a festival poster set in the plain type of an official tax form.
a page from a paperback novel.
an old certificate.
a ransom note.

why.A: That example comes in paragraph 4, in a different context.
why.B: The printer handed the narrator a novel to make the opposite point.
why.C: Old certificates are linked to blackletter in paragraph 5.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 1 states this directly.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the narrator could not name the paperback’s typeface because:

choices.text: the printer had chosen a typeface too rare for anyone to know.
the narrator had never read a novel before that day.
the typeface had done its job of going unnoticed.
the book was printed in blackletter.

why.A: The printer opened the book “at random”; nothing suggests the face was rare.
why.B: Nothing in the passage suggests this.
why.C: Correct — the printer says that this “was the point,” and paragraph 3 notes that readers almost never can name such faces.
why.D: Blackletter comes up only in paragraph 5, about German readers.

context: In paragraph 3, the author calls typography a craft “whose greatest success is to go unremarked.” As used here, “unremarked” most nearly means:

choices.text: unmarked by errors.
unnoticed.
unpublished.
unpaid.

why.A: The word concerns being noticed, not being free of mistakes.
why.B: Correct — the sentence before says all the labour “is spent so that nobody will see it.”
why.C: The typefaces are in print everywhere; they are simply not noticed.
why.D: Pay is never mentioned.

context: Paragraph 4 mainly serves to:

choices.text: limit Warde’s claim to long stretches of reading.
argue that posters should be set in the same typefaces that are used in novels and newspapers.
explain why German readers preferred blackletter.
describe the narrator’s first meeting with the printer.

why.A: Correct — it grants that posters and shop fronts should be noticed and says Warde’s argument “is an argument about reading.”
why.B: The paragraph says a poster in a plain face “would fail at its one job.”
why.C: Blackletter is discussed in paragraph 5.
why.D: That meeting is in paragraph 1.

context: In the final sentence, the author says that “the glass is only clear to eyes that have learned to see through it.” This statement suggests that:

choices.text: most readers need spectacles to read small type comfortably.
wine is best served in clear glasses.
readers should be taught to notice typefaces.
a typeface seems transparent only to readers who have grown used to it.

why.A: This reads “eyes” and “glass” literally; the passage is not about eyesight.
why.B: The wine glass is Warde’s image for type, not a claim about wine.
why.C: The author still wants a book typeface “to disappear.”
why.D: Correct — paragraph 5 explains that each typeface “had become transparent through habit.”

context: The author’s attitude toward Warde’s argument is best described as:

choices.text: critical, since the author finds a deeper difficulty that defeats her argument about clear glass.
uncritically admiring.
largely in agreement, with qualifications.
uninterested, since the author no longer thinks about typefaces.

why.A: The author names a “deeper difficulty,” but then says “That does not defeat the argument, but it changes it.”
why.B: The author raises two separate objections.
why.C: Correct — the author says she was “mostly right” but adds limits (paragraph 4) and a “deeper difficulty” (paragraph 5).
why.D: The author still thinks of the printer when choosing a typeface.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: A history of printing is traced in order, from the invention of movable type to the word processors of today.
An anecdote leads to an idea, which the author endorses, limits, revises, and then returns to with a reservation.
Two typefaces are compared and one is recommended.
An argument is stated and then abandoned.

why.A: The passage gives no such history; its examples are selected, not chronological.
why.B: Correct — the printer (1), Warde (2), agreement (3), limit (4), revision (5–6), and a return to the printer (7).
why.C: No specific typefaces are named or recommended.
why.D: The author revises the argument but says it is not defeated.

context: According to paragraph 5, how did German readers of the past regard roman type compared with blackletter?

choices.text: Roman type could look foreign and thin, while blackletter was their clear glass.
Roman type was their clear glass, while blackletter looked foreign and thin.
They found both equally hard to read.
They preferred whichever was cheaper.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 5 states both points.
why.B: This reverses the paragraph.
why.C: Blackletter was transparent to them.
why.D: Cost is never mentioned.

context: Which detail best supports the author’s claim that a typeface’s invisibility “can be learned”?

choices.text: Designers worry over the height of a lowercase letter and the tiny gap between an r and an n.
Warde compared good printing to a crystal wine glass.
The narrator now chooses one of about three dull typefaces.
Readers often dislike a new face at first and then stop noticing it a few years later.

why.A: This shows invisibility being designed into a face, which is the side of the argument the claim about learning qualifies.
why.B: This states the ideal of invisibility, not how it is acquired.
why.C: This reports the narrator’s habit, not how readers come to stop noticing type.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 6 presents this change over time as evidence that the letters “had to be looked at before they could be looked through.”

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Opera kept the prompter’s box because singers face practical demands that actors in spoken plays do not.
An actor who needs prompting on opening night has not prepared properly.
The prompter’s box matters less for the mistakes it rescues than for what its presence admits and allows.
The prompter’s box should be brought back into the spoken theatre.

why.A: This is the point of paragraph 4, and the author agrees with it, but the passage moves past usefulness to what the box admits and allows.
why.B: The author agrees with directors on this in paragraph 3, but it is a passing concession.
why.C: Correct — the author says what interests him is “less its usefulness than what it admits,” and that the net “changes the act even when it is never touched.”
why.D: The author never proposes this and grants that the spoken theatre had good reasons to drop it.

context: According to the passage, besides supplying words a singer has forgotten, an opera prompter may:

choices.text: conduct the orchestra from inside the box when the conductor cannot be seen by the players.
signal when singers should come in and pass on the conductor’s beat.
rehearse the singers in their roles before each performance.
operate the stage lighting.

why.A: She relays the conductor’s beat to singers; she does not conduct the orchestra.
why.B: Correct — paragraph 4: she “gives entrances” and “relays the conductor’s beat to singers who cannot see it.”
why.C: Nothing in the passage describes the prompter leading rehearsals.
why.D: Audiences mistake the box for “a piece of the lighting,” but that is a mistake.

context: In paragraph 7, a tenor who never needed the prompter all season thanks her anyway. The passage suggests that he did so because:

choices.text: knowing she was there had let him sing with the freedom to take risks.
it is the custom for performers to thank every member of the crew at the end of a season.
she had quietly prompted him on nights when he did not realize it.
he wanted to apologize for leaving her with nothing to do.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 6 says performers who know “a fall will be caught can attempt more,” even if the net is never used.
why.B: Such a custom may exist in some houses, but the passage never mentions it; it offers a different explanation in paragraph 6.
why.C: The passage says he “had not needed her once.”
why.D: Nothing suggests an apology; the author treats the thanks as a compliment.

context: In paragraph 5, the author says that what interests him is “what it admits.” As used here, “admits” most nearly means:

choices.text: lets in.
accepts as a member.
allows as evidence.
acknowledges.

why.A: That sense fits a door or a ticket, but the paragraph is about what the box confesses, not whom it allows inside.
why.B: The box does not enrol anyone.
why.C: That legal sense does not fit; nothing is being judged in court.
why.D: Correct — the box is described as “a permanent, visible acknowledgment” that a performance might fail.

context: Paragraph 3 mainly serves to:

choices.text: argue that actors in the spoken theatre are less skilled and less hardworking than opera singers.
describe the author’s first night inside the box.
grant that the spoken theatre had good reasons to give up the box.
explain how the prompter gives entrances.

why.A: The paragraph explains a change in practice; it does not rank actors against singers.
why.B: That experience is in paragraph 2.
why.C: Correct — it lists the reasons (less thorough learning, carrying whispers, weekly new plays) and agrees with directors who expect actors to know their lines.
why.D: Entrances are explained in paragraph 4.

context: In paragraph 2, the author says that from inside the box “the stage is a forest of ankles.” This image conveys that:

choices.text: the stage was decorated with painted trees for the production that summer.
from the box one sees mostly the singers’ feet and lower legs.
the singers stood very still.
the author felt lost in the theatre.

why.A: This takes “forest” literally; nothing is said about scenery.
why.B: Correct — the next sentence adds that “You cannot see the singers’ faces unless they lean toward you.”
why.C: The image is about what can be seen from below, not about movement.
why.D: The image describes a view, not the author’s feelings about the building.

context: In paragraph 6, the author’s attitude toward the prompter’s box is best described as:

choices.text: appreciative, while insisting that relying on it is a sign of failure.
romantic, since he treats the box as a charming relic of theatre history.
disapproving, since he regards any use of a prompter as evidence that rehearsal has failed.
indifferent to whether prompters survive.

why.A: Correct — he says a production leaning on the prompter “is not a good production,” yet argues the net frees performers to take risks.
why.B: He opens the paragraph with “I do not want to romanticize this.”
why.C: His first sentences invite this reading, but the paragraph turns on “But”: the net “changes the act even when it is never touched.”
why.D: He calls his nights in the box among his best.

context: How does paragraph 5 relate to paragraph 4?

choices.text: It gives a further practical reason that opera houses kept their prompters after the theatre did not.
It contradicts paragraph 4 by denying that singers need prompters.
It returns to the author’s summer as a student.
It turns from the box’s practical uses to what the box signifies.

why.A: Paragraph 5 sets practical reasons aside rather than adding one.
why.B: Paragraph 5 does not deny this.
why.C: The summer returns in paragraphs 6 and 7.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 4 gives opera’s practical reasons; paragraph 5 opens with “less its usefulness than what it admits.”

context: According to paragraphs 3 and 4, how does the spoken theatre differ from opera in its use of the prompter’s box?

choices.text: The spoken theatre uses the box for entrances, while opera uses it only for forgotten words.
The spoken theatre invented the box, while opera borrowed it.
The spoken theatre has mostly given it up, while opera has kept it.
Both have abandoned it.

why.A: This reverses who gives entrances; paragraph 4 says opera prompters give them.
why.B: The passage does not say where the box began.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 3 says the spoken theatre “abandoned” it in most places; paragraph 4 says “Opera kept the box.”
why.D: Opera kept it.

context: Which quotation best supports the author’s claim that the net “changes the act even when it is never touched”?

choices.text: “A prompter who is needed too often is a sign that something has gone wrong in rehearsal”
“Performers who know that a fall will be caught can attempt more”
“Some singers say that they barely need her.”
“the whole arrangement belongs to an era when companies staged a new play every week or two”

why.A: This concerns a prompter who is used, not one who is never needed.
why.B: Correct — the knowledge of the net, not its use, changes what performers try.
why.C: This reports how little some singers use her, not how her presence changes them.
why.D: This explains why the spoken theatre once needed the box.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Schools should present the five-paragraph essay as training, not as the essay itself, which is an open attempt at thinking.
Schools should stop teaching the five-paragraph essay, because it keeps students from ever learning to think for themselves.
Montaigne revised his Essais mostly by adding new thoughts rather than by cutting old ones.
The English word essay comes from a French word meaning a trial.

why.A: Correct — the author proposes telling students the form is “a set of training wheels, useful for a while, and not the thing itself,” which “is an attempt.”
why.B: The last paragraph says “I am not proposing that schools abandon the five-paragraph essay.”
why.C: This is true of paragraph 5 but serves as an example for the larger point.
why.D: This origin opens the passage but is not its main idea.

context: According to paragraph 1, what does the French word essai mean?

choices.text: A report of conclusions the writer reached in advance
A short book of the writer’s opinions
A letter addressed to a friend or patron
A trial or an attempt

why.A: That describes the school essay in paragraph 2, which the author calls “the opposite of an attempt.”
why.B: The passage never defines the word this way.
why.C: The passage never defines the word this way.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 1 states this directly.

context: The last sentence says that an essay “is, in fact, only worth reading if it might have” failed. It can be inferred that, for the author, a worthwhile essay is one whose:

choices.text: argument contains a contradiction the writer failed to notice while drafting it.
length is exactly five paragraphs.
conclusion was not settled before the writing began.
writer has never revised it.

why.A: Paragraph 6 says nobody should hand in an essay “that contradicts itself without noticing.”
why.B: That is the school form the author wants put in perspective.
why.C: Correct — the author criticizes essays defending “a position that had never been at risk”; an essay that might fail is one still searching.
why.D: Montaigne, the author’s model, revised for the rest of his life.

context: In paragraph 4, the author describes some student essays as “perfectly organized and entirely inert.” As used here, “inert” most nearly means:

choices.text: chemically unreactive.
lifeless.
careless in their details.
too brief to matter.

why.A: That is the chemist’s sense of the word, for substances; here it describes writing without life.
why.B: Correct — the essays had no movement of thought, because the position “had never been at risk.”
why.C: The essays are “perfectly organized,” so carelessness is not the fault.
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph concerns length.

context: Paragraph 3 (“I do not think the five-paragraph essay is useless”) mainly serves to:

choices.text: credit the form’s real lessons, so that the criticism that follows is aimed at its misuse.
show that the author has abandoned his objections to the form.
argue that adult writers write worse than students do.
describe how Montaigne organized his essays.

why.A: Correct — after naming what it teaches, the author says the trouble begins only “when the scaffold is mistaken for the building.”
why.B: Paragraph 3 might read as a retreat, but it opens “before I complain about it,” and paragraph 4 goes on to complain.
why.C: The remark about adult writers is an aside, not the paragraph’s purpose.
why.D: Montaigne’s method is described in paragraph 5.

context: In paragraph 4, the author says that “The essay becomes a container rather than a search.” This means that the essay:

choices.text: must be kept in a folder until the writer has finished all of the revisions.
is too short to hold a proper argument.
