helps students find sources in a library.
holds finished thoughts instead of working toward new ones.

why.A: This takes “container” literally.
why.B: Length is not the issue.
why.C: This takes “search” literally.
why.D: Correct — the sentence before says such writing is “a way of displaying thought that is already finished.”

context: The author’s attitude toward the five-paragraph essay is best described as:

choices.text: contemptuous, since he regards it as a form with nothing to teach any student about writing.
enthusiastic.
critical of how it is treated, but appreciative of what it teaches.
neutral, since he takes no position on it.

why.A: The author does “complain,” but he says the form’s lessons “are not small.”
why.B: He calls the essays it produces “entirely inert.”
why.C: Correct — the author objects when “the scaffold is mistaken for the building” but says the form “teaches something real.”
why.D: He takes a clear position: keep it, but explain what it is.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It tells the story of Montaigne’s life from his first published book in 1580 to his death.
It defines the essay by its origin, contrasts the school version, concedes its value, criticizes its misuse, and offers Montaigne as a model.
It compares several teachers’ methods of teaching the essay and chooses the best.
It lists common errors in student essays.

why.A: The passage gives only one detail of his life’s work; it is not a biography.
why.B: Correct — origin (1), the school form (2), its value (3), its misuse (4), Montaigne’s method and its lesson (5–6), and a proposal (7).
why.C: No teachers’ methods are compared.
why.D: The only fault discussed is a settled conclusion, not a list of errors.

context: According to paragraph 5, how did Montaigne’s way of revising differ from what a “tidy final draft” would do?

choices.text: He added new thoughts beside old ones instead of cutting what he no longer believed.
He cut everything he no longer believed.
He rewrote each essay into five paragraphs.
He stopped revising after 1580.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph says he wrote new thoughts “into the margins beside the old ones,” which a tidy draft would have hidden.
why.B: This reverses the paragraph: he did not cut.
why.C: The five-paragraph form belongs to schools, not Montaigne.
why.D: He revised “for the rest of his life.”

context: Which detail best supports the claim that Montaigne did not know his conclusions before he began writing?

choices.text: Later editors have marked the layers of his revisions so that readers can see his younger and older selves disagreeing.
He wrote on subjects as various as cannibals and thumbs.
He published the first books of his Essais in 1580.
He admits more than once that he does not know where a piece will end up when he begins it.

why.A: This shows his views changed over years of revision, not that he began each piece without knowing its end.
why.B: Variety of subject says nothing about whether he knew his conclusions.
why.C: A date says nothing about his method.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 1 states this about the start of each piece.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: An octopus has nine separate brains, one in its head and one in each arm.
An arm separated from an octopus can go on responding for some time.
An octopus’s arms do much of their own sensing and acting, which suggests intelligence need not be centralized.
Octopuses see poorly and hunt only by touch.

why.A: Paragraph 6 says most researchers regard the phrase as “an exaggeration.”
why.B: This is evidence in paragraph 4, not the main idea.
why.C: Correct — the passage describes arms that taste, grasp, and even tell self from food, and closes on “a different design” for intelligence.
why.D: The passage mentions its eyes and says it can hunt blind in a crevice, not that it always does.

context: According to paragraph 2, about what share of an octopus’s neurons are in its arms?

choices.text: About one-third, with the other two-thirds in the head
About two-thirds
About half, with the other half in the head
Nearly all of them, with only a few in the head

why.A: This reverses the paragraph.
why.B: Correct — “about two-thirds of them are not in the head at all. They are in the arms.”
why.C: The paragraph gives two-thirds.
why.D: The paragraph gives two-thirds.

context: Based on the passage, an octopus probing a dark crevice most likely tells a crab from a stone by:

choices.text: tasting it with its suckers.
seeing it with its large, well-developed eyes, which are adapted for seeing in dim light.
hearing the crab move among the rocks.
sensing the warmth of the crab’s body.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 3 says the suckers respond to chemicals, and that this may be how an octopus “hunting blind” tells a crab from a stone.
why.B: Octopuses do have large eyes, but the passage describes this search as done “without seeing either.”
why.C: Hearing is never mentioned.
why.D: Heat is never mentioned.

context: In paragraph 3, the author says of the arm, “It samples.” As used here, “samples” most nearly means:

choices.text: collects specimens for later study in a laboratory.
picks things out at random.
borrows a phrase from a song.
tests by tasting.

why.A: That scientific sense does not fit an arm exploring a crevice.
why.B: The arm is not choosing at random; it is tasting what it touches.
why.C: That musical sense has no place here.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph has just explained that an octopus “can taste what it touches.”

context: Paragraph 4, about arms separated from the animal, mainly serves to:

choices.text: argue that experiments on octopuses are cruel and should be stopped by the researchers who run them.
explain how octopuses regrow lost arms.
offer evidence that the arms can act without the brain.
show that the arms cannot taste.

why.A: The author winces, but does not argue that the experiments should stop.
why.B: Regrowth is mentioned only in passing.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph ends: “Whatever is guiding these movements, it cannot be the brain.”
why.D: The paragraph says nothing against their tasting.

context: In paragraph 1, the movement of the shrimp along the arm is compared to “a conveyor belt.” The comparison emphasizes that the prey is:

choices.text: carried to a factory.
passed along smoothly and steadily, without the animal seeming to watch.
dropped several times.
moving away from the mouth.

why.A: This takes the image literally.
why.B: Correct — the same sentence describes a “smooth, rolling motion,” and the next says the eyes may be elsewhere.
why.C: The motion is described as smooth.
why.D: The prey moves “toward the mouth.”

context: The author’s attitude toward describing the octopus as “an animal with nine brains” is best described as:

choices.text: understanding of its appeal, but doubtful of its accuracy.
approving, since the numbers of neurons in each arm make the phrase an accurate description.
scornful of the popular writers who use it.
uncertain what the phrase means.

why.A: Correct — the author calls it “tempting” and common, then says most researchers “would regard it as an exaggeration.”
why.B: The large number of arm neurons might suggest this, but the author says “The arms are not independent minds.”
why.C: The author calls the phrase “tempting,” not foolish.
why.D: The author explains the phrase clearly.

context: How does paragraph 5 relate to the paragraphs before it?

choices.text: It retracts the claim that the arms can taste, replacing it with a claim that they respond only to touch.
It begins a new topic unrelated to the arms.
It summarizes the passage.
It raises a puzzle that follows from the arms’ independence and reports a possible answer.

why.A: Paragraph 5 builds on the arms’ tasting rather than retracting it.
why.B: The paragraph is about the arms.
why.C: It adds new evidence; the summary comes later.
why.D: Correct — if each arm grabs anything that tastes like food, why not each other? The skin study offers an answer.

context: According to paragraph 5, how did separated arms treat material coated with an extract of octopus skin compared with the same material left plain?

choices.text: They grabbed the coated material more often, because it tasted of food.
They grabbed both equally.
They grabbed the coated material less often.
They ignored both entirely.

why.A: This reverses the finding.
why.B: The study found a difference.
why.C: Correct — the arms grabbed it “less often than the same material left plain.”
why.D: The arms “readily grabbed a range of objects.”

context: Which finding best supports the claim that the central brain “can overrule the arms’ local chemistry”?

choices.text: A separated arm offered food may grasp it and try to pass it toward where the mouth would have been.
A living octopus sometimes handled a severed arm as though it were prey.
Each sucker is lined with thousands of sensory cells.
An octopus can open a jar.

why.A: This shows the arm acting on its own, the opposite of the brain overruling it.
why.B: Correct — the arms’ chemistry says “self,” but the whole animal treated the arm as food.
why.C: This concerns the arm’s senses, not the brain’s control.
why.D: This shows coordination in general, not overruling chemistry.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A narrow, sugar-based strategy lets the wood frog survive freezing, showing such survival is possible though limited.
Freezing is lethal to most animals because ice both tears their cells apart and dries them out.
Research on wood frogs will soon make it possible to freeze human organs for transplant.
Wood frogs in Alaska are a separate species from those farther south.

why.A: Correct — the passage explains the strategy, stresses that it is “a narrow one,” and ends on what it shows is “possible in principle.”
why.B: This is the point of paragraph 2; it sets up the frog’s solution but is not the main idea.
why.C: The author says “Nobody expects to freeze a kidney the way a frog freezes itself.”
why.D: The passage calls the differences a matter of populations, not species.

context: According to paragraph 3, what substance does the frog’s liver pour into its blood as ice begins to form?

choices.text: Salt, which lowers the freezing point of the blood
Oxygen drawn from the air
Starch from its stores
Glucose

why.A: Paragraph 2 says salts left behind by ice are part of the danger, not the defence.
why.B: The frog stops breathing; oxygen is not what the liver supplies.
why.C: Starch is what the liver stores and converts; glucose is what enters the blood.
why.D: Correct — the liver converts stored starch “into glucose.”

context: Based on paragraph 3, a wood frog in air that is cooling slowly but has not yet dropped below freezing would most likely:

choices.text: already have flooded its cells with glucose in preparation for the coming cold weather.
have stopped breathing.
not yet have raised the sugar in its blood.
have begun to thaw.

why.A: This is the natural expectation the passage calls a “surprise”: preparation waits for ice.
why.B: The frog stops breathing once frozen, not before.
why.C: Correct — the frog “does not begin preparing as the air grows cold”; it begins “when it actually starts to freeze.”
why.D: A frog that has not frozen cannot thaw.

context: In paragraph 1, the author says the frozen frog is “Not chilled, not sluggish, but frozen.” As used here, “sluggish” most nearly means:

choices.text: lazy by nature and habit.
slow-moving.
like a slug in shape.
poisonous to predators.

why.A: The word describes the effect of cold, not the frog’s character.
why.B: Correct — it names a milder state than frozen, like “chilled.”
why.C: The word concerns movement, not shape.
why.D: Nothing in the sentence concerns poison.

context: Paragraph 6 (“It is easy to make too much of all this”) mainly serves to:

choices.text: temper the account by noting the limits of the frog’s ability.
argue that the wood frog’s survival has been exaggerated by the researchers who first described it.
introduce the frog’s use of glucose.
describe frogs in Alaska.

why.A: Correct — it says freezing too fast, too often, or too long can kill the frog, and that its trick “is a narrow one.”
why.B: The paragraph does not accuse any researchers; it limits the reader’s conclusions.
why.C: Glucose is introduced in paragraph 3.
why.D: Alaskan frogs are in paragraph 5.

context: Paragraph 2 ends by saying a freezing animal faces “ice that tears and ice that dries.” This phrase refers to:

choices.text: ice that forms on a frog’s skin and ice that forms in the leaf litter above it.
freezing in winter and drying in summer.
two kinds of weather.
crystals piercing membranes, and salty liquid drawing water out of cells.

why.A: The two dangers are about cells, not where ice forms outdoors.
why.B: Summer drought is never discussed.
why.C: The phrase describes damage to cells.
why.D: Correct — the paragraph has just described both dangers in these terms.

context: In paragraph 7, the author’s attitude toward the frog’s value for medicine is best described as:

choices.text: confident that frozen human organs will be stored routinely once the frog’s method is copied.
dismissive of the researchers’ interest.
hopeful, but careful not to promise too much.
alarmed about the risks of freezing organs.

why.A: The paragraph’s hopeful ending pulls this way, but the author says the frog offers only “a hint” and that medicine “cannot yet do” this at all.
why.B: The author presents their interest respectfully.
why.C: Correct — the frog is “proof that the thing is possible in principle,” yet “Nobody expects to freeze a kidney the way a frog freezes itself.”
why.D: No risks of the research are raised.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.text: It follows one wood frog through a single winter, from its first night of hard frost under the leaves to the pond where it breeds in spring.
It presents a striking fact, explains why freezing kills, shows how the frog copes, notes variation and limits, and ends on wider significance.
It compares the wood frog with several other freeze-tolerant animals.
It argues against a theory about frogs.

why.A: The passage describes the species in general, not one frog.
why.B: Correct — the frozen frog (1), the dangers (2), the solution (3–4), variation (5), limits (6), and medicine (7).
why.C: No other freeze-tolerant animals are discussed.
why.D: No opposing theory is stated.

context: According to paragraph 5, how do wood frogs from Alaska differ from those in milder parts of the range?

choices.text: They survive much colder temperatures and store more protective compounds.
They survive only a few degrees below zero Celsius.
They do not freeze at all, because they spend the winter underwater in ponds.
They thaw from the outside in.

why.A: Correct — Alaskan frogs survive “well below minus fifteen degrees” and “build up larger stores of sugar and other protective compounds.”
why.B: That describes frogs from the milder parts of the range.
why.C: Nothing suggests they avoid freezing; they stay frozen for months.
why.D: Thawing direction is not compared.

context: Which statement from the passage best supports the idea that a frozen wood frog is not in fact dead?

choices.text: By every ordinary test, a frozen wood frog would appear to be dead.
A frozen frog is not breathing and its heart is not beating.
Many frogs do not survive a hard winter.
Its tissues get by on the small amount of energy they can make without oxygen.

why.A: This is a statement about appearances; it supports the opposite reading, which the passage goes on to correct.
why.B: These are signs that would ordinarily mean death.
why.C: This is about frogs that die, not the ones that live.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 4 shows the tissues still working while the frog is frozen.

context: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Lake Nyos released a deadly cloud of carbon dioxide in 1986, killing some seventeen hundred people.
Ice floats because it is less dense than water.
Because water is densest near four degrees, many lakes mix twice a year, which is vital to life in them.
Warmer summers have stopped most lakes from turning over.

why.A: This is an example in paragraph 6 of a lake that does not mix.
why.B: This is one step in the explanation in paragraph 2.
why.C: Correct — the passage traces the turnover to water’s density and shows how it supplies oxygen and nutrients.
why.D: Paragraph 7 says effects “are still being worked out”; it does not say turnover has stopped.

context: According to paragraph 2, at about what temperature is water densest?

choices.text: At zero degrees, its freezing point, because that is where it is coldest
About four degrees Celsius
About ten degrees Celsius
At its boiling point

why.A: The paragraph says the densest water “is not the coldest water.”
why.B: Correct — “It is water at about four degrees.”
why.C: No such figure appears.
why.D: Boiling is not discussed.

context: The passage suggests that the deep water of a productive lake runs low on oxygen by late summer mainly because:

choices.text: it is cut off from the surface while bacteria use up what oxygen it has.
fish crowd into the deep water to escape the heat and consume the oxygen there.
warm water from the surface sinks and pushes the oxygen out.
ice forms over the lake.

why.A: Correct — paragraph 5 says oxygen enters at the surface and that bacteria breaking down dead plankton “use up what oxygen there is.”
why.B: Fish do use oxygen, but the passage never attributes the loss to them; it names bacteria.
why.C: In summer the warm water “stays on top.”
why.D: Ice forms in winter, not summer.

context: In paragraph 5, the author refers to “the deepest water of a productive lake.” As used here, “productive” most nearly means:

choices.text: busy with fishing boats and other commercial activity.
efficient.
profitable.
rich in living growth.

why.A: The paragraph concerns plankton, not human activity.
why.B: The lake is not doing work for anyone.
why.C: Money plays no part in the paragraph.
why.D: Correct — such a lake produces much plankton, which dies, sinks, and uses up oxygen as it decays.

context: The account of Lake Nyos in paragraph 6 mainly serves to:

choices.text: argue that pipes should be installed in every deep lake to vent gas before a disaster strikes.
prove that turnovers are always deadly.
show that a lake’s failure to mix can be dangerous.
explain why ice floats.

why.A: The pipes are reported for Nyos only; no general policy is proposed.
why.B: The passage calls ordinary turnovers vital to life.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph says isolation is usually “merely a curiosity” but occasionally “a danger,” and Nyos is the example.
why.D: Ice is explained in paragraph 2.

context: In paragraph 5, the author says, “The lake, in effect, breathes twice a year.” This refers to:

choices.text: the wind that ruffles the lake’s surface each day.
the two turnovers that carry oxygen down to the deep water.
fish rising to the surface.
the lake freezing and thawing.

why.A: Daily wind does not reach the deep water in summer.
why.B: Correct — the sentence before describes the autumn turnover bringing “fresh oxygen down to the bottom,” and the spring one repeats it.
why.C: Nothing in the paragraph mentions fish rising.
why.D: The breathing is the mixing that brings oxygen, not the freezing.

context: In paragraph 7, the author’s attitude toward the effect of a warming climate on lakes is best described as:

choices.text: concerned, but careful not to claim more than is known.
alarmed, since the author predicts that every lake will soon stop turning over.
unconcerned.
angry at the researchers.

why.A: Correct — researchers have “begun to worry,” yet the effects “are still being worked out” and “will differ from lake to lake.”
why.B: The word “worry” invites this reading, but the author makes no such prediction and stresses uncertainty.
why.C: The author reports real grounds for worry.
why.D: Nothing is said against researchers.

context: How does paragraph 2 relate to paragraph 1?

choices.text: It describes what the turnover does for the plants and animals living in the lake.
It gives an example of a lake that never turns over.
It disputes paragraph 1.
It explains the property of water that causes the turnover paragraph 1 introduces.

why.A: That is the subject of paragraph 5.
why.B: That comes in paragraph 6.
why.C: It explains paragraph 1 rather than disputing it.
why.D: Correct — paragraph 1 describes the turnover; paragraph 2 opens, “The reason it happens lies in an odd property of water.”

context: According to paragraphs 3 and 4, how does the layering of a deep lake in summer differ from its layering in winter?

choices.text: In summer the coldest water lies on top; in winter warm water does.
The lake is layered in winter but fully mixed all summer long.
In summer warm water lies on top; in winter the coldest water does, above water near four degrees.
There is no difference.

why.A: This reverses both seasons.
why.B: The summer layers “resist mixing” for months.
why.C: Correct — paragraph 3 describes warm water above cold; paragraph 4 says in winter “the coldest water now floats on top.”
why.D: Paragraph 4 says “the order reverses.”

context: Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that the densest water in a lake “is not the coldest water”?

choices.text: Most liquids grow steadily denser as they cool.
Under winter ice, the bottom of a lake settles at about four degrees.
Wind that ruffles the surface stirs only the top layer.
Dead plankton are broken down by bacteria.

why.A: This describes other liquids; taken alone it suggests the opposite of the claim.
why.B: Correct — the bottom holds the densest water, and it is warmer than the near-freezing water at the top.
why.C: This concerns mixing, not which water is densest.
why.D: This concerns oxygen, not density.

context: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

choices.text: argue that the four-day week has real costs that should be admitted as part of a trade-off.
argue that the four-day week should be banned in every district, whatever its trouble hiring.
describe one district’s experience of switching.
show that rural districts cannot hire teachers.

why.A: Correct — Passage B reviews the declines and the shifted costs, then says “that is a trade-off, and it should be described as one.”
why.B: Passage B grants that in some places the benefit “may well outweigh a small loss.”
why.C: That is Passage A.
why.D: Hiring is Passage A’s concern; Passage B only grants it.

context: According to Passage A, what was the district’s main reason for switching to a four-day week?

choices.text: To save money on buses, heating, and substitute teachers
To raise the district’s test scores
To give families a day for appointments
To hire teachers

why.A: Passage A says outsiders assume this, and that the savings “were smaller than the board had hoped.”
why.B: Passage A says scores “have not risen dramatically.”
why.C: That is a side benefit mentioned later, not the reason.
why.D: Correct — “The real reason was hiring.”

context: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A’s statement that the district’s test scores “have not fallen, either” by saying that:

choices.text: this proves the four-day week has no effect on achievement in districts that lengthen the school day.
the district must have reported its scores inaccurately.
flat scores do not show the schedule did no harm, since they might otherwise have risen.
the district should have added a fifth day.

why.A: Passage B says a district’s own scores “cannot tell us” whether the schedule helped or hurt.
why.B: Passage B calls such stories “sincere.”
why.C: Correct — Passage B says a district whose scores stayed flat “may have been headed for a rise.”
why.D: Passage B does not advise that specific district.

context: In Passage B, the author says of the stories districts tell, “The stories are sincere.” As used here, “sincere” most nearly means:

choices.text: proven.
honestly meant.
brief.
angry.

why.A: The author says the evidence cannot prove them.
why.B: Correct — the author does not doubt the districts believe them; the problem is what the scores can show.
why.C: Length is not at issue.
why.D: Nothing in the sentence concerns anger.

context: The last sentence of Passage A (“It was between four days with a teacher and five days without one”) mainly serves to:

choices.text: recast the choice as one about staffing rather than schedules.
admit that the district could not in the end fill its chemistry post, even with a four-day week.
argue that every district should switch to a four-day week.
report the results of a study.

why.A: Correct — the author says the real choice “was never between four days and five days with a good teacher in every room.”
why.B: Passage A says the four-day week drew many applicants for that post.
why.C: The paragraph opens “I would not recommend the four-day week to every district.”
why.D: No study is reported in Passage A.

context: In Passage A, the letters to the local paper predicted that the district would become “the laughing stock of the county.” The phrase means the district would be:

choices.text: a county leader in raising farm animals and livestock.
the most cheerful district in the county.
a financial investment.
an object of ridicule.

why.A: This reads “stock” literally, as livestock.
why.B: The letters predicted disaster, not cheer.
why.C: This reads “stock” as a share in a company.
why.D: Correct — the letters predicted the district would be laughed at by its neighbours.

context: The tone of the last paragraph of Passage B toward the four-day week is best described as:

choices.text: approving, since the author does not doubt that the schedule helps districts hire teachers.
hostile, condemning districts that switch.
conceding a real benefit while insisting that its costs be admitted.
amused by the districts’ stories.

why.A: “I do not doubt” invites this reading, but the paragraph turns to what districts are “not telling” parents.
why.B: The author allows that the benefit may outweigh the loss.
why.C: Correct — the author does “not doubt” the hiring benefit, then says the change should be described as a trade-off.
why.D: Nothing in the paragraph is amused.

context: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.text: Passage B rejects the four-day week outright and argues that no district should ever adopt it.
Passage A defends the change from one district’s experience; Passage B questions how such experience is judged and names costs, while granting a benefit.
Both passages argue that every district should adopt the four-day week.
Passage A reports research that Passage B summarizes.

why.A: Passage B’s criticism pulls this way, but it grants that the benefit “may well outweigh a small loss.”
why.B: Correct — Passage B doubts that a district’s own scores can settle the question, adds the costs, and allows that hiring may outweigh them.
why.C: Passage A says it would not recommend it to every district.
why.D: Passage A reports one district, not research.

context: Both passages agree that the four-day week:

choices.text: can help a district hire teachers.
saves a large share of a district’s budget.
raises test scores.
suits every district.

why.A: Correct — Passage A calls hiring the real reason; Passage B says, “I do not doubt that the four-day week helps some districts hire teachers.”
why.B: Passage A says the savings were smaller than hoped; Passage B calls them “usually modest.”
why.C: Neither passage reports gains; Passage B says “Almost none found gains.”
why.D: Passage A says it would not recommend it to every district.

context: Which detail from Passage A shows that the district tried to make up for the lost day of classes?

choices.text: Families schedule dental appointments and trips on the day off.
The district had many applicants for one chemistry post after the change was advertised.
Letters to the paper predicted disaster.
The school days are longer by a little over an hour.

why.A: This explains better attendance, not making up hours.
why.B: This concerns hiring, not class time.
why.C: This is the reaction, not the district’s plan.
why.D: Correct — Passage A says this keeps class hours across the year nearly the same.

context: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

choices.text: dismiss the genetic science behind the project as unsound.
describe how mammoth genes would be added to elephant cells.
argue that recreating the mammoth would draw effort away from protecting living species.
explain how mammoths kept the far north as grassland.

why.A: Passage B says, “I do not dismiss the science.”
why.B: That is described in Passage A.
why.C: Correct — the author sees mainly “what they would cost the animals we still have” and ends by urging help for “the species that are still here.”
why.D: That idea appears in Passage A.

context: According to Passage A, which traits would scientists try to give elephant cells?

choices.text: Long tusks, great size, and a trunk
A thick coat, small ears, and a layer of insulating fat
A shorter pregnancy
The ability to eat grass

why.A: Passage A never mentions tusks or trunks.
why.B: Correct — the first paragraph of Passage A lists these three.
why.C: Pregnancy length is raised in Passage B, not as a trait to edit.
why.D: Grazing is discussed, not edited.

context: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A’s point that the project’s techniques could help endangered species by:

choices.text: welcoming the tools but saying they should be developed for living species directly.
rejecting any use of genetic tools in conservation, because such tools make extinction seem reversible.
agreeing that the project would pay for itself.
denying that the Asian elephant is endangered.

why.A: Correct — Passage B says it would “welcome” such tools but that “they should be developed for the species that are still here.”
why.B: Passage B does fear that belief, which gives this pull, but it says of the tools, “I would welcome them.”
why.C: Passage B stresses the project’s costs to living animals.
why.D: Passage B says the species “is itself endangered.”

context: In Passage A, the author says the idea that grazers kept the far north as grassland “is contested” but that “it is not fanciful.” As used here, “fanciful” most nearly means:

choices.text: decorative.
expensive.
popular.
unrealistic.

why.A: A “fanciful” design can be ornate, but this sentence concerns an idea’s plausibility.
why.B: Cost is not the issue.
why.C: Popularity is not the issue.
why.D: Correct — the author grants the idea is disputed but denies that it is mere imagination.

context: In Passage B, the question “Why spend money protecting a habitat today if a species can be rebuilt from its DNA tomorrow?” mainly serves to:

choices.text: state the author’s own view that it is no longer worth spending money on protecting habitats.
quote a scientist involved in the projects.
voice the reasoning the author fears the public might adopt.
ask the reader for money.

why.A: The author opposes this reasoning; the whole passage urges protecting living species.
why.B: The passage says “No scientist involved in these projects has made that argument.”
why.C: Correct — it follows the worry that “the urgency of preventing it may fade” and is not the author’s own view.
why.D: No appeal for donations is made.

context: At the end of Passage B, the author contrasts species that are “not frozen in the ground but alive.” The phrase “frozen in the ground” refers to:

choices.text: animals that hibernate through long northern winters.
extinct animals known from their remains.
plans that have been stopped.
elephants kept in cold places.

why.A: Hibernation is never discussed.
why.B: Correct — it points back to mammoths known from remains in frozen ground, set against species still living.
why.C: The phrase is about animals, not plans.
why.D: The phrase contrasts the extinct with the living.

context: The attitude of the author of Passage A toward the mammoth project is best described as:

choices.text: committed to it, but candid that it may not work.
certain that a herd of cold-adapted elephants will slow the thaw of the Arctic’s permafrost.
doubtful that the attempt is worth making.
indifferent to its results.

why.A: Correct — the author thinks the attempt justified, yet concedes it “is a long way off, and that it may not work.”
why.B: The author’s enthusiasm pulls this way, but the claim is hedged: “If that is right,” and “might one day.”
why.C: The author says “that is enough to justify the attempt.”
why.D: The author cares about both the goal and what the work teaches.

context: Which choice best describes how Passage B is organized?

choices.text: It explains the steps of the project in the order they would happen, from editing elephant genes in a laboratory to raising the first calf.
It reports an experiment and its results.
It tells the history of the mammoth’s extinction.
It grants the project’s appeal, raises practical and welfare objections, adds a subtler risk, and closes by redirecting the tools.

why.A: Those steps are Passage A’s subject; Passage B raises objections.
why.B: No experiment is reported.
why.C: The extinction is mentioned only in Passage A.
why.D: Correct — the appeal (first paragraph), the elephant problem (second), the public’s belief (third), and the redirection (fourth).

context: Both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.text: the project is justified by what it might teach, even if no mammoth-like calf is ever born.
the result of the project would be a true mammoth.
tools from such projects might help living endangered species.
elephant pregnancies for the project are easy to justify.

why.A: This is Passage A’s view; Passage B argues the tools should be developed for living species instead.
why.B: Passage A says it “would not be a mammoth in the strict sense.”
why.C: Correct — Passage A hopes they could help species that have lost genetic diversity; Passage B says some “may yet prove useful to conservation.”
why.D: Passage B says they are hard to justify.

context: Which detail from Passage B most directly challenges Passage A’s hope for “a herd of cold-adapted elephants”?

choices.text: Few images capture the public imagination like a shaggy giant walking out of the ice age.
Asian elephants carry a calf for nearly two years and are endangered.
No scientist involved has argued that extinction can be reversed.
The tools may prove useful to conservation.

why.A: This grants the project’s appeal; it does not challenge the herd.
why.B: Correct — producing a herd would need many such pregnancies, which Passage B says are hard to justify.
why.C: This concerns public belief, not the practicality of a herd.
why.D: This is a concession, not a challenge.
